title: Gentle King
text: The name About This Site Conquering kings came on warhorses. Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey ( Zechariah 9:9 , Matthew 21:5 ). He has all authority, and he will judge the living and the dead. Yet he says he is meek and lowly in heart, and newer Bibles translate that word gentle . A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. Isaiah 42:3 (KJV) This site is confessionally Reformed and Presbyterian, and it holds the Westminster Confession and Catechisms. It’s one layman’s work. About this site says who writes it and what it believes.

title: Sojourner
text: What it is What Sojourner Is Sojourner is a free Bible study program for your phone, tablet, or computer. You read the Bible beside the commentaries, confessions, and reference works the Reformed church has used for four hundred years. The Hebrew and Greek are underneath, with tools on top for preparing a sermon and leading family worship. It runs in any browser at app.gentleking.org , or as a program on Windows and Linux. Your notes stay on your own device, and you never sign in. Most study software wants something from you first. An account. A subscription. A connection. A tier that hides the good commentaries until you pay. Sojourner asks for none of it. You install it, and the Bibles, the commentaries, and the reference works are already there. It’s for the pastor, the elder, the family, and the student who want Scripture and the best of the old books close at hand for free. Sojourner is what believers called themselves on their way through this life. You’re passing through, and you need the road marked. That’s the idea behind the name. It’s a tool, not a substitute. A program can't preach to you, baptize you, or feed you at the Lord’s Table. Use it through the week, and be under the Word in your own church on the Lord’s Day.

title: Sojourner
text: Convictions Private and Offline Sojourner uses the network for exactly one thing. You press a button on the About page to check whether a newer version exists. That’s all. There’s no account, no sync service, and no telemetry of any kind. Nothing you read, search, write, or pray is reported anywhere, because there’s nowhere for it to go. Even the book shelves install from files you download yourself, so they can also come on a USB stick. That’s the desktop program. The web app keeps the same promise in a browser. Your notes stay in your browser’s private storage on your own device. There’s no account, and the app sends nothing about you. It fetches the books from this ministry’s own server as you read them. It can also download the whole library once so that it never needs the network again. More on the web app and your data . Everything you write lives in one file on your machine. Snapshots and automatic backups run in the background. You can export the whole database and import it again, and run an integrity check. You can keep a copy in a OneDrive or Dropbox folder if you want one, and see your own reading statistics on a heatmap. If the program ever crashes, the log stays on your computer. This is the only arrangement that makes sense for a book you’re meant to read for the rest of your life. Companies fold and services shut down. A file on your own disk doesn’t.

title: Sojourner
section: Free Bible Software for Your Phone and Computer
text: For every device Free Bible Software for Your Phone and Computer If you’re looking for a free Bible app for your iPhone, your Android, your Mac, your Windows PC, or your Linux machine, Sojourner is one. It’s the same program everywhere. It costs nothing and needs no account. Once it’s installed it works with no internet connection at all. In the browser it can download its whole library and do the same. Anyone who has used e-Sword or theWord will know the idea. The Bible sits in one pane and the commentaries follow along in another. Sojourner differs in what comes with it. Matthew Henry, Calvin, the Westminster Standards, the Three Forms of Unity, the Psalter, and the Hebrew and Greek with their lexicons are there when it opens. They were chosen for readers in the Reformed and Presbyterian tradition. The Reformed library is ready to use when you open the program. Logos and Accordance do far more, and they cost far more. Sojourner isn’t trying to be them.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: How it works Panes That Follow Each Other You can open up to eight panes and split the window however you like. Drag a pane to dock it, stack tabs in it, pick a ready-made arrangement, or save the layout as a named workspace that survives a reinstall. Side lists, like an index or a table of contents, can be narrowed or folded away. Then you link them. Click a verse in one pane and every linked pane turns to it. The commentary, cross references, confession proofs, encyclopedia, and atlas all go to that verse. So do the people and places it names, its place on the timeline, and the books on your shelves that cite it. One click, and the whole shelf opens to the same page. You can also set translations side by side, or compare one verse in every translation at once. Any Scripture reference in the program, in a commentary, a confession, or your own notes, shows the verse on hover. Opens the full size picture. Psalm 23 in the King James, the Berean Standard Bible, and the Hebrew, which reads right to left.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: New in 0.4.0 Color Text Every person, place, time, and number in the Bible, each in its own color. You can see who, what, where, when, and how many at a glance. Opens the full size picture. Genesis 22 with Color text on. Turn it on with Color text in the Bible’s toolbar, beside Interlinear. Each word that answers one of those questions takes its family’s color. Who? God, in purple. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each have a shade of their own, with every name, title, and pronoun that means them. Who? Angels, in olive. Angels are bright, and demons, false gods, and idols are dark. Who? People, in blue. Named people, then nations and tribes, then words like king and servant, then the pronouns. What? Nature, in teal. Animals and plants. Where? Places, in green. Named places, then words like city and wilderness, then words like up and there. When? Time, in brown. Days, years, and feasts, then words like when and then, and it came to pass. How many? Numbers, in crimson. Numbers, measures like cubits and shekels, and amounts like all and many. Within a family the most specific word is the brightest. Jerusalem is brighter than city, and city is brighter than there. Verbs, objects, and ideas stay black, so the page still reads normally. How Christ is marked Every colored word was checked by hand. Where the New Testament says an Old Testament passage speaks of Christ, his color follows. The Servant of Isaiah 53 takes it, and the Son of Psalm 2 , and the ruler “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” in Micah 5:2 , and the one in Zechariah 12:10 of whom God says “they shall look upon me whom they have pierced.” Opens the full size picture. Isaiah 53 . The Servant is in the Son’s color, because the New Testament says he is Christ. Click any colored word A colored word opens a card that says what it is and lists every verse where that word has that color. A person or a place opens in the Factbook, and a place opens on the map. The strip under the toolbar shows how much of each family the chapter holds, and a click hides or shows a family. The In this chapter list shows every person and place the chapter names. Pick one and it’s circled wherever it appears. Opens the full size picture. Moriah’s card, with the other verse that names it, 2 Chronicles 3:1 , where Solomon built the temple. In every translation, and in the Greek and Hebrew The colors are carried from the King James to the other English translations word by word, so the World English Bible’s Yahweh is colored like the LORD. They reach the Greek and Hebrew through Strong’s numbers, and a translation you add yourself is colored the same way. The Vulgate and the Septuagint have no word tagging, so they get only the names and the most common words. Opens the full size picture. John 1 in the Greek. λόγος, the Word, is in the Son’s color. Who’s speaking Who’s speaking is in the Color text menu. God’s own words are set in small capitals, as “Take now thy son” is in Genesis 22 , and every “Thus saith the LORD” in the prophets. Scripture quoted inside a speech is in italics, as when Jesus answers the tempter from Deuteronomy, and speech within speech is a shade lighter. Turn on the words of Jesus in red as well, and every speaker in a passage can be told apart. If you can't see every color Underline each family, in the same menu, also gives each family its own line under the words. One is solid, and the others are dotted, wavy, dashed, double, and a line above. Opens the full size picture. Underline each family, for a reader who can’t tell every color apart. Where color text shows up Color text can also color a sermon’s passages and tonight’s reading in family worship. There it adds Look closer, which asks the family who is in the reading, what animals and plants, where it happens, when, and how many. Each answer stays hidden until you show it. Opens the full size picture. Look closer, after the reading in Family worship. The numbers are still hidden here. Search can look for a color or a speaker too, such as every verse that names the Son, or every place in Isaiah where God himself speaks. Copied verses keep their colors when you paste them into Word, Google Docs, or an email.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: Greek and Hebrew Greek and Hebrew for Beginners Every phrase of the King James is tagged with its Strong’s number in both testaments. The interlinear is laid out like Blue Letter Bible’s, in a compact table with one row for each English phrase. Each row gives the Strong’s number, the Hebrew or Greek word, its root and how to say it, and its grammar. Small words the King James leaves untranslated, like the Greek article, share the row of the word they go with. One switch puts the words back in the original order. Another hides the Hebrew accent marks while keeping the vowels. Opens the full size picture. John 1 in the interlinear. Opens the full size picture. Genesis 1 in Hebrew. The Cantillation box shows or hides the accent marks. The grammar is spelled out in plain English, such as aorist active indicative, third person singular, rather than in code letters. Hover over a word to see it, or open its card, where a Parsing section explains each term, such as what the aorist is, what a piel does, and why a noun is genitive. The Hebrew and Greek were checked word by word against their sources in both testaments. A Hebrew font sets the vowel points where they belong. Opens the full size picture. The card for logos . The Parsing section says what each term means. Double-click any word in the text and its entry opens in the lexicon you choose. You can search the Greek and Hebrew without typing accents or vowel points. Word study Pick any Hebrew or Greek word and Sojourner shows how often it occurs, how the King James translates it, the forms it takes and the grammar of each, the related words, and every place it appears. Opens the full size picture. The word study for logos , with every form of the word and how often each appears. Search by grammar Every Hebrew and Greek word is parsed, which means its grammar is labeled, such as its tense or whether it’s a command. Search by grammar finds every word of one kind, such as every command in Ephesians. You pick from lists, so you don’t need to know the code letters. Where the Greek editions differ Set the five Greek editions side by side on a verse to see where they differ. At 1 John 5:7 , the words about the three that bear record in heaven, known as the Comma Johanneum, appear only in the Textus Receptus. None of this requires you to have studied the languages. A man with a concordance and some patience has done real work in the text for two hundred years. This makes the same work quicker.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: Who, where, and when People, Places, and Maps A page of text can’t easily show you who a man was, where something happened, or what else was happening at the time. The Factbook, the timeline, the atlas, and the harmonies are for that. The Factbook A page for each of four thousand two hundred and seventy-five people, places, and things in the Bible. The Bible has several men named Zechariah, and the Factbook tells them apart by the verses that name them. Each page gives the family, every verse, and what the encyclopedia and dictionary say. Double-click a name in the text to open the person that verse means. The timeline Four hundred and sixty-four events, from the Creation to Paul in Rome, on a line you can zoom. The eras are marked, and the kings of Judah and Israel run side by side. A strip beside the text shows where the chapter you’re reading falls. The dates are approximate, taken from a traditional chronology. Turn on Church history and the line runs on past the apostles to the present, with two hundred and ninety-six events in ten eras. They include councils, creeds and confessions, lives, writings, and missions. Every date comes from a source, mostly Philip Schaff’s History of the Christian Church, and each event quotes it. Where the sources give no date, the event is left out rather than guessed. A creed or confession opens its text, and a writing opens its book if it’s on your shelves. A strip beneath the timeline shows where you are, and you can drag it to move along. Opens the full size picture. Church history on the timeline, from the early councils to the Westminster Assembly and after. Opens the full size picture. Luther posts the Ninety-five Theses, with the words from Schaff that date it. Opens the full size picture. David’s reign on the timeline, his Factbook page below, and 2 Samuel 5 beside it. The atlas One thousand three hundred and forty-two places, each with its coordinates, its modern identification where there's one, and every verse that names it. Fourteen journeys are traced on the map, from Abraham leaving Ur to Paul reaching Rome. Each stop has its own reference and a line saying what happened there. The old regions are lightly shaded inside a dashed line, because no one ever surveyed their borders. A sharp line would claim more than anyone knows. Opens the full size picture. Paul’s second missionary journey. Place data from OpenBible.info, coastlines from Natural Earth. The map packs Two add-on packs show the land itself. They’re on the releases page beside the book shelves, under Sojourner Library Packs, and they need Sojourner 0.3.6 or later. The Terrain pack, about 271 MB, shades the hills and valleys of the whole biblical world, with the most detail over the Holy Land. Turn on Raise the land in 3D under Layers and the map tilts to show the relief. You can see the Jordan rift, the Judean hills, and the high plateau east of the Jordan. The Imagery pack, about 1.26 GB, adds a view from the sky, switched on under Layers. The base layer is NASA’s Blue Marble. Over it lies a cloud-free picture from the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites, sharp down to ten meters over the Holy Land, Lebanon, and Transjordan. It’s a step less sharp over Syria, Sinai, the Nile delta, Asia Minor, Greece, and Cyprus. It’s a step less again over the Nile up to Thebes, Mesopotamia, and Italy. In this view the drawn coasts and lakes are hidden so the land shows through. To add one, open Settings, choose Library packs, and pick Install a map pack. Like the shelves, they’re files you download yourself, so they can also come on a USB stick. The harmonies Two harmonies of the Gospels, both laid out in four columns. Robert M. Sutherland’s of 2020 has a hundred and thirty-six events, and A. T. Robertson’s of 1922 has a hundred and eighty-five. Each event lists where it’s told in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, with Acts 1 for the ascension. Where an event appears in more than one Gospel, one button sets the accounts side by side. Opens the full size picture. The feeding of the five thousand, with Matthew, Mark, and Luke set side by side.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: One Search Box One box searches Scripture, the commentaries, the lexicons, the Factbook, the confessions, the encyclopedia, your books, and your own notes, prayers, sermons, and illustrations, with the same rules everywhere. Put an exact phrase in quotation marks. Ask for either of two words with OR, or leave a word out with a minus sign. You can also group words in parentheses, ask for words near each other, match the start of a word, or use regular expressions. A plus sign asks for the exact form and its capitals. So +LORD finds the covenant name as the King James prints it and skips the ordinary word Lord . You can also narrow a search by typing a filter into the box. There are filters for a book, a translation, a Strong’s number, the words of Christ, and the verses you have notes on, and they’re saved with the search. Older spellings match, so shew finds show . Results can be counted by book and by translation, or laid out like a printed concordance. Opens the full size picture. Faith, in Hebrews, laid out like a concordance.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: Reading Book and chapter navigation, paragraph mode, verse numbers on or off, and red letters. Five named highlight colors and an underline, bookmarks, a find bar for the open chapter, a focus mode that hides everything else, and printing. Seven themes, including sepia, true black, and two high contrast themes. A font made for dyslexic readers, adjustable text size, and reduced motion for anyone who needs the screen to hold still. The built-in voice reads any chapter, commentary, or book aloud. In a book it starts at your page, and the page follows the voice. Select a passage and choose Read aloud from here to start somewhere else. A commentary is read a verse or a paragraph at a time, and a list in the player jumps to any piece of it. Opens the full size picture. Barnes on Romans 8:28 , read aloud.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: Private Notes Write on a verse, a chapter, or a highlight. There are templates for observation and interpretation and application, for question and answer, for a sermon outline, and for a prayer in response. Type a reference inside any note and that verse is marked in the text from then on. Highlighting works the same way. Five colors and an underline, each named for what it marks rather than for its color. Promise in yellow, command in green, doctrine in blue, warning in orange. You can then pull up every promise you’ve marked, across every book, in one list. The Mine pane gathers everything you’ve written on the open chapter. Deleted notes, prayers, sermons, and illustrations wait thirty days in a trash before they’re gone.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: For preachers Preparing and Preaching The sermon editor treats your points as the outline, so the structure comes from the manuscript instead of being kept beside it. Passage blocks show live in the sermon’s translation. Drag a point to a new place and its sub-points, and everything written under them, move with it. Open another page while you write and it opens in a new tab beside the sermon, so the manuscript is only a click away. Part of a point can be set apart as a block for the explanation, the illustration, or the application. A block can also mark a transition, or carry a name you give it. Each kind has its own color, and the colors carry through to preaching mode and print. So you can spot the application under any point at a glance. Opens the full size picture. Explanation, illustration, and application blocks, with the outline giving the words and minutes of every point. Every verse, commentary entry, confession section, lexicon entry, word study, encyclopedia article, and book selection has a small microphone button. Press it and that text drops into the open sermon with its source line attached, so you always know where a quotation came from. A single shortcut catches a sermon idea from anywhere in the program. A selection in the Bible can start one with its verses already attached. Ideas wait in an inbox beside every manuscript and on the Sermons page, until you drag one into a sermon or start a new sermon from it. Opens the full size picture. Catching an idea for a funeral on Saturday. Illustrations go into a file of their own, each with its source and where you’ve used it. If you reach for one you’ve already told in this series, it tells you before you put it in. Twelve templates give you a starting point. One sets out three points, each with an explanation, an illustration, and an application. Others give a verse-by-verse outline, a defender’s outline for answering an objection, and an outline for preaching to children and youth. Opens the full size picture. The twelve sermon templates. Around that sit a six-stage preparation track, timed rehearsals that measure your speaking rate, and a preaching mode with pulpit-sized type and a clock. It makes slides and exports them to PowerPoint, and any line you mark gets a slide of its own. It builds fill-in handouts, prints, and exports to Markdown. Sermons group into a series with a reading plan for the congregation. A series can give the church a verse a week to learn, printed on cards to hand out. After a sermon is preached, there’s a place to write down how it went. Opens the full size picture. Preaching mode, with the clock and the next point along the foot. If you preach from a phone or a tablet, there’s a podium file. It’s the whole manuscript as one small web page with every passage written into it. So it needs no internet and no program but a browser. A tap turns the page, the text size can change, and a clock keeps time against the minutes you planned. Opens the full size picture. The podium file on two phones.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: The Today Page The Today page gathers what’s in front of you. Where your reading left off, today’s portion of your plan, the sermons coming up, the memory cards that are due, and the people you meant to pray for. A new install opens on it. Once your household has begun family worship, it also shows what you’ll read and learn the next time you gather. Opens the full size picture. The Today page. Reading plans come with catch-up tools for the weeks you fall behind, and you can build your own. The prayer journal follows the ACTS pattern and keeps a list of people. It nudges you toward the ones you haven’t prayed for in a while, and it prints. Memory covers Scripture and the catechism together, on a spaced repetition schedule, with three ways to practice. One shows only the first letter of every word. It’s harder than it looks and works better than reading it over again. A whole psalm or chapter is learned a part at a time. The next part comes once you’ve recalled the one before twice in a row, and at the end you say it through from the top. A card can also be turned around, to show you the words and ask where they’re found. Ready-made sets range from the Romans Road and the Ten Commandments to short verses for little ones. The Heidelberg Catechism and the Catechism for Young Children can be learned beside the Shorter and the Larger. For the Westminster catechisms, one button turns a proof text for each question you’re learning into a Scripture card. The program will read a Scripture card aloud, or every one that’s due, so you can practice with your eyes shut or your hands busy. Instead of a streak there’s a calendar of the days you practiced. Opens the full size picture. The prayer journal, a first-letter memory card, and the reading plans. The Psalter is there for singing too, on its own page under Devotion. Open a psalm, choose a tune, and press play. The words are set under the melody one stanza at a time, and each psalm remembers the tune you last sang it to. The page opens on your last psalm, the music can be made larger, and a long line breaks onto a second staff in a narrow pane. The words are set line by line as the book of 1650 prints them, checked against two old editions and the Free Church of Scotland’s text. Nothing is modernized, so chuse , shew , and heav’n stay as the book has them. Opens the full size picture. Psalm 23 on the Psalter page, set to St. Flavian.

title: Everything Sojourner Does
text: For the household Family Worship Matthew Henry preached a sermon on family religion and called it A Church in the House. Sojourner has a page for keeping that church. It’s made for the one who leads, even if they feel the least ready of anyone. A gathering takes a few minutes. You read a short passage, sing a psalm, go over the catechism, and pray. If you choose a verse to learn by heart, you say it together before you pray. The page walks through each step in order, so nothing has to be prepared and no one has to preach. Opens the full size picture. The Family worship page, with tonight’s steps and a dot for each day the family met. And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. Deuteronomy 6:6-7 (KJV) If you’ve never done this before, begin with the first four weeks. That’s twenty-eight short readings that tell the story of the Bible, from the creation to the new creation. Each week has a psalm from the 1650 Psalter with its tune to play, and a new catechism question comes every other time you meet. You start with the Catechism for Young Children or the Shorter Catechism. You can choose the Heidelberg instead, and the Larger, with its long answers, is there for when the children are older. Each reading comes with three questions to talk over, one each for faith, love, and hope. What does this passage teach us to believe about God? How does it call us to love God and our neighbour? What does it give us to hope for? You can reword them, add one, or take one away in the family settings, and your own go on the printed sheet too. Tonight’s catechism question comes with its answer, to say together until the children know it. Earlier questions come round again with the answer hidden until someone has had a try, so they aren’t lost. At prayer time the page offers the three names from your prayer list you’ve gone longest without praying for. The Lord’s Prayer is there for the nights when words won’t come. Opens the full size picture. The three questions, which you can reword or add to. The Gather round button puts the same steps on the whole screen in large type, for the kitchen table or the television. Press Amen at the end and the reading and the catechism move on. The page counts the times you gather, not the days on the calendar, so a missed night costs nothing. You pick up where you left off. There’s no streak to break, only a mark for each day you met. Opens the full size picture. Gather round at the catechism step. The Print this week button puts the next seven readings, the psalm, the catechism questions, the memory verse, and the names to pray for on one sheet. For the one leading, the page gives some plain advice and points you to the old helps. The Directory for Family-Worship, which the Church of Scotland approved in 1647, is on the Confessions page beside the Catechism for Young Children of 1840. James W. Alexander’s Thoughts on Family-Worship is on the Sojourner Library shelf.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
text: The same Bible study companion, in your browser. Open it on an iPhone, an Android, an iPad, or a Mac, put it on your home screen, and take it offline if you like.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
text: In your browser The Same Sojourner, Anywhere Sojourner now runs in a web browser, on a phone, a tablet, or a computer. It’s the same Bible study program as the Windows and Linux program, with the same Bibles, commentaries, confessions, Hebrew and Greek, atlas, and notes. There's nothing to buy and nothing to fetch from an app store. Open app.gentleking.org and it’s there. It’s a progressive web app. That means you can put it on your home screen or in your dock, and then it opens in its own window like any other app. After your first visit, it’ll offer to do that for you. Open Sojourner in your browser The Windows and Linux program

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
section: Putting It on Your Home Screen
text: Installing it Putting It on Your Home Screen iPhone and iPad. Open it in Safari or Chrome. Tap the Share button, then Add to Home Screen. Please do this. Safari clears a website’s data after a week or so without a visit, but it keeps an app that lives on the home screen. Android. Tap Install when the app offers. Or open the menu in Chrome, the three dots, and choose Install app. Mac. In Safari, open the File menu and choose Add to Dock. That needs macOS Sonoma or later. In Chrome or Edge, click the install icon at the right of the address bar. Windows and Linux. In Chrome or Edge, click the install icon in the address bar. Firefox can’t install web apps, but Sojourner works fine in a Firefox tab. If you want everything on your own disk, the desktop program is still there. Keep it open in one tab at a time. The app’s storage allows only one open copy, and a second tab will tell you so and offer to take over.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
section: The Books, and Using It Offline
text: The library The Books, and Using It Offline The desktop program carries its whole library inside the installer. The web app fetches the Bibles, commentaries, lexicons, and reference works in small pieces as you open them. It keeps each piece on your device once you’ve read it. So it starts quickly and grows as you use it. To use it with no connection at all, open Settings, choose Data and backups, and pick Use without the internet. That downloads the whole library, about 900 MB. From then on the app works on a plane, in a waiting room, or anywhere without a signal. The book shelves, such as the Puritans and the Church Fathers, are added from Settings and read online. Keep on this device stores a single book for reading offline. The Atlas has its terrain and satellite maps built in.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
section: Your Notes Stay on Your Device
text: Privacy Your Notes Stay on Your Device Your notes, highlights, prayers, and sermons are kept in your browser’s private storage on the device you’re using, the way the desktop program keeps them in a file on your computer. There’s no account and no sync. Nothing you read, search, write, or pray is sent anywhere. The books come from data.gentleking.org. Cloudflare, which hosts both addresses, keeps ordinary request logs the way any web host does. The app itself sends nothing about you. Back up now and then. A browser can clear a site’s data, and Safari does it after a few weeks without a visit unless the app is on your home screen. Open Settings, choose Data and backups, and Export. That saves everything to one file, and the app will remind you to do it. The desktop program uses the same kind of file. So you can carry your notes from your phone to Windows or Linux and back again with Import.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
section: What the Web Version Leaves Out
text: Honest limits What the Web Version Leaves Out Almost everything in the desktop program is here. A few things aren’t, because a browser can’t do them. The natural reading voice. The desktop program reads aloud with a voice built into it. In the browser, Sojourner uses your device’s own voices instead. Backups to a folder. Use Export instead, and keep the file somewhere safe. Your own audio, video, and MOBI files. Your own EPUB and PDF books do work. They stay in the browser and are not part of an export. Sync. Each device keeps its own notes. Export and Import carry them across. If you want all of it on your own computer, with nothing fetched from anywhere, the Windows and Linux program is unchanged and free.

title: Sojourner on Your Phone
text: Try It Now It’s free and needs no account. Open it, read a chapter with Matthew Henry beside it, and see whether it helps you. Open Sojourner Everything it does

title: What Comes With Sojourner
text: The translations, the original texts, the lexicons, the commentaries and confessions, the four book shelves, and where every one of them came from.

title: What Comes With Sojourner
text: What is inside What Is Included All of this installs with the program. Nothing is locked, and none of it needs a connection to open. Thirteen translations Public domain or free to share The eight older ones are the King James of 1769, the American Standard of 1901, Young’s Literal, Darby, Webster’s, the Geneva of 1599, Douay-Rheims, and Tyndale, which has the New Testament, the five books of Moses, and Jonah. The five modern ones are free because their makers allow them to be shared. They’re the World English Bible, the Berean Standard Bible, the Literal Standard Version, and unfoldingWord’s Literal and Simplified Texts. The original texts Hebrew, Greek, and Latin The Hebrew Old Testament from the Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete copy of the Hebrew Bible, read right to left. Five editions of the Greek New Testament. The Textus Receptus is the Greek text behind the King James. The Byzantine text follows the many later copies, and the Westcott and Hort, Tregelles, and SBL editions weigh the oldest copies most heavily. Also the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, and the Latin Vulgate in its Clementine edition. All of them follow English chapter and verse numbering, so they line up with the English beside them. The lexicons For readers with no Greek or Hebrew, and for those with some A lexicon is a dictionary of the Hebrew or Greek words. Strong’s and Thayer’s are the ones most readers start with. The full Brown, Driver, and Briggs is here for Hebrew, with Abbott-Smith and Liddell, Scott, and Jones for Greek, and STEPBible’s brief lexicons for both. Double-click any word in the text for its entry. There’s more on the original languages with the rest of the features. Commentaries Henry, Calvin, Jamieson, Barnes, Spurgeon The six volumes of Matthew Henry’s Commentary on the Whole Bible, the forty-five volumes of Calvin, Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Barnes’ Notes on the New Testament, and Spurgeon’s Treasury of David on all one hundred and fifty Psalms. The footnotes Calvin’s translators added are marked as theirs and kept apart from his own words. The Westminster Standards With proofs and a topic index The Confession, the Larger Catechism, and the Shorter Catechism, each with its Scripture proofs and a doctrinal index. Hodge and Shaw on the Confession and Vincent on the Shorter Catechism are beside them. For the household there are also the Catechism for Young Children of 1840, written to lead a child on to the Shorter, and the Church of Scotland’s Directory for Family-Worship of 1647. The wider confessions The creeds and the Three Forms of Unity The Apostles’, Nicene, Athanasian, and Chalcedonian creeds, the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort with their Rejection of Errors, all in old public domain translations. The Psalter 1650, with tunes you can play The 1650 Scottish Metrical Psalter in full, all one hundred and sixty-three settings, on a page of its own. Thirty-nine tunes play in the program, so you can hear the line before you sing it. Read aloud A voice that runs on your machine A neural voice ships with the program and reads any chapter, commentary, or book aloud with no connection. It starts at the page you’re on, or at any passage you select, and a list in the player jumps ahead. Words light up as it reads. There’s a sleep timer, and you can correct how it says a name. A reference like John viii. 23 is read as John 8 , verse 23. Opens the full size picture. The Shorter Catechism’s first question, with Thomas Vincent’s comment and 1 Corinthians 10:31 , one of its proof texts, open beside it.

title: What Comes With Sojourner
text: Reference How Much Is in There These count very different things, so don’t compare them with each other. 9,349 Encyclopedia articles, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia of 1915 69,580 Entries in Noah Webster’s American Dictionary of the English Language of 1828 5,998 Dictionary entries, Easton’s and Smith’s merged by headword 344,757 Cross references 4,275 People, places, and things in the Factbook, each with its own page 1,342 Atlas places, each with coordinates and every verse that names it 464 Events on the timeline, from the Creation to Paul in Rome 296 Events of church history, from the apostles to the present, each dated by its source 271 Puritan and Reformed works on the Sojourner Library shelf 38 Volumes of the Church Fathers on a shelf of their own 39 Tunes for the 1650 Scottish Metrical Psalter, playable 14 Atlas journeys, from Abraham to Paul’s voyage to Rome 6 Reading plans, including M’Cheyne, a chronological year, and four weeks of family worship 2 Harmonies of the Gospels in four columns, Sutherland’s of 2020 and Robertson’s of 1922 Opens the full size picture. Acts 17 beside the encyclopedia’s article on the Areopagus, the hill where Paul preached in Athens. Webster’s 1828 Many King James words meant something different four hundred years ago. Prevent meant to go before, and conversation meant the whole way a man lived. Noah Webster’s dictionary of 1828 still gives those older senses, and his Scripture citations are linked. Double-click an English word and his entry appears beside the others. This works even for a word as the King James spells it, such as letteth . The Dictionary page has a switch between the Bible dictionaries and Webster. Opens the full size picture. Prevent in Webster’s 1828. To go before, as in Psalm 119 , I prevented the dawning of the morning. Opens the full size picture. 1 Thessalonians 4:15 . Double-click prevent and Webster is there beside the Greek, saying the word once meant to go before. There’s more on the shelves below . Once installed, their books are read, searched, and linked exactly like the books you add yourself.

title: What Comes With Sojourner
text: The book library Add-On Books and Your Own The books come as four shelves, each a separate download on the releases page, so you take only the ones you want. To install one, open Settings, choose Library packs, and pick Install from file. Once a shelf is in, that button reads Install or update a shelf. You can remove a shelf there too. The Sojourner Library Two hundred and seventy-one Puritan and Reformed works. The Church Fathers The writers of the early church. The Ante-Nicene Fathers, from before the Council of Nicaea, and both series of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, as Roberts, Donaldson, Schaff, and Wace edited them, with Lightfoot’s Apostolic Fathers. Thirty-eight volumes in all. Ancient literature The writers around the Bible. Josephus and Philo, 1 Enoch, and three Roman writers, Tacitus on the reign of Tiberius, the letters of Pliny the Younger, and Suetonius’s Lives of the Twelve Caesars. The nineteenth century Schaff’s History of the Christian Church and his Creeds of Christendom, and Edersheim’s Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, with his books on the Temple and on Jewish social life. Inside the program, Resources sorts every book by shelf and by subject. Books of sermons, theology, commentary, and the Christian life are each grouped together, and the Fathers are grouped by series. Cited in your library Beside each verse, a small count shows how many times the books on your shelves cite it. Click it for the list, and click a citation to open the book at that page. It shows you who else has written on the verse you’re reading. Opens the full size picture. Romans 8:28 , cited 201 times in 86 books. Each book shows where it cites the verse, and a click opens it there. Your own books and recordings Bring in your own EPUB, PDF, and MOBI books and your own audio and video. All of it goes into the search box and is scanned for the verses it cites. You can group it by author, by date, or by topic. Recordings play at the speed you choose. A passage can link straight to the moment in a recording where it’s discussed.

title: What Comes With Sojourner
text: Where the Texts Came From Every text in Sojourner is in the public domain or used under an open license, except one harmony of the Gospels. That one is used with its author’s permission, as explained below. The About page in Settings lists each source and its terms, with every Creative Commons credit the licenses ask for. The Hebrew and Greek texts, the lexicons, and the Factbook’s people and places come from STEPBible and Tyndale House, and the parsing and lexicon data from OpenScriptures. The Berean Standard Bible was given to the public domain by its makers in 2023, and the Literal Standard Version and unfoldingWord’s two texts are used under their open licenses. The timeline draws on the Theographic Bible Metadata, and the atlas on OpenBible.info, with coastlines from Natural Earth. The Terrain pack’s heights come from the Terrain Tiles on AWS, with SRTM and GMTED2010 courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey, ETOPO1 from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and EU-DEM produced using Copernicus data and information funded by the European Union. The Imagery pack’s whole-world view is NASA’s Blue Marble Next Generation, from the NASA Earth Observatory and in the public domain, and the rest of it contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2024. Most of the books on the shelves come from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library. Others come from Project Gutenberg and from old scans kept at the Internet Archive. Alexander on family worship was made for Sojourner by comparing six of those scans word by word, and it hasn’t yet been proofread line by line. The OpenDyslexic font, and the Ezra SIL font that sets the Hebrew, are under the SIL Open Font License. Webster’s dictionary of 1828 is in the public domain, and this edition of it comes from DataWar’s under the MIT license. The Psalter’s words come from two public domain editions kept at the Internet Archive, checked against the Free Church of Scotland’s text and the printing of 1650. The dates of the church history on the timeline come from Schaff’s History of the Christian Church and his Creeds of Christendom, the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, and the New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia. The creeds and the Three Forms of Unity come from Philip Schaff’s Creeds of Christendom of 1877. Schaff printed Dort’s Rejection of Errors only in Latin, so its English comes from Thomas Scott’s translation of 1818. Calvin is the Calvin Translation Society’s edition. The 2020 harmony of the Gospels is the work of Robert M. Sutherland , copyright 2020. His stated terms permit reproduction with attribution, so its order of events and their references are used here with acknowledgment of his authorship. His commentary, his Greek text, and the verse text he sets in parallel aren't. The 1922 harmony is A. T. Robertson’s and is public domain. None of the Bibles, commentaries, confessions, books, or reference data in Sojourner was written by AI. Where a source came with summaries written by AI, they were left out. None of this is my work. It’s the labour of Calvin, Henry, Spurgeon, Barnes, Orr, Easton, Smith, Strong, Thayer, Brown, Driver, Briggs, Schaff, the Westminster divines, and the many people who typed their books into machines and gave them away. Sojourner only puts them on one shelf.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: What to expect when you install it, how to update without losing anything, and how to add the book shelves and the map packs.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: The first time Installing It Go to the releases page and download the one file for your computer. All three hold the same full program. On a phone, a tablet, or a Mac, use Sojourner in the browser instead. On Windows Download the file ending in x64-setup.exe and run it. It installs for you alone, so it doesn’t need administrator rights. It includes the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime that Sojourner draws with, so it installs on a machine that has never been online. It runs on Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. On Linux Sojourner needs a 64-bit Linux system from 2024 or later. Ubuntu 24.04, Linux Mint 22, Debian 13, or newer. Download the file ending in .deb and open it in your software installer. Or, in a terminal in the folder where it landed, run sudo apt install ./Sojourner_0.4.1_amd64.deb . Most other systems, such as Fedora 40 or newer. Download the file ending in .AppImage . It runs without installing. Make it executable, then open it. You can do that in its Properties by allowing it to run as a program, or with chmod +x in a terminal. It needs the libfuse2 package, which Ubuntu 24.04 calls libfuse2t64 . Moving from Windows to Linux? On the Windows computer, open Settings, choose Data and backups, and Export. Copy that file across, then choose Import in the same place on Linux. The book library isn’t in any of the three. The books come as four shelves, each a separate download. They’re further down the releases page, under Sojourner Library Packs. The same shelf files work on Windows and Linux. Adding a shelf is explained below. New to the program? A built-in tutorial walks through every feature. It’s in Settings, under Tutorial.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: Before you double-click Two Things to Know First Neither of these is a problem with the program, but you should know about both. Windows will warn you. The Windows installer isn’t code-signed, because a certificate costs money this work doesn’t have. So SmartScreen shows a blue box the first time you run it. Click More info , then Run anyway . The release page lists each file’s SHA-256 checksum, a kind of fingerprint for the file. Anyone who knows how can use it to confirm the file is the one that was published. All three files are built by GitHub from the public source code, not on anyone’s own computer. The release page links the record of that build. If the warning makes you uneasy, that’s a good instinct, and you’re welcome to pass on it. It's a large download. About 594 MB for Windows, 519 MB for the .deb, and 626 MB for the AppImage, because the texts and the reading voice are all inside it rather than fetched from a server later. That’s the trade. One long download once, and then the program never needs the network again. Version 0.4.1 means what it says. It’s early, real, and in use, but it isn’t finished. Things will change and some of them will break. If something goes wrong, tell me and I’ll fix it.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: A new version Updating Sojourner doesn’t update itself. To see whether a newer version exists, open the About page in Settings and press the button there. That button is the only thing in the program that goes online. On Windows, download the new installer and run it over the old one. On Linux, install the new .deb the same way you installed the first, or put the new AppImage in place of the old one. Your notes, highlights, sermons, prayers, bookmarks, and installed shelves are stored apart from the program, and they’re kept. Even so, make a backup first, in Settings under Data and backups. Version 0.4.1 brought Sojourner to Linux, the same program with everything the Windows version has. Version 0.4.0 brought Color text , which puts every person, place, time, and number in the Bible in its own color, and Who’s speaking, which sets God’s own words apart from the story around them.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: Library packs Adding Books and Maps The book shelves are on the releases page under Sojourner Library Packs 0.3.6, with two map packs that add terrain and satellite views to the Atlas. To install one, open Settings, choose Library packs, and pick Install from file. Once a shelf is in, that button reads Install or update a shelf. What is on each shelf is listed with the rest of the library. If your Puritan and Reformed shelf is older than 0.3.6, install the new one. It was rebuilt from cleaner texts. It replaces the old one and keeps your notes on its books. The other three shelves have the same books as before, so they work as they are. The map packs need Sojourner 0.3.6 or later. To add one, open Settings, choose Library packs, and pick Install a map pack. What each pack shows is described with the atlas. Like the shelves, they’re files you download yourself, so they can also come on a USB stick.

title: Installing and Updating Sojourner
text: If something goes wrong Bug Reports and Corrections If something doesn’t work, or a text is wrong, or you want the program to do something it doesn’t, write to sojourner at gentleking.org . Bug reports are welcome, and corrections to the texts most of all.

title: Mortify
text: A free app for the daily work of putting sin to death by the Spirit. It meets you in the hour of temptation, morning and evening, and after a fall, and it sends you back to Christ every time.

title: Mortify
text: Begin Open Mortify Mortify Free · Works in any browser · Sign up to begin Open it on your phone and add it to your home screen. Then it opens like an app. Open Mortify What it will ask of you Works on Any phone or computer with a current web browser. It’s made for the phone. Install Add it to your home screen from the browser. There’s nothing to get from an app store. Account Needed. You sign in with a code sent to your email, with no password to remember. Price Free Privacy No ads, no analytics, and no tracking. Your journal and confessions are encrypted with your PIN. For Adults, eighteen and older Scripture The Berean Standard Bible, all of it, inside the app Made by Colt, who writes this site . Published by gentleking.org . Address mortify.gentleking.org

title: Mortify
section: Help to Put Sin to Death by the Spirit
text: What it is Help to Put Sin to Death by the Spirit Mortify is a simple help for the daily work every Christian is called to. It follows John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers. It keeps sending you back to Christ, to his Word and prayer, to the Lord’s Day, and to his people in your church. For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. Romans 8:13 (KJV) It begins with grace, not with effort. Before it asks you anything about your sin, it sets out the gospel. It says plainly, “You do not put sin to death to make God love you. You put sin to death because in Christ he already loves you.” Opens the full size picture. The home page. Flee comes first, then the way back after a fall, then the day’s word.

title: Mortify
text: Flee When You're Tempted The first thing on its home page is Flee. Press it when temptation comes, and it takes you through five steps. Attend to the Word. A verse for the sin you’re fighting. Receive counsel. Usually a few lines from one of the Puritans, who knew this fight well. Sometimes a word of Scripture. Turn to prayer. A prayer for this sin, to pray then and there. Ask your brethren to pray. One press asks the believers in your circle to pray for you. Or you can call any of them who has shared a phone number. If you have no circle yet, it tells you to call someone you trust. Now get up and go. Something plain to do right now. For lust at a screen, it might tell you to put the phone in another room, or to get up and go where people are. Then it asks, Did you stand firm? If the answer isn't yet, it doesn’t leave you there. It offers another prayer and a way to ask your circle again if you've linked with anyone. It also offers the way back if you've fallen. Flee opens without your PIN, so nothing stands between you and help. If you ask for prayer with no signal, the request waits on your phone. It goes to your circle when you’re back online. For despair, and for drink and drugs, it shows a number to call before anything else. Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart. 2 Timothy 2:22 (KJV) Opens the full size picture. Flee’s first step, the Word. Opens the full size picture. The third step, a prayer for the sin you’re fighting.

title: Mortify
text: I've fallen When You've Fallen Beside Flee is I've fallen. It doesn’t scold you or count the days since. It walks you back to Christ. There are five steps, Return to Christ, Confession, Seek the care of brethren, A short look back, and Rest in Christ. You can write a private confession. It’s encrypted on your phone before it’s saved, and no one but you can read it. If you choose, your circle can be told plainly that you fell and confessed, with none of what you wrote. Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much. James 5:16 (KJV)

title: Mortify
text: Every day Morning and Evening The fight isn’t only won in the moment of temptation. It’s won in the ordinary days around it, so Mortify gives you a morning and an evening. The morning reading At a time you choose, there’s a passage of Scripture and the next question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism. There’s a word of counsel, a chapter for the sin you’re fighting, and the chapter of Proverbs for the day of the month. There are sermons to hear as well, which open on SermonAudio. On Saturday it helps you prepare for the Lord’s Day. On Sunday it tells you to put the app down and spend the day with the Lord and his people. The evening examination At night there's a psalm, a verse, a word of counsel, and three honest questions about the day. You can mark what lay under a temptation, such as weariness, self-pity, or pride, and where it found you, such as alone, at night, or at a screen. You can write a private examination. At any time you can look back over what you marked in the past week and see the patterns. Opens the full size picture. The morning reading. Opens the full size picture. The evening examination. The whole Bible The Berean Standard Bible is inside the app, every book and chapter. Every verse in the readings and in Flee opens its chapter.

title: Mortify
text: Your battles Fifteen Sins by Name When you begin, you choose the sins you’re fighting. Each has its own Scripture, counsel, prayers, questions for the evening, and plain things to do when temptation comes. Lust and pornography Anger Bitterness and an unforgiving heart Pride Envy Fear of man Covetousness and the love of money Discontent and grumbling Worry and unbelief Despair Drunkenness and drugs Gluttony Sins of the tongue Lying and deceit Sloth and wasted time The counsel comes from Thomas Watson, John Owen, William Gurnall, Richard Sibbes, Thomas Brooks, and John Bunyan. Some of the prayers are Matthew Henry’s, from his Method for Prayer. Every prayer opens in adoration and closes in praise.

title: Mortify
text: Brethren Accountability With Friends From Church God didn’t mean for you to fight alone. If you choose, you can link with up to eight believers you already know, best of all from your own church. Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. Galatians 6:2 (KJV) Opens the full size picture. Your private code, and the believers you’ve linked with. Brothers link with brothers, and sisters with sisters. There’s no public feed and no search for strangers. You give your private code to someone you trust, and they ask to link with you. You choose what they see. It can be the sins you’re fighting, and when you asked for help and when you stood firm. If you wish, it can also be that you fell and confessed. Your journal and your confessions are never shared. They can pray for you, ask how your soul is, and send a short word of encouragement. When you ask for prayer, you see how many are praying for you.

title: Mortify
text: Your privacy Private by Design What you write in your journal is encrypted on your phone with your PIN before it’s saved. That means your examinations, your confessions, and your reflections. No one who runs Mortify can read them. Some things aren’t encrypted, so that the app can work. These are your email, whether you’re a brother or a sister, your answer about trusting in Christ, and the sins you chose. They also include your reading times and time zone, the dates of what you record and what you marked about it, and whether you stood firm when you used Flee. Your profile and anything you send to your circle aren’t encrypted either. There are no ads, no analytics, and no tracking, and your data is never sold. From Settings you can download your examinations, your confessions, and the rest of your record. You can also delete your account there. The privacy policy sets it all out in full. When you begin, you set a PIN and are given a recovery code to keep somewhere safe. If you lose both, what you wrote can’t be opened by anyone, not even you.

title: Mortify
section: What It Will Ask of You
text: Getting started What It Will Ask of You Mortify is for adults. When you begin, it asks you to confirm you’re eighteen or older, and then it sets out the gospel before anything else. After the gospel, you make your account with your email. There's no password. A code comes to your email, and you type it in. You say whether you’re a brother or a sister. Then it asks whether you’re trusting in Christ alone. If you’re not sure, it points you to the Gospel of John, to a faithful church, and to a pastor, and lets you go on. Then you choose your battles, set a time for the morning reading and the evening examination, and choose a PIN. Write down the recovery code it gives you. On an iPhone, add it to your home screen from Safari, then open it from there. The home screen app keeps its own sign-in. So you sign in once more, enter your recovery code, and choose a PIN for it. Mortify needs a connection the first time it opens on a phone.

title: Mortify
text: Plainly What It's Not It isn’t your Savior. The app says so on its first page. It can’t save you, and fighting sin won’t make you right with God. Only Christ can do that. It isn’t counseling or crisis care, and it can’t answer an emergency. Speak with your pastor. In danger, call 911 . If you’re thinking of ending your life, call 988 or text 988 . There are no streaks, scores, or trophies, because your assurance rests on Christ and not on a winning streak. It isn’t made to keep you in it longer than you need. It doesn’t filter the internet. For the battle with lust, it shows you how to turn on filtering in your phone’s own settings. That means Screen Time on an iPhone or a free family filter on Android. It tells you to do it with a trusted believer beside you.

title: Mortify
text: Questions Contact Me If something doesn’t work, or something in it isn’t right, write to mortify at gentleking.org . Corrections are welcome, most of all to anything it teaches. Mortify is published by Gentle King and given away free. The same site sets out the gospel of Jesus Christ , help in the fight against sin , and Sojourner , a free Bible study app for your phone or computer. Open Mortify

title: The Gospel
text: Christ died for His people and is freely offered to every sinner who hears the gospel. He rose bodily from the dead, and everyone who trusts in Him alone is forgiven and counted righteous for His sake.

title: The Gospel
text: His command and promise Come to Him If you haven't trusted Christ, come to Him. Your sin is a reason you need Him. Don't make waiting until you feel worthy an excuse for refusing His mercy. Come to Christ now. Your warrant is His command and promise, not an inward sense of being elect. You do not have to finish these explanations before trusting Him. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. Matthew 11:28-30 (KJV)

title: The Gospel
text: The God who saves Who God Is God made us, and we owe Him our worship and obedience. He is eternal, holy, and unchanging. There is one God in three Persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Persons are distinct, yet each is fully God. They share one divine being and one will. God's holiness means He cannot approve of evil. His mercy means sinners have reason to come to Him. These aren't competing parts of His character. At the cross, He saves His people without setting His justice aside. Salvation begins in His eternal purpose of grace, not in anything He foresaw in us. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. Isaiah 6:3 (KJV) God governs all that he has made and judges in righteousness. His mercy never sets aside his holiness. To understand the salvation he gives, we must understand our need before him.

title: The Gospel
section: What Sin Is and What It Has Done
text: Our need What Sin Is and What It Has Done Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God. It includes what we fail to do as well as the wrong we commit ( Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 14 ). God made Adam upright and placed him under a covenant requiring perfect obedience. Adam disobeyed as the representative head of mankind. All who descend from him by ordinary generation inherit his guilt and a corrupted nature. Christ alone was conceived without sin. We also commit sins of our own. We break God's law because our hearts are turned from Him. Being spiritually dead doesn't mean we're incapable of thought or choice. It means we won't turn to God in saving faith unless His Spirit makes us alive. We need forgiveness and a new heart. Neither can be earned. For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Romans 3:23 (KJV) Sin affects every part of us. Total depravity doesn’t mean everyone is as wicked as possible. It means no part of our nature is untouched by sin, and we can’t turn ourselves to God or earn his favor.

title: The Gospel
section: The Wrath of God and the Judgment to Come
text: God judges sin The Wrath of God and the Judgment to Come God's wrath is holy and just. It is never a loss of control. He judges sin because he is righteous, and every one of us must answer to him ( Romans 1:18 , Hebrews 9:27 ). Jesus warned of everlasting punishment and spoke of it alongside life eternal ( Matthew 25:46 ). Those who remain outside Christ will face conscious punishment that does not end. Our need is greater than relief from guilt or help to live better. We need deliverance from sin and its just condemnation. For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans 6:23 (KJV)

title: The Gospel
text: His person and saving work Jesus Christ, the Gentle King Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God who took a true human nature to Himself. He was conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of the virgin Mary. He is one Person, fully God and fully man. His two natures are neither mixed nor divided. And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth. John 1:14 (KJV) His humanity includes a true body and a reasonable soul. He shared our human weakness and suffered real temptation, yet he was without sin ( Hebrews 2:14-17 , 4:15). He obeyed the law His people had broken. His whole life was righteous, and His death was willing obedience to His Father. We need more than the removal of our guilt. We need the righteousness that Christ alone supplies. God counts His obedience and satisfaction to believers, who receive Him through faith alone. Christ fulfilled the law perfectly and bore the punishment his people deserved. His obedience continued through his death, and his suffering extended throughout his humiliation. Active and passive obedience name these two aspects of his one saving work ( Philippians 2:8 ). Christ died as the substitute for His people and is freely offered to every sinner who hears the gospel. He bore the judgment His people's sins deserved and fully satisfied God's justice. His suffering included the anguish of bearing divine wrath, not only the pain inflicted by men. Propitiation means that Christ's sacrifice satisfied God's justice and turned away His wrath from His people. The Father Himself provided this sacrifice in love. Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; Romans 3:25 (KJV) Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. 1 John 4:10 (KJV) But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. Isaiah 53:5 (KJV) For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2 Corinthians 5:21 (KJV) His cry of forsakenness must be taken seriously. He was deprived of the comforting sense of His Father's presence as He bore the curse. Yet the Trinity was never divided, the Father never ceased loving the Son, and Christ's divine and human natures remained united. His sufferings were real, and His trust in His Father did not fail. His sacrifice fully satisfied God's justice and secured salvation for all whom the Father gave him. He reconciles his people to God and redeems them from bondage by his blood. The Father sent his Son in love. Christ's death accomplished the salvation that divine love purposed ( John 6:37-39 , Romans 5:8-10 , Westminster Confession 8.5 , 8.8). On the third day He rose bodily from the dead. He later ascended into heaven, where He reigns and intercedes for His people. His resurrection confirms the victory of His finished work. He will return bodily to raise the dead and judge the world. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 (KJV)

title: The Gospel
text: Salvation is God's gift Grace Alone God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world. His choice was according to his own good pleasure, without any foreseen faith, obedience, or merit in them. The faith through which they receive Christ is itself his gift ( Ephesians 1:4-5 , 2:8-9, Westminster Confession 3.5 ). For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV) Man by his fall having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace; wherein He freely offereth unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ; requiring of them faith in Him, that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal life His Holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. Westminster Confession of Faith 7.3 In effectual calling, the Spirit renews the sinner and brings him willingly to Christ. Regeneration is the source of faith, not its reward. God justifies the believer through faith alone, on the basis of Christ's righteousness. Faith doesn't merit acceptance. It receives the Savior who has secured it. In those able to receive the outward call of the gospel, the Spirit's renewing work enables their response of faith. This priority isn’t a period in which they should wait before believing. They are commanded to trust Christ now ( Westminster Confession 10.1-2 ). Elect infants dying in infancy, and other elect persons incapable of receiving the outward call through the ministry of the Word, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit. He works when, where, and how he pleases ( Westminster Confession 10.3 ).

title: The Gospel
text: The call of the gospel Repentance and Faith God commands everyone who hears the gospel to repent and believe in Jesus Christ. You don't have to discover whether you're elect before coming to Him. Your warrant to come is His command and promise, not an inward sense of being elect. Saving faith receives and rests upon Christ alone for salvation. Repentance is a turning from sin to God, with grief for sin and a purpose to walk in obedience. Neither is a payment for mercy. Both are gifts of God's grace, and neither should be confused with merely knowing religious facts or feeling afraid of judgment. Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 87 Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 86 Repentance is necessary and always accompanies saving faith. It doesn’t satisfy God's justice or earn pardon. Faith is the only instrument of justification, and the faith that receives Christ is never without the other saving graces ( Westminster Confession 11.2 , 15.3). Christ is freely offered to every sinner who hears the gospel. His command and promise are your warrant to come. Religious interest or fear of judgment alone doesn’t prove that you’ve been born again. You don’t need to settle that question before obeying his call. Receive and rest upon Christ himself. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. John 6:37 (KJV)

title: The Gospel
text: Accepted for Christ's sake Justification by Faith Alone Justification is God's act of pardoning sin and accepting a sinner as righteous for Christ's sake. It changes our standing before him. Its ground is Christ's perfect obedience and satisfaction, credited to us. Faith alone receives this righteousness. Neither faith itself nor any work in us earns God's acceptance. Justification is an act of God’s free grace, wherein he pardoneth all our sins, and accepteth us as righteous in his sight, only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 33 Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: Romans 5:1 (KJV) Justification is a complete declaration of acceptance. Sanctification is the Spirit's work of renewing us inwardly. Both belong to everyone united to Christ, but our acceptance rests wholly on Christ's righteousness. Our progress in holiness adds nothing to it ( Westminster Confession 11.1-2 , 13.1). Believers cannot fall from the state of justification. Through sin they can fall under God's fatherly displeasure and lose the comfort of his countenance. They must confess their sins and renew their faith and repentance. God's continuing forgiveness doesn’t mean sin is harmless or that repentance can be neglected ( Westminster Confession 11.5 ).

title: The Gospel
text: Life with Christ Life After You Believe Everyone united to Christ is justified and adopted into God's family. Justification changes our standing before God. Sanctification changes us inwardly as the Spirit teaches us to hate sin and walk in obedience. These blessings belong together, but they aren't the same thing. We obey because God has received us in Christ. Our obedience contributes nothing to the righteousness by which we're justified. It is nevertheless necessary as the fruit of living faith. Repentance continues throughout the Christian life because sin remains in us. The same Christ who saves His people ordinarily feeds and strengthens them through His Word, the sacraments, and prayer. Read your Bible and belong to a faithful church. Receive the ministry Christ has appointed rather than measuring spiritual health by the strength of an experience. Christians suffer, and some endure long seasons of darkness. Their suffering isn't God's condemning wrath. A Father's discipline may correct particular sins, but we shouldn't assume every illness or loss can be traced to a particular offense. Job warns against that judgment. God preserves His people in faith. He uses warnings, correction, and the help of other believers to keep them. Assurance can weaken, but Christ doesn't become a weaker Savior when our confidence falters. Look first to His promises. Then consider the imperfect but real fruits of His Spirit without making them the foundation of your acceptance. There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. Romans 8:1 (KJV) At death, believers' souls are made perfect in holiness and received into God's presence. Their bodies remain united to Christ and await the resurrection. When He returns, He will raise them in glory. They will enjoy Him forever, free from sin and suffering. Baptism and the Lord's Supper are signs and seals of the covenant of grace. Their benefit comes from Christ through the work of his Spirit, rather than from a power in the outward elements. Receive them as Christ appointed, within the fellowship and oversight of a faithful church ( Westminster Confession 27.1-3 ). For practical help, read How to Find a Faithful Church . If you’re fighting a persistent sin, read Struggling With Sin . If you already belong to Christ, continue in the same faith. Confess your sins and depend on his mercy. If assurance is weak, read Assurance and Doubt . These pages can help explain the gospel, but they can’t replace Scripture or the ministry of a faithful local church. Go on to Reformed doctrine Open Bible Reading Helps

title: Grief and Hard Times
text: For the day the hard news comes, and the long days after. King James Scripture and plain counsel, gathered by sorrow. Find yours below.

title: Grief and Hard Times
text: What Are You Facing? In danger, or thinking of ending your life? Call 911 , or call 988 or text 988 , now. Someone at home hurting you? Call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 , or text START to 88788 . If a child is being hurt, call 911 . If someone checks your phone, they may see this page and your calls. A friend’s phone leaves nothing on yours. Outside the United States, call your local emergency number. Choose what has happened. Each one opens a page of its own. You don’t need to read any other. When someone has died Someone I love has died My husband or wife has died My child has died, before birth or after I fear they didn’t know Christ Someone I love took their own life In body and mind A serious illness, new or long My own mind has gone dark I’m afraid of dying At home and at work My marriage is breaking My parents are splitting up My child has turned from the Lord My work or my home is gone I’m alone Fear and doubt I’m afraid I’m not really his God feels far away It feels as if God is against me What I did is too great to forgive A sin has hold of me and won’t let go Danger I’m not safe I’m thinking of ending my life The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. Psalm 34:18 (KJV) A contrite spirit is a crushed one. Choose the page that speaks to your trouble. You can begin with a single Psalm and a simple prayer. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus read that he was sent to heal the brokenhearted, and then he said, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears ( Luke 4:18 , 21). That’s still his work.

title: Grief and Hard Times
text: The Savior Christ Knows Grief Firsthand Whatever brought you here, the Son of God has been near it. He didn’t save us from a distance. He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. Isaiah 53:3-4 (KJV) He wept at a grave. He was betrayed by a friend who ate his bread. In the garden he asked for the cup to pass. On the cross he cried out that God had forsaken him, so that those who trust him will never be forsaken ( Matthew 27:46 , Hebrews 13:5 ). On the third day he rose, and he lives now. The Larger Catechism says the Son became man so that he might have a fellow feeling of our infirmities, and so that we might have comfort and access with boldness unto the throne of grace (Q&A 39). For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. Hebrews 4:15-16 (KJV) This is your time of need. Come.

title: Grief and Hard Times
text: Prayer When You Can't Pray Grief can take the words out of your mouth. God has provided for that too. Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Romans 8:26 (KJV) If you belong to Christ, a groan with no words in it can be a prayer. The Spirit himself carries it. And if you’re his, the Son is praying for you at the right hand of God, as he prayed for Peter before Peter ever fell ( Romans 8:34 , Luke 22:32 ). When you have no words, borrow the prayers God gave his people. Read Psalm 13 aloud, or Psalm 42 , or Psalm 88 . Psalm 88 ends in the dark, yet its first words call God the God of my salvation. David asked God to put his tears into his bottle ( Psalm 56:8 ). God has no bottle and needs none. The picture means that he keeps count of every tear, and not one is lost.

title: Grief and Hard Times
text: The church Do Not Carry It Alone This page can hand you Scripture. It cannot sit with you, pray over you, or bring you a meal. Christ gave those things to his church. Call your pastor or an elder today. If one of them is the one hurting you, call another pastor you trust. You do not have to explain it well. Say that something has happened and ask him to pray with you. If the need is money or meals or rides, tell your deacons. That is what the office is for. Peter told the elders, Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof ( 1 Peter 5:2 ). Letting them do it is not a burden you lay on them. It is the work Christ gave them. When an elder comes, ask when he will come again. Go to worship on the Lord’s Day, even if you only sit and weep. Sit under the Word, and pray with God’s people. If you are a communing member, come to the Lord’s Table. It was given for the relief of weak and doubting Christians too (Larger Catechism Q&A 172). The Word, the sacraments, and prayer are the means by which Christ gives his people the benefits of his redemption (Shorter Catechism Q&A 88), and by them weak faith is strengthened ( Westminster Confession 14.1 ). Yours may be weak this week. Where you can, put off large decisions for a while, and do not make any of them alone. Getting safe is never a decision to put off.
