If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die. Owen said that a man who finds no fight in himself against his sin is at peace with it, not dying to it. Although hypocrites and other unregenerate men may vainly deceive themselves with false hopes and carnal presumptions of being in the favour of God and estate of salvation, which hope of theirs shall perish: yet such as truly believe in the Lord Jesus, and love him in sincerity, endeavouring to walk in all good conscience before him, may in this life be certainly assured that they are in the state of grace, and may rejoice in the hope of the glory of God, which hope shall never make them ashamed. Westminster Confession of Faith 18.1 Carnal presumptions are hopes the sinful heart takes for granted. What divides the hope that perishes from the hope that never shames is a true faith in the Lord Jesus. Sincere love for him and an honest effort to walk with him always come with it. If you love a sin and mean to keep it, you have no ground to call yourself safe, whatever you once prayed or professed. God’s foundation carries two sayings on one seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his, and, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity ( 2 Timothy 2:19 ). That’s hard to hear. It’s said plainly because the door is still open. Go to your elders and tell them the truth. Paul says, Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat ( 1 Corinthians 11:28 ). A man who means to keep his sin shouldn’t come to the Table until he has turned from it ( Westminster Confession 29.8 ). Christ has given his church power to keep him from it until he does (Larger Catechism Q&A 173). That discipline is care that aims to bring you back ( Where Christ Feeds His People ). Owen’s rule, that only a believer can put sin to death, reaches you too. You may need to come to Christ as if for the first time, and you may come today. The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance ( Romans 2:4 ).

title: Struggling With Sin
text: The end of the fight The Fight Will End For all who are his, this fight has an end. The last look at Christ will finish what the first look began. Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure. 1 John 3:2-3 (KJV) Beholding him by faith changes us slowly now. Seeing him will finish it. At death the souls of believers are made perfect in holiness ( Afraid of Dying ). The sin you’ve fought won’t come with you. If you’re his, take the same road again tomorrow. The King you fight under will not break a bruised reed ( Matthew 12:20 ). Of faith set on Christ, Owen wrote, live in this, and thou wilt die a conqueror. If you’re not his yet, all of this can be yours. Christ died for sinners and rose again, and he is gentle with those who come. Turn from your sin and trust him. Come as you are, today, and he will do the cleaning. Let your elders know you. If you have no church, find a faithful one. If you’d like someone to pray for you, write to me . I’m not a pastor, so in an emergency don’t wait on me. Come to Him

title: Doctrine
text: Explore Reformed doctrine one subject at a time, from Scripture to the things to come.

title: Doctrine
text: Begin With One Subject Doctrine teaches us who God is and what he has done. Start with the Word of God, or choose the subject you need. Each page keeps the fuller teaching and its Scripture references. Why Doctrine Matters Why sound teaching belongs to the Christian life. The Bible Why Scripture is our final rule of faith and life. God and the Trinity The one living God, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. The Five Solas Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. The Doctrines of Grace How God brings sinners to Christ and keeps them. Covenant Theology One covenant of grace across the Old and New Testaments. Law and Gospel What God commands and what he gives in Christ. The Church and Worship The church, worship, and the ordinary means of grace. The End Times Christ’s return, the resurrection, and the judgment. The Westminster Standards Where to begin with the Westminster Standards. Providence God's government of his creatures and all their actions. Union With Christ How believers share in Christ and his saving benefits. Adoption Received as children of the Father through the Son. Sanctification The Spirit's continuing work of making believers holy. Church Government Elders, discipline, the keys, and church courts. Baptism The covenant sign for believers and their children. Justification Accepted through Christ's righteousness alone. Christ the Mediator True God and true man, our Prophet, Priest and King. The Fall and Original Sin Adam's headship and why sinners need grace. Christian Liberty Conscience and lawful obedience under the original Confession. Oaths and Vows The solemn promises Scripture permits and requires. Westminster Study Center All thirty-three chapters, with their proofs.

title: Apologetics
text: Straight answers for the one who objects to the faith, and comfort for the one who holds it with a shaking hand. Each has pages of his own.

title: Apologetics
text: Before you begin Choose Your Question These pages are written for two readers who could hardly be further apart. One doesn’t believe and has his reasons. The other believes and is afraid he doesn’t. If you’re the first, the first part is yours. It takes the common objections one at a time and answers them straight. It won’t flatter you, and it won’t pretend the question is only about evidence. If you’re the second, the second part is yours, and the arguments will stay out of your way. Each fear has a page of its own, written for you. But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: 1 Peter 3:15 (KJV) If you’re a Christian who wants help answering a friend, borrow the first part. Peter asks for the answer to be given with meekness, the word the King chose for himself. An argument can clear rubble out of the road, but only the Spirit gives life. So the aim is never to win. It’s to see your friend at the feet of Christ. I have objections I am a Christian with doubts

title: Apologetics
text: Part one For the One Who Objects Most arguments about God treat him as a question you can settle when you like. The Bible treats you as a witness who already knows the answer. The usual approach puts God on trial and seats you in the jury box. That picture is false. No one comes to the question of God neutral. You come already sure of what’s possible and what could count as proof, and so do I. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse: Romans 1:20 (KJV) Paul says that men knew God, yet didn't glorify him as God and were not thankful, and so they held the truth down ( Romans 1:18-21 ). Unbelief isn’t a lack of light. It’s a quarrel with it. Where your objection is about facts, you’ll get facts, and only ones that hold. Where it goes deeper, you’ll see that you must borrow from God to make it at all. These pages will also keep speaking to your conscience. The trouble between you and God is moral before it’s intellectual. The pages are meant to be read in order, but begin with whichever question is yours. Is God Real? Every argument against God is made with tools that only work if he is there. 5 min read Can the Bible Be Trusted? The Bible claims that when it speaks, God speaks. It does not wait on your verdict to be true, and it has nothing to fear from your questions. 6 min read Did Jesus Rise From the Dead? The faith rests on an event at a real time and place. If Jesus did not rise, set it all aside. If he did, you will have to deal with him. 6 min read Why Does God Allow Evil? Many who ask this are carrying a grief of their own, and they should be answered with care. 6 min read Can You Be Good Without God? Nearly everyone is sure that some things are really wrong. Very few ask what makes them so. 3 min read Is Hell Fair? Hell is real, and it is felt without end. It should never be spoken of lightly, and never left out. 3 min read Is Jesus the Only Way? Few things Christians say offend more in our day than that Jesus is the only way to God. 3 min read What About the Hypocrites? Some of the strongest arguments against Christ come from people who carry his name, and they deserve an honest answer. 3 min read Is It Fair That God Chooses? The Bible teaches that God chooses whom he will save. Some hear that as a way off the hook. 3 min read Am I a Good Person? Every objection on these pages has had an answer. Jesus said the reason men stay away from him lies somewhere else. 4 min read

title: Apologetics
text: Assurance and Doubt If you believe and are afraid, find help for your fears here . Each question has a page of its own.

title: Is God Real?
text: Every argument against God is made with tools that only work if he is there.

title: Is God Real?
text: There's no evidence for God What would you count as evidence? That's worth asking before either of us begins. The Christian doesn't believe the world is silent about its Maker. Psalm 19 says the heavens declare his glory, and Romans 1:19-21 says God's power and divinity are shown in what he has made. Scripture also says we suppress that truth in unrighteousness. So the disagreement reaches further than a shortage of facts. You can look through a telescope, examine a cell, and study the laws of nature without admitting that God made them. The same observations can be interpreted in different ways. That doesn't make observations worthless. It means our starting beliefs about what exists and what can be known matter when we discuss them. Reason itself raises questions. We reason as though truth matters, contradictions must be avoided, and our minds can know something about a world outside us. The Christian understands these gifts as coming from a wise Creator who made man in his image. Someone who doesn't believe in God may give other accounts of logic and knowledge. We need to examine those accounts fairly rather than declaring that unbelievers can't reason. They plainly can, and Scripture says they still live in God's world. Science also depends on an orderly world. We test an idea because we expect nature to behave with enough regularity for a test to mean something. That expectation is useful, but the method of science doesn't by itself explain why there is a world to investigate. The Lord made and upholds all things ( Genesis 8:22 and Colossians 1:17 ). And he is before all things, and by him all things consist. Colossians 1:17 (KJV) There's an important distinction. The orderly world isn't a mathematical demonstration that compels every mind to confess the Trinity. The God of Scripture has also spoken through prophets and apostles and, at last, in his Son ( Hebrews 1:1-2 ). The resurrection of Christ is a historical claim that deserves serious attention. So I won't merely tell you to look at a tree and pretend every question has been answered. If you say that nothing could convince you, consider whether you've ruled the answer out before examining it. If you have honest questions, ask them. Christians shouldn't fear serious examination. But the Bible doesn't promise that any argument, by itself, can give a sinner a new heart. That is the Spirit's work through the Word ( 1 Corinthians 2:14 ). For the moral question, see Can You Be Good Without God? . For the records of Christ's person and work, read Can the Bible Be Trusted? and Did Jesus Rise From the Dead? . The message I want you to hear is larger than a debate about first causes. Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again. The gospel calls you to repent and believe him.

title: Is God Real?
text: Who made God? God never began. He is eternal and has life in himself ( Psalm 90:2 and John 5:26 ). Christians don't claim that everything has a maker, including God. We claim that the created world depends on the uncreated Lord. The question is whether the world has its source in something sufficient to account for its existence. Saying that God is eternal isn't an attempt to make an exception to a rule that all things must have a cause. It's a claim about the difference between the Creator and what he made.

title: Is God Real?
text: Science has replaced God Science studies how the world normally works. Why there's a world at all is another question. A man who learns how an engine runs hasn’t learned that no one built it. Many of the men who built modern science, Kepler and Boyle and Faraday and Maxwell among them, believed in the God of the Bible. They looked for laws in nature because a wise God had made it.

title: Is God Real?
text: Faith is believing without evidence Not in the Bible. When Jesus blessed those who have not seen and yet believe ( John 20:29 ), he was speaking to Thomas. Thomas had refused the word of the disciples who saw him ( John 20:25 ). Believing good witnesses isn’t believing without evidence. Faith as the Bible means it's trust in someone who has proved trustworthy, and Luke wrote so that his reader could know for certain ( Luke 1:1-4 ). You trust the record that Julius Caesar lived. You trust your memory, though you can only check it with your memory. What matters is whether your trust rests on something that can hold it. If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater, and God has testified of his Son ( 1 John 5:9 ).

title: Is God Real?
text: Examine the Claims Read John start to finish. It ends with Thomas, the doubter, and with why the book was written ( John 20:24-31 ). Read it as testimony and weigh it as you would any witness. Write down your strongest reason for unbelief. Then ask what you’re assuming to make it. Take both to a pastor and ask him to answer. Visit a faithful church on Sunday. Don’t go to argue. Sit and listen to the God you doubt being addressed as if he’s there.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: The Bible claims that when it speaks, God speaks. It does not wait on your verdict to be true, and it has nothing to fear from your questions.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: Men wrote it They did, and the Bible never hides it. It says holy men spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost ( 2 Peter 1:21 ). If God made the mind, he can speak through a man without the man ceasing to be himself. To deny it's to take for granted that there’s no such God. The question under this one is Jesus. He treated the Scriptures of Israel as the word of God that cannot be broken ( John 10:35 ). He promised his apostles that the Holy Ghost would bring to their remembrance all that he had said to them and guide them into all truth ( John 14:26 , 16:13). His word settles the Old Testament, and his promise stands behind the New. God set his seal on that word when he raised him from the dead, and so declared him to be the Son of God with power ( Romans 1:4 ).

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
section: Men chose which books went in
text: Men chose which books went in The church didn’t make any book Scripture by voting on it. The Bible’s authority rests wholly on God who wrote it and not on the word of any man or church ( WCF 1.4 ). The churches received the books that bore his voice. The four Gospels and Paul’s letters were read as Scripture long before any council drew up a list. The Council of Nicaea, which is often blamed for choosing them, issued no list at all. The gospels that were left out were mostly written in the second century or later, after the apostles were dead.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: It contradicts itself A contradiction is two statements that can’t both be true in the same sense at once. Most of what gets called one is two witnesses telling an event from different places. Matthew tells of one angel at the tomb and Mark of a young man in white. Luke tells of two men, whom the women later reported as angels ( Luke 24:23 ), and John tells of two angels. Neither Matthew nor Mark says there was only one. There are harder places, and Christians have worked through them in the open for centuries. A difficult passage deserves careful comparison of the accounts before anyone declares a contradiction.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
section: It has been changed over time
text: It has been changed over time God has kept his word pure in all ages ( WCF 1.8 ), and the copies bear that out. The New Testament survives in more than five thousand Greek manuscripts, some copied within about two centuries of the originals. The first six books of the Annals of Tacitus survive in one manuscript, copied more than seven hundred years after he wrote, and historians trust that text. The New Testament copies differ mostly in spelling and word order. No doctrine hangs on any place where the wording is truly uncertain. The great scroll of Isaiah found among the Dead Sea Scrolls is about a thousand years older than the oldest Hebrew copies known before it, and it reads substantially the same.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: You're arguing in a circle Every final authority has to vouch for itself, or whatever vouched for it would be the final authority instead. For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself, Hebrews 6:13 (KJV) If your final authority is your own reason, you can’t defend reason without using it. The man who says only what science can prove is true has said something science can’t prove. So everyone has a circle at the bottom. The question is which one can hold the weight of the world. The page on God argued that yours can’t account for the tools you used to make this charge. And the Christian circle touches history at a point where it could have been proved false, a tomb in Jerusalem that was found empty.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
section: Nobody can take it all literally
text: Nobody can take it all literally Read each biblical writer according to his intended meaning and the kind of writing he used. The Bible usually tells you what kind of writing you’re reading, a song or a letter or a vision. Read the history as history and the poetry as poetry. When a psalm tells the floods to clap their hands, no one looks for hands. Scripture is its own interpreter, the Westminster Confession says, so a hard place is read by the light of clearer ones ( WCF 1.9 ). This objection is usually aimed at Genesis, and there the clearer places settle what matters most. Jesus spoke of the man and woman God made at the beginning ( Matthew 19:4 ). Paul compares Adam with Christ as one real man with another ( Romans 5:12-19 ). Where faithful readers have differed over details in the visions of Daniel and Revelation, those details can be held with an open hand. None of that's reason to doubt what is written as history, and the Gospels are written as history. Luke dates the start of John the Baptist’s preaching by the fifteenth year of Tiberius and names the governor and the high priests ( Luke 3:1-2 ). Paul says that if Christ was not raised, your faith is vain ( 1 Corinthians 15:17 ). That isn’t how anyone speaks of a metaphor.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: Read the Accounts for Yourself Read Luke start to finish. Read it as you’d read any other ancient history, in two or three sittings. Notice the names, places, and dates he gives, and ask whether it reads like legend. Write down your strongest objection. Pick the one place you think the Bible fails, and put it in a sentence. Then ask a pastor about it, face to face or by email. Go to a faithful church on Sunday. Sit in the back if you like, and just listen. Hear how the Bible is handled by people who believe it.

title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
text: Check the Manuscript Evidence The Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts maintains a searchable collection of manuscript photographs and records. You can examine the witnesses rather than relying on a number repeated in an article. Manuscript catalogs change as fragments are identified and dated. Numerous copies give scholars a large body of evidence to compare. They also contain variant readings, which must be studied carefully. The authority of Scripture rests on God its author ( WCF 1.4 ), while the study of manuscripts concerns the transmission of the text.

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: The faith rests on an event at a real time and place. If Jesus did not rise, set it all aside. If he did, you will have to deal with him.

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: He may never have lived Almost no historian of the ancient world doubts that Jesus lived and was crucified. Tacitus, a Roman historian who despised Christians, recorded that Christ was put to death under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius. In 2012 Bart Ehrman, an agnostic scholar, wrote a whole book to answer those who say Jesus never lived.

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: The resurrection is a legend Paul's testimony to the resurrection circulated while people who knew Jesus and his earliest followers were still alive. Paul wrote to the Corinthians within about twenty-five years of the cross. He handed on a summary that many scholars, including some who deny the resurrection, date to within a few years of it. And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep. After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles. And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time. 1 Corinthians 15:5-8 (KJV) Most of the five hundred were still alive when Paul wrote. He names Cephas and James, and he had met them both ( Galatians 1:18-19 ). A man inventing a story doesn’t point you to living witnesses who could expose him. The resurrection was preached in Jerusalem, a short walk from the grave, and there’s no record that anyone produced the body. His enemies said the disciples had stolen it, which grants that the tomb was empty. Matthew says that story was still being told when he wrote ( Matthew 28:13-15 ).

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
section: The disciples lied, or they were fooled
text: The disciples lied, or they were fooled The disciples gained nothing by the story but trouble, and some were killed for it. Herod put James the brother of John to the sword ( Acts 12:2 ). The Jewish historian Josephus records that James the brother of Jesus was stoned in Jerusalem. Men will die for a falsehood they believe. They don’t choose prison and death for a story they know they invented. These men said they had seen him and eaten with him. Even scholars who reject the resurrection generally grant that the disciples believed they had seen him alive. Were they fooled by grief? A vision doesn’t empty a tomb, and the appearances didn’t come only to grieving friends. That same James was one of the brothers who did not believe in him ( John 7:5 ), and he became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. Paul was hunting Christians down when Christ met him. Grief doesn’t turn a doubting brother into a leader, or an enemy into an apostle.

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: Dead men don't rise They don’t, and the disciples knew it as well as you do ( Luke 24:11 ). The Christian claim isn’t that dead men rise on their own. It’s that God raised this one. To rule it out because dead men stay dead is to assume there’s no God who could raise them. That’s the very thing in question. Hume put the objection more carefully, saying a report of a miracle is always more likely false than true. But how likely it's that God raised this man depends on whether there’s a God who would. So it comes back to whether God is there. And experience is all against it only if you first leave out the men who said they saw him. Paul told the philosophers of Athens what the resurrection means for every man alive. Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. Acts 17:31 (KJV) The empty tomb is God’s assurance to all men that the Judge has been named. It’s empty, and you'll stand before the man who left it. So God now commands all men everywhere to repent ( Acts 17:30 ), and the man who will judge you is the same man who receives sinners today ( Luke 15:2 ).

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: Read the Resurrection Accounts Read Luke start to finish, then 1 Corinthians 15 . Luke ends with the empty tomb and the meals with the risen Jesus. Paul’s chapter shows what the earliest church staked on it. Write down your best explanation of the empty tomb. Check it against each fact on this page. Then take it to a pastor and ask where it breaks. Go to a faithful church on Sunday and listen. Christians meet on the first day of the week because of what happened that morning. Hear what they say about it.

title: Did Jesus Rise From the Dead?
text: Check the Historical Record Tacitus describes Christ's execution under Pontius Pilate in Annals 15.44 . Josephus records the death of James, whom he identifies as the brother of Jesus called Christ, in Antiquities 20.9.1 . Both are non-Christian sources that can be examined directly. These records support historical claims about Jesus and the earliest church. Neither writer says he witnessed the resurrection. The resurrection testimony itself is found in the Gospels and the apostolic preaching, particularly 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 . The difference between a source's words and the conclusion drawn from them matters.

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
text: Many who ask this are carrying a grief of their own, and they should be answered with care.

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
section: A good and powerful God would stop it
text: A good and powerful God would stop it The argument assumes that God could have no good purpose in allowing evil for a time. Our knowledge is too limited to rule out every good purpose God may have in allowing suffering. A small child can’t see why his father lets the doctor hurt him. He’s in no position to say there’s probably no reason. The gap between you and God is far wider than that ( Romans 11:33 ). The Bible shows God with exactly such a purpose. Joseph’s brothers sold him into slavery, and years later he told them they had meant it for evil and God had meant it for good ( Genesis 50:20 ). If you mean only that Christians contradict themselves, they don’t. There’s nothing contradictory in a good God allowing evil for a good reason. If you mean that evil is really evil, you’re appealing to a moral law only God can give, as the page on right and wrong shows. Sickness and disaster spring from the same root as the evil that men do. When Adam sinned, God cursed the ground for his sake ( Genesis 3:17 ), and the whole creation has groaned under that curse ever since ( Romans 8:20-22 ). A cancer is a mark of a fallen world. And God will stop evil. He has set the day. But if he ended all evil tonight, where would he stop? It runs through every human heart, yours included. That he hasn’t ended it yet is his patience, and his goodness is leading you to repentance ( Romans 2:4 ).

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
text: Then God is to blame The Bible holds two things together. God ordains all that comes to pass, and the men who do evil are guilty of it. The clearest case is the cross. Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain: Acts 2:23 (KJV) God planned the death of Jesus, and the hands that carried it out were wicked. God meant it for the saving of sinners, and the men meant murder. Guilt belongs to the one whose purpose is evil, and God’s never is. He isn’t the author of sin, and he never forces a man’s will ( WCF 3.1 ). He ordained the worst evil ever done without sharing its guilt. He brought from it the greatest good ever given. He can be trusted with the rest.

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
section: The God of the Old Testament is cruel
text: The God of the Old Testament is cruel The hardest case is Canaan, where Israel was told to leave nothing alive that breathed in the cities God gave them ( Deuteronomy 20:16-17 ). It was judgment after four centuries of patience, for the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full ( Genesis 15:16 ). By then they were burning their own children to their gods ( Deuteronomy 12:31 ). God showed no favoritism. He later threw Israel out of the land for the same sins ( Leviticus 18:28 , 2 Kings 17:7-8 ). Mercy was open even then. Rahab of Jericho confessed Israel’s God and was spared, and her name stands in the line of Jesus ( Matthew 1:5 ). Those commands belonged to one nation at one point in history, and they were never a standing order. Anyone who says God has told him to kill is claiming a word from heaven the Bible doesn’t allow. As for the children, every life is God’s to give and his to take back. Job said as much on the day he lost all ten of his own ( Job 1:18-21 ). What was unusual in Canaan is that God commanded men to carry out his sentence on those nations, and told us why.

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
text: The Bible approves of slavery The law of Moses made it a crime worthy of death to steal a man and sell him ( Exodus 21:16 ), and Paul names menstealers among the lawless ( 1 Timothy 1:10 ). That’s how the Atlantic trade filled its ships. The law did allow servitude. An Israelite who grew poor and was sold served as a hired servant until the jubilee. Those bought from the nations around Israel could be kept as bondmen for life ( Leviticus 25:39-46 ). But the law hemmed it in. A servant who escaped from his master was not to be handed back ( Deuteronomy 23:15-16 ). A master who struck out his servant’s eye or tooth had to let him go free ( Exodus 21:26-27 ). The law of Moses bore with some things because men’s hearts were hard, as Jesus said of divorce ( Matthew 19:8 ). The apostles told a Christian slave to take his freedom if he could ( 1 Corinthians 7:21 ). They told a master to receive his runaway as a brother beloved (Philemon 16). Some Presbyterians in the American South defended slavery from the Bible, and they were wrong. You’re right to call the slave trade evil. But you can say so only by a law above every nation, and that law is God’s. It condemns the menstealer, and it finds the rest of us guilty too. Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin, and only the Son can make a man free indeed ( John 8:34-36 ).

title: Why Does God Allow Evil?
text: Bring the Question to Scripture Read Luke start to finish. Pay close attention to the last chapters, where the worst evil ever done falls on Jesus himself. Ask what kind of God would walk into suffering like that. Write down the evil that troubles you most. If it’s something that happened to you or someone you love, say so plainly. Then take it to a pastor and talk it through. Go to a faithful church on Sunday and listen. You’ll be among people who have buried children and sat in cancer wards. Hear what they pray.

title: Can You Be Good Without God?
text: Nearly everyone is sure that some things are really wrong. Very few ask what makes them so.

title: Can You Be Good Without God?
section: I can be good without God
text: I can be good without God In one sense you can, and Christians have never denied it. God’s law is written on every heart, so men who never read a Bible know a great deal about right and wrong ( Romans 2:14-15 ). But good by whose measure? Jesus said the first and great commandment is to love God himself with everything you are ( Matthew 22:37-38 ). A man can be kind to his neighbor and break that commandment every day he lives. Even his good works, the Confession says, are sinful and can't please God. They don’t come from a heart purified by faith or aim at the glory of God. Yet leaving them undone would be more sinful still ( WCF 16.7 , Hebrews 11:6 ).

title: Can You Be Good Without God?
section: Morality is only evolution or culture
text: Morality is only evolution or culture An evolutionary account may describe how moral habits developed, but description alone can't establish what anyone ought to do. Nature has produced cruelty as surely as kindness, and it can’t tell you which is right. If moral rules depend entirely on a society's approval, there's no standard above that society by which to judge its conduct. The men who ended the slave trade weren’t right, only different. No one lives that way. You say torturing a child for fun is wrong everywhere and always, and you’re right. That’s a law above every culture. You might call it simply a fact, like two and two making four. But a sum doesn’t accuse you, and you wrong no one when you add it up badly. A law that binds every man and accuses him when he breaks it needs a Lawgiver with the right to bind him. His law is no whim, as if he could have made cruelty good. He commands what agrees with his own nature, and he cannot deny himself ( 2 Timothy 2:13 ). And you don’t only know that law. You hold other people to it every time they break their word to you or run you down behind your back. You’ve done both. Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things. Romans 2:1 (KJV)

title: Can You Be Good Without God?
text: Examine Your Life Read Matthew start to finish. Slow down at the Sermon on the Mount in chapters 5 to 7. Measure yourself by it, not by your neighbors. Write down where your sense of right and wrong comes from. Try to ground it without God, in a sentence or two. Then ask a pastor to read it with you. Visit a faithful church on Sunday and listen. Listen for how the prayers and the sermon speak about sin. Ask yourself whether you could honestly say amen.

title: Is Hell Fair?
text: Hell is real, and it is felt without end. It should never be spoken of lightly, and never left out.

title: Is Hell Fair?
section: A loving God wouldn't send anyone there
text: A loving God wouldn't send anyone there When a cruel person dies without answering for his deeds, we still know that judgment is owed. A man murders and is never caught, and dies old and comfortable in his bed. Something in you says that can’t be the end of it. God's judgment will reach every evil, including the sins we would rather overlook in ourselves. No one in the Bible warned of hell more often than Jesus, the gentlest man who ever lived. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him. Luke 12:5 (KJV) The warning comes from a God who swears by his own life that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked ( Ezekiel 33:11 ). And hell is exact. Some will be beaten with many stripes and some with few, and the many are for the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not do it ( Luke 12:47-48 ). No one will bear a stroke more than he deserves.

title: Is Hell Fair?
section: Forever is too long for a short life of sin
text: Forever is too long for a short life of sin A crime isn’t measured by how long it took. A murder can take a second. We weigh a wrong by what was done and by who was wronged, and striking your mother is worse than striking a stranger. Sin is a wrong done to the infinitely holy God, to whom you owe all you have. Every sin, even the least, being against the sovereignty, goodness, and holiness of God, and against his righteous law, deserveth his wrath and curse, both in this life, and that which is to come; and cannot be expiated but by the blood of Christ. Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 152 In Matthew 25:46 the Authorized Version calls the punishment everlasting and the life eternal. In the Greek they’re the same word. If one ends, so does the other. The catechism ends where it must, with the blood of Christ , who bore that wrath so that those who trust him never will.

title: Is Hell Fair?
text: Read Christ's Warnings Read Luke start to finish. Notice how often the warnings of hell and the offers of mercy come from the same mouth. Luke 12 and Luke 15 sit only a few pages apart. Write down what seems unjust to you. Put it in one sentence. Then ask a pastor how he answers it, and listen to the whole answer. Go to a faithful church on Sunday and listen. Hear whether the preacher warns of judgment and still holds out Christ to you. Both are there for your good.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
text: Few things Christians say offend more in our day than that Jesus is the only way to God.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
text: All religions lead to God They can’t all lead to the same place, because they don’t agree about where it is. Islam teaches that Jesus wasn't crucified, though almost every historian holds that he was. Christianity puts his cross at the center of everything. To say all religions are the same is to say each is wrong about what it cares about most. That claim dismisses the central teachings of the religions it claims to respect. Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. John 14:6 (KJV) Only one faith says that God became a man and died for the sins of his enemies. If there were another way, the cross would be the most needless cruelty in history. The night before he died, Jesus asked his Father, if it were possible, to let the cup pass from him ( Matthew 26:39 ). It didn’t pass, because there was no other way.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
section: What about those who never heard?
text: What about those who never heard? No one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ he never heard of. Men are judged for sinning against the light they had, in creation and in conscience ( Romans 1:20 , 2:12-15). But ignorance saves no one. If it did, the kindest thing the church could do would be to keep quiet. Christ sent his church to every nation because men cannot call on one they have not heard of ( Romans 10:14 ). Apart from him no one is saved, however carefully he lives by the light of nature or his own religion ( WCF 10.4 ). You've heard the gospel. Christ commands you to repent and believe now.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
section: It's arrogant to say you're right
text: It's arrogant to say you're right Every claim to truth rules out its opposite, including the claim that Christians are wrong. Arrogance lies in how a man holds what he believes and why he thinks he came by it. We didn’t find God by being wiser or better than anyone. We were lost, and he found us, and we have nothing we did not receive ( 1 Corinthians 4:7 ). A man pulled out of the river isn’t boasting when he tells you where the rope is.

title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
text: Consider Christ's Claim Read John start to finish. Mark each time Jesus says I am. Ask whether a good teacher who wasn’t the only way could talk like that. Write down the religion or view you find most fair. Set down what it says about sin and how a person is put right with God. Then ask a pastor to compare it with the gospel. Go to a faithful church on Sunday and listen. Notice who gets the credit for salvation in what is sung and preached. Listen for the rope.

title: What About the Hypocrites?
text: Some of the strongest arguments against Christ come from people who carry his name, and they deserve an honest answer.

title: What About the Hypocrites?
section: The church is full of hypocrites
text: The church is full of hypocrites Some who sit in churches are hypocrites, and Jesus said there would be ( Matthew 7:21-23 ). His hardest words were for religious men who looked clean outside and were rotten within ( Matthew 23:27-28 ). So on this point you and he agree. But a hypocrite fails to live by what he claims. That tells you about the man and nothing against the claim. Counterfeit money is only worth making because real money exists. Many of the Christians you have in mind aren’t hypocrites at all. They’re sinners who know it, which is why they’re in church. They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Mark 2:17 (KJV)

title: What About the Hypocrites?
text: Religion has done great harm It has, and some of it was done in the name of Christ. There’s no excuse to make, and Reformed Christians have no clean hands to hold up. Geneva burned Michael Servetus for heresy in 1553, and Calvin had pressed for his death. Cruelty like that defies Christ. He rebuked James and John when they wanted to call down fire on a village that would not receive him ( Luke 9:54-55 ). But the harm doesn’t leave when religion does. The officially atheist governments of the last century killed their own people by the millions. The trouble is the human heart, which goes wherever men go, into churches and into prison camps alike. Am I a Good Person? turns to it.

title: What About the Hypocrites?
text: Consider the Objection Read Mark start to finish. It’s the shortest Gospel, and you can read it in an evening. Judge Jesus by what he said and did, not by his followers. Write down what you hold against Christians. Be specific. Then ask a pastor about it and see whether he defends it or owns it. Visit a faithful church on Sunday. Listen to what they confess about themselves in the service. Ask whether these people claim to be good, or claim to need a Savior.

title: Is It Fair That God Chooses?
text: The Bible teaches that God chooses whom he will save. Some hear that as a way off the hook.

title: Is It Fair That God Chooses?
section: If God chooses, how can he blame me?
text: If God chooses, how can he blame me? Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Romans 9:19-20 (KJV) Paul raised your objection himself, and he had to, because he taught that God chooses. No one would raise it if God’s choice only followed ours. His first answer is a rebuke. The thing formed doesn’t put its maker on trial. Then see what the Bible never says, that a man is condemned for not being chosen. He is condemned for his sin ( WCF 3.7 ), and no one ever sinned against his own will. Every sin you’ve committed, you committed because you wanted to. Election pushes no one into sin. It pulls some out who would have stayed in it gladly. God wrongs no one when he leaves a man to the sin he loves.

title: Is It Fair That God Chooses?
section: Then there's no point in trying
text: Then there's no point in trying God’s decree about you is hidden, and you don’t need to know it before you come. What is revealed is his command to repent and believe, and his promise that Christ will cast out no one who comes ( John 6:37 ). Nothing has ever kept a sinner from Christ but that he would not come ( John 5:40 ). The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law. Deuteronomy 29:29 (KJV) The God who ordains the end ordains the means, and the means is the gospel, heard and believed. The gospel page says more about election and the sinner who wants to come.

title: Is It Fair That God Chooses?
text: Christ's Invitation Read John start to finish. Watch for chapter 6, where Jesus speaks of the Father giving and drawing, and in the same breath invites all who come. See how he holds the two together. Write down your objection and ask a pastor. Put the hardest form of it in one sentence. A Reformed pastor has heard it before and won’t brush it off. Go to a faithful church on Sunday and listen. Notice that the gospel is offered to everyone in the room. Take that offer as meant for you.

title: Am I a Good Person?
text: Every objection on these pages has had an answer. Jesus said the reason men stay away from him lies somewhere else.

title: Am I a Good Person?
text: I'm a good person You've lied, and no lie is too small for God to count. You’ve taken what wasn’t yours, whether money or time or credit. Jesus said that whoever looks on a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart ( Matthew 5:28 ). John calls hatred murder ( 1 John 3:15 ), and you know whether you’ve hated. God’s name has been a curse in your mouth, or a word that meant nothing, and he will not hold that man guiltless ( Exodus 20:7 ). And have you loved God with all your heart for a single hour? You haven’t even thanked him for the breath you argue with. Perhaps you hope the good you’ve done will outweigh the bad. It won’t. Whoever keeps the whole law and yet breaks it in one point is guilty of all ( James 2:10 ), because the God who said do not commit adultery also said do not kill ( James 2:11 ). Break his law at any point and you’ve defied the one who gave all of it. Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. Romans 3:19 (KJV) Jesus said that evil thoughts, adulteries, murders, thefts and deceit come from within, out of the heart ( Mark 7:21-23 ). Ask yourself whether you want to be free of your sins, or only free of what they cost you. There are some you’d keep if you could keep them without the judgment. That’s what it means to love darkness. You aren’t a good man with a few faults and some questions. You’re a sinner by nature and by choice. You were born that way , a child of Adam, and Paul says we were all by nature the children of wrath ( Ephesians 2:3 ). I don’t say it from above you. The same law shut my mouth.

title: Am I a Good Person?
section: Then what hope is there for me?
text: Then what hope is there for me? Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them. Luke 15:1-2 (KJV) His enemies meant it as a charge, and it’s the best news you’ll ever hear. Christ came for sinners exactly like you. He kept the law you’ve broken. On the cross he bore its curse for everyone who trusts him, and God raised him from the dead. The gospel page tells it in full. So the call is the one Jesus preached. Repent, and believe the gospel ( Mark 1:15 ). Turn your back on your sin, and rest on Christ alone, not your own record, to answer for you before God. Come to Christ now, even with questions you haven't resolved. Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord , and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. Isaiah 55:7 (KJV) The unrighteous man must forsake his thoughts as well as his way, and some of those thoughts may be the objections you brought here. Leave them with the rest, and take the pardon. Call on him. You don’t need fine words. A tax collector asked God to be merciful to him as a sinner, and Jesus said he went home justified ( Luke 18:13-14 ). Read the Gospel of John. A chapter a day is enough. John wrote it so that you would believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life through his name ( John 20:31 ). Hear the Word preached. Go to a faithful church this Sunday. Faith comes by hearing the word of God ( Romans 10:17 ), and no one has to believe anything to walk in and listen. Write to me. If an objection is still standing in your way, tell me what it is .

title: Am I Really Saved?
text: God does not want his children living on guesses. John wrote his first letter to believers so that they would know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13).

title: Am I Really Saved?
section: I don't know if I'm saved
text: I don't know if I'm saved You can know. The Confession calls assurance something far firmer than a guess. It names three grounds for it, in an order that protects a frightened conscience. This certainty is not a bare conjectural and probable persuasion grounded upon a fallible hope; but an infallible assurance of faith, founded upon the divine truth of the promises of salvation, the inward evidence of those graces unto which these promises are made, the testimony of the Spirit of adoption witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God: Westminster Confession of Faith 18.2 Start with the promises, because they don’t change when you do. God has promised everlasting life to everyone who believes on the Son ( John 3:36 ). That was as true on the morning you felt nothing as on the morning you wept for joy. Then look at the graces with an honest eye. A weak trust in Christ counts. So does hatred of the sin you keep falling into, and grief that you love him so little. Every grace is imperfect in this life, so the graces confirm the promise and never replace it. Start with them and you’ll find a reason to doubt each one. Last comes the Spirit himself, who bears witness with our spirit that we are the children of God ( Romans 8:16 ). He bears that witness through the Word, often quietly. You see it in the simple fact that you come to God as a child comes to his father.

title: Am I Really Saved?
section: Maybe my faith was never real
text: Maybe my faith was never real The Confession says in 18.3 that assurance isn't of the essence of faith, and that a true believer may wait long before he has it. A lack of certainty doesn’t prove a lack of faith. The Larger Catechism goes further. One who doubteth of his being in Christ, or of his due preparation to the sacrament of the Lord’s supper, may have true interest in Christ, though he be not yet assured thereof; and in God’s account hath it, if he be duly affected with the apprehension of the want of it, and unfeignedly desires to be found in Christ, and to depart from iniquity: Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 172 Maybe it troubles you that you aren’t sure, and you truly want to be found in Christ and done with your sin. Then the Catechism says you may belong to Christ before you’re sure of it, and that in God’s account you do. That answer asks what you want. It doesn’t ask whether you’ve won the fight yet. Some people are certain they're saved because they once made a profession, grew up in church, or had a powerful experience. The Confession warns that hypocrites and other unregenerate people may deceive themselves with false hopes ( WCF 18.1 ). Assurance isn't the same as confidence in an old decision. Scripture calls us to examine whether we're in the faith ( 2 Corinthians 13:5 ), and to look for repentance and love as fruits of genuine faith ( 1 John 2:3-6 ). Yet those fruits don't purchase salvation, and constant self-inspection can't give life. Christ saves sinners who trust him. There’s also a shorter road than weighing your faith. You don’t have to settle whether the first time was real. You can come to Christ today.

title: Am I Really Saved?
text: I'm afraid I wasn't chosen You don't need to discover the secret decree before believing Christ. The gospel commands you to repent and believe, and Christ promises to receive those who come to him ( John 6:37 ). Election is true, and the Confession says it should bring abundant consolation to all who sincerely obey the gospel. The gospel is obeyed by believing it, and Paul puts the two words side by side ( Romans 10:16 ). You aren’t asked to read the decree to find your name there. Nobody can read it and find his name left out. Jesus said no one can come to him unless the Father draws him ( John 6:44 ). If you’ve come to Christ, however weakly, the Father drew you. So believers may be assured of their election from the certainty of their calling ( WCF 3.8 ), and Peter tells us to make our calling and election sure ( 2 Peter 1:10 ). Look for your election in the call you answered.

title: Am I Really Saved?
text: Return to Christ's Promises Read one promise a day. Try John 3:36 , John 6:37 , Romans 10:13 , and 1 John 5:13 . Read it slowly and ask, is this true? Then rest on it. Pray simply. Tell God you want Christ and want to be done with your sin. Ask him to make you sure. You don’t need the right words. Stop checking your feelings every hour. Feelings rise and fall. When the fear comes, turn it into a short prayer and get back to your day. Talk to your pastor or an elder. Tell them you aren’t sure you’re saved. This is part of their job, and they’ve heard it before. Be in church Sunday. God strengthens faith through the preached Word and the sacraments. Go even if you feel nothing.

title: When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back
text: Few things shake a Christian like meeting the same sin again, years after he first wept over it. Your fear draws one conclusion from that. God has drawn another, and he has written it down.

title: When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back
section: I keep going back to the same sin
text: I keep going back to the same sin If you think a real Christian would be free of this by now, read Romans 7 . Paul wrote it as an apostle, and he says he does the very thing he hates. There’s a war in every believer between the flesh and the spirit, and it lasts as long as this life ( WCF 13.2 ). God doth continue to forgive the sins of those that are justified; and although they can never fall from the state of justification, yet they may by their sins fall under God’s fatherly displeasure, and not have the light of his countenance restored unto them, until they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith and repentance. Westminster Confession of Faith 11.5 God gave his verdict when you believed, and he doesn’t reopen the case. What your sin can bring on you is his fatherly displeasure. He may hide the light of his face until you come back humbled and confess it. He may use the rod. Yet he won’t take his lovingkindness from you ( Psalm 89:30-33 ). That’s a father correcting his son, and there’s nothing of the judge in it. My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous: And he is the propitiation for our sins: 1 John 2:1-2 (KJV) Your advocate doesn’t plead that you’re innocent. He pleads his own blood. That plea doesn’t wear thin as your record grows, because it never rested on your record. There's a difference between falling into sin and making peace with it. A man who plans his sin, excuses it, and refuses correction shouldn't use perseverance as permission to go on. Scripture warns against hardening the heart ( Hebrews 3:12-13 ). If that's you, repent today. Don't reassure yourself with an old profession while resisting the Lord's commands. So don’t hide the sin, and don’t make peace with it. Remaining sin may win for a time, but the part of you that's born again will overcome, because the Spirit of Christ keeps giving it strength ( WCF 13.3 ). For the long fight itself, read Struggling With Sin .

title: When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back
section: What I did is too great to forgive
text: What I did is too great to forgive You may carry one sin heavier than all the rest. If you did it after you came to Christ, it may feel heavier still. As there is no sin so small but it deserves damnation, so there is no sin so great that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent. Westminster Confession of Faith 15.4 David took another man’s wife and had the man killed to cover it. When he confessed, Nathan told him the Lord had put away his sin ( 2 Samuel 12:13 ). The consequences stayed in his house, but the guilt was gone. Paul had hunted Christians into prison. He called himself the chief of sinners. He said Christ showed him mercy as a pattern for everyone who would believe after him ( 1 Timothy 1:15-16 ). If your sin is great, that pattern was set up for sinners like you. Once you’ve confessed it and turned from it, trusting Christ’s blood and not your confession, the pardon is yours. The memory may come back for years, and the shame with it, but the guilt doesn’t. Take him at his word, and thank him for it.

title: When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back
section: He must be tired of forgiving me
text: He must be tired of forgiving me We get tired of forgiving because every pardon costs us something. Your pardon cost God his Son, and that price was paid once and in full. He isn’t paying it again each time you come. Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy. He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. Micah 7:18-19 (KJV) He has promised to subdue the very sins he pardons. When Peter asked how often he must forgive his brother, Jesus said seventy times seven ( Matthew 18:22 ). He doesn’t ask more mercy of you than he shows you.

title: When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back
text: When the Sin Returns Confess it each time, right away. Don’t wait until you feel sorry enough. Name the sin to God plainly and thank him for the blood of Christ. Change the place and the hour. Romans 13:14 says to make no provision for the flesh. If you keep falling in the same place at the same time, change your routine there. Move the phone, leave the room, go to bed earlier. Tell one person. Pick a mature Christian of your own sex, or an elder, and tell them what you’re fighting. Ask them to check on you every week. Go to church Sunday. Don't stay home because you fell. Sit under the preached Word. If you're a communicant member, examine yourself and speak with your elders if you're unsure about coming to the Lord's Table ( WLC 171-173 ). Write down one verse. Put 1 John 1:9 or Micah 7:18-19 where you’ll see it, and read it when the shame comes back.

title: The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away
text: Some fears come back at night, when the house is quiet and there is nothing to do but think. Each of these has an answer that will not give way under you.

title: The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away
section: I think I've committed the unpardonable sin
text: I think I've committed the unpardonable sin The scribes from Jerusalem couldn’t deny that Jesus was casting out devils. So they said he did it by the prince of the devils. Jesus answered them. Verily I say unto you, All sins shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, and blasphemies wherewith soever they shall blaspheme: But he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation: Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit. Mark 3:28-30 (KJV) The sin Jesus named was a settled verdict. These men saw the Holy Spirit’s work in Christ and called it the devil’s. They weren’t asking for mercy. They were accusing the Savior. If you’re asking Christ for mercy, you’re doing the opposite of what they did, and whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved ( Romans 10:13 ). No exception is written into that promise, so whatever you fear you did, it hasn’t shut you out. If the fear began with a blasphemous thought that came against your will, that’s no settled verdict. What’s written about thoughts you would never choose is for you.

title: The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away
text: Hebrews 6 and 10 frighten me Hebrews 6 speaks of people who were enlightened and tasted the good word of God and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and then fell away. They had stood close to Christ and walked away from him with their eyes open. They were like ground that drinks the same rain as a good field and bears only thorns. The passage says such people can’t be renewed to repentance. If you’ve come back to Christ in repentance, or are coming now, you aren’t the person it describes. But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak. Hebrews 6:9 (KJV) Being enlightened, tasting the good Word, and sharing in the life of the visible church aren't identical to regeneration. Some receive great outward privileges and experience the Spirit's work among God's people without possessing saving faith. Hebrews 6 distinguishes these experiences from the "things that accompany salvation" in verse 9. The warning concerns deliberate apostasy. Don't apply it to a repentant believer's ordinary battle with sin. The writer expected better things of his readers ( Hebrews 6:9 ). His warning was one means by which God would keep them watchful. And the chapter ends with an anchor. It’s a hope sure and steadfast, given with a promise and an oath, so that all who have fled to it for refuge might have strong consolation (6:17-20). If you’ve fled to Christ for refuge, that anchor is yours. Hebrews 10:26 frightens many for the same reason. It says no sacrifice remains for those who sin wilfully after they've received the knowledge of the truth. A man who keeps falling into a sin he knows is wrong fears it means him. Verse 29 says who is meant. It’s the man who has trodden under foot the Son of God and counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing. If you keep running back to that blood, you aren’t trampling it. You’re among them that believe to the saving of the soul (10:39).

title: The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away
text: I might lose my salvation My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand. John 10:27-29 (KJV) Jesus said that no man can pluck his sheep out of his hand, and he said more. They shall never perish. If a sheep could slip away and be lost for good, that promise wouldn’t be true. This perseverance of the saints depends, not upon their own free will, but upon the immutability of the decree of election, flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ; the abiding of the Spirit and of the seed of God within them; and the nature of the covenant of grace: Westminster Confession of Faith 17.2 Not one of those supports is your willpower. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus told Peter that Satan wanted to sift the disciples like wheat. He said he had prayed for Peter himself, that his faith would not fail ( Luke 22:31-32 ). Within hours Peter swore with curses that he didn’t know him. His courage failed. His faith didn’t finally fail, because Christ had prayed for it. Before Peter ever fell, Jesus told him to strengthen his brethren once he was turned back. God preserves his people through warnings like these. Don't turn the doctrine of perseverance into a reason to ignore them. The same Christ who promises to keep his sheep causes them to hear his voice and follow him ( John 10:27 ). True believers may fall into grievous sins and stay in them for a time ( WCF 17.3 ). They won’t fall all the way, and they won’t fall for good.

title: The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away
text: When You Fear Falling Away Ask for mercy out loud. Tonight, pray Romans 10:13 back to God. Tell him you’re calling on his name and ask him to save you. That prayer is the opposite of the sin you fear. Read the whole chapter. Don’t live on one scary verse. Read all of Hebrews 6 down to verse 20, and all of John 10 . Notice how each one ends. Stop searching online at night. Late-night searching feeds the fear. Close the phone and pray instead. Come back to it in daylight with your Bible open. Tell an elder what you’re afraid of. Name the verse or the thought that scares you. Fears grow in secret and shrink when they’re spoken.

title: When God Feels Far
text: There are seasons when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling and the Bible is only ink. They do not mean that God has gone.

title: When God Feels Far
section: I've prayed, but God still feels far away
text: I've prayed, but God still feels far away You read the Bible, and the words seem to stop at the page. You pray, and you wonder whether God hears. If his promises once brought comfort and now seem distant, tell the Lord how much that grieves you. The Psalms give words to believers who know this darkness. Who is among you that feareth the Lord , that obeyeth the voice of his servant, that walketh in darkness, and hath no light? let him trust in the name of the Lord , and stay upon his God. Isaiah 50:10 (KJV) Notice who is walking in darkness. It's someone who fears the Lord and obeys his servant. Isaiah doesn't tell him to manufacture a feeling. He tells him to trust his God. The Lord's promise remains true when you can barely feel its comfort. Psalm 88 ends in darkness. Heman doesn't receive a tidy answer before the last verse, yet he begins by calling upon the God of his salvation. In Psalm 77 Asaph asks whether God's mercy has clean gone for ever. He brings the question to God, then remembers how the Lord led Israel through the sea. He couldn't see God's footsteps, but God was there ( Psalm 77:19-20 ). You may not be able to trace what the Lord is doing now.

title: When God Feels Far
section: Has God withdrawn his love from me?
text: Has God withdrawn his love from me? There's a difference between losing the comfort of God's love and being cast out of his family. A believer can lose the sense of God's fatherly countenance for a time. He can't lose the justification Christ purchased for him ( Romans 8:1 and WCF 11.5 ). Christ doesn't cease to intercede because your heart has gone cold ( Hebrews 7:25 ). Westminster Confession 18.4 says true believers may have their assurance shaken, diminished, and interrupted. It doesn't say this happens only to people who haven't prayed enough. It names negligence, particular sins, sudden temptation, and God's withdrawing the light of his countenance for a time. The Confession also says that God never leaves his own utterly destitute of the seed of God and the life of faith. Don't make today's feelings your final judgment on the Lord's faithfulness. The promise of Christ is a better witness than your present comfort ( John 6:37 and John 10:27-29 ).

title: When God Feels Far
section: What if my sin has brought this darkness?
text: What if my sin has brought this darkness? Sometimes it has. David knew what it was to keep silent about his sin and feel the Lord's hand heavy upon him. Read Psalm 32 . If you know you're cherishing a sin, don't excuse it by calling your trouble a dry season. Confess it plainly. Turn from it. If you've wronged someone, seek to make it right. God's fatherly displeasure is real. The Confession says a justified believer may lose the light of his countenance until he humbles himself, confesses, seeks pardon, and renews his faith and repentance ( WCF 11.5 ). Yet the Father isn't demanding that his child pay for sins Christ has already borne. He calls his child back through repentance. But don't search for a secret sin behind every hard day. Job's friends were wrong to assume his suffering proved some hidden wickedness. Christ also rejected the disciples' attempt to trace a man's blindness to a particular sin ( John 9:1-3 ). Examine yourself honestly, and repent where Scripture exposes sin. Don't invent guilt where God hasn't shown it.

title: When God Feels Far
section: I've repented. Why hasn't the comfort returned?
text: I've repented. Why hasn't the comfort returned? Because comfort isn't something we can command. David prayed for the joy of salvation to be restored ( Psalm 51:12 ). That prayer itself shows that a forgiven man may long for a joy he doesn't presently have. You might confess your sin sincerely and still feel low the next morning. That doesn't mean your repentance was false. Don't keep confessing the same matter merely to obtain a particular feeling. Believe what God says about pardon, and go on putting sin to death. If there's a duty you've neglected, take it up again. Some darkness lasts longer than we expect. Psalm 88 doesn't hide that. The Lord may restore assurance gradually, through his Word and the ministry of his church. WCF 18.3 says a true believer may have to wait long and struggle with many difficulties before he has assurance. Come to Christ now, even while assurance remains weak.

title: When God Feels Far
section: How do I seek him while I feel nothing?
text: How do I seek him while I feel nothing? Keep going where the Lord has promised to meet and strengthen his people. Hear the Word preached. Read Scripture in its context, even if you only manage a short passage. Pray honestly. If all you can say is that you're afraid and need help, say that. Pray Psalm 13 or Psalm 77 when your own words fail. Don't withdraw from the church because you feel empty. Tell your pastor or an elder what's happening. Ask for prayer and counsel. If you're a communicant member troubled by doubts, speak with your elders about coming to the Lord's Table. The Supper is given to strengthen weak faith, but it must be received with repentance and self-examination ( WLC 171-173 ). These are means of grace, not a bargain with God. You aren't earning his presence by keeping a schedule. You're coming to the places where he ordinarily nourishes his people ( WCF 14.1 ).

title: When God Feels Far
section: What about exhaustion, grief, or illness?
text: What about exhaustion, grief, or illness? Your body matters. Severe weariness, grief, depression, or illness can make it harder to think and pray. Elijah was afraid and worn down under the juniper tree, and the Lord provided rest and food ( 1 Kings 19:4-8 ). But that's not the whole account. At Horeb the Lord questioned him, corrected him, and sent him back to his calling ( 1 Kings 19:9-18 ). Don't turn the passage into a claim that spiritual darkness is cured by a meal and a nap. Get the rest and care you need, and don't treat medical help as unbelief. If the heaviness persists or interferes with daily life, speak to a doctor as well as your elders. Physical care can help you bear the burden. It can't replace the promises of Christ or the ordinary means of grace. If you're thinking of ending your life, tell someone near you today. In the United States you can call 988 or text 988 at any hour. Elsewhere, seek immediate help through your local emergency service.

title: When God Feels Far
text: What to do now Bring the real question to God. If you fear he has forsaken you, tell him so. Read Psalm 13 and pray it rather than pretending all is well. Deal with known sin. Confess it and turn from it. Don't keep hunting for a hidden offense just because the feeling won't lift. Go hear the Word. Be at public worship this Lord's Day, even if you're numb. Ask an elder to pray with you. Hold to a promise. Read John 6:37 in its setting. Your warrant to come to Christ is his invitation, not a feeling of being chosen. Receive appropriate care. If your health or mood has suffered, seek practical and medical help. Don't ask a night's sleep to do what only the Lord can do.

title: Doubts and Unwanted Thoughts
text: Some believers are afraid it is not true, and the question will not leave them alone. Others are afraid of what their own minds keep saying to them.

title: Doubts and Unwanted Thoughts
section: Sometimes I wonder if any of it's true
text: Sometimes I wonder if any of it's true The pull to walk away isn’t new. When many of his disciples turned back, Jesus put the question to the twelve. Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. John 6:67-68 (KJV) Peter answered with a question of his own. He knew the other voices on offer, and none of them had the words of eternal life. When doubt tells you to leave, ask it where it means to take you. The arguments are real, and the answers to objections set them out for a day when your mind is clear. But you didn’t come to faith by argument alone. The Confession says in 1.5 that our full persuasion of the truth of Scripture comes from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts. So when doubt comes, go back to the Word, and pray as a desperate father once prayed. And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. Mark 9:24 (KJV) He had just admitted he wasn’t sure Jesus could help. Jesus healed his son anyway. He didn’t first make the man measure how much of him believed.

title: Doubts and Unwanted Thoughts
section: I have thoughts I would never choose
text: I have thoughts I would never choose It may be a blasphemy that flashes through your mind in prayer. The harder you push it away, the louder it comes back. John Bunyan, who later wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress, went through a season like this. Blasphemies against God and Christ poured through his mind until he feared he was lost. His book Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners tells the story. He came through it and preached Christ for the rest of his life. A thought that frightens you may have entered your mind without your consent. Ask whether you've embraced it or resisted it, and speak to an elder when you need counsel. A thought you hate isn’t a thought you hold. Satan once told the Son of God himself to fall down and worship the devil, and Christ was without sin ( Matthew 4:9-10 ). Being tempted isn’t the same as sinning. Whatever in these thoughts rises from the old nature still in you is pardoned in Christ with the rest of your sin. Your horror at them shows where your heart is. Temptation and consent to sin must be distinguished ( Hebrews 4:15 and James 1:14-15 ). So don’t argue with them or keep checking whether you meant them. Turn from them to Christ, the way you’d walk past a man shouting in the street. If they come in a loop you can’t break, don’t keep them secret. See a doctor, and if you’re young, tell your parents first. It’s a known problem, sometimes a form of OCD, and there’s real help for it.

title: Doubts and Unwanted Thoughts
text: When Doubts Keep Returning Write down your hardest question. Then read the page in the answers to objections that speaks to it, on a morning when you’re rested. Read one Gospel straight through. Mark is short enough to read in an evening or two. Look at Jesus himself, not only the arguments about him. Don’t fight unwanted thoughts head on. When one comes, say a short prayer like Mark 9:24 and go on with what you were doing. Don’t go back to check it. Tell someone. Tell your pastor, an elder, or a parent. If the thoughts come in loops, ask your doctor about OCD.

title: Is God Punishing Me?
text: The diagnosis comes, or the child dies, or the marriage comes apart. Under the grief a harder question rises, about what God thinks of you.

title: Is God Punishing Me?
section: It feels as if God is against me
text: It feels as if God is against me Paul asks who can be against us if God is for us, and he answers with the cross. He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Romans 8:32 (KJV) God has already given the most he had to give. If he meant you harm, he wouldn’t have paid so much for you. A few verses earlier Paul says all things work together for good to those who love God. He doesn’t say all things are good. Many aren’t, and you may be living inside one. Romans 8:29 tells you what the good is. God means to make you like his Son. For the Lord will not cast off for ever: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men. Lamentations 3:31-33 (KJV) He does bring grief, but he takes no pleasure in it, and his compassion outlasts it. You may weep. Jesus wept over Lazarus, though he knew he was about to raise him.

title: Is God Punishing Me?
section: I think he is punishing me
text: I think he is punishing me The punishment for a believer’s sin fell on Christ, and God doesn’t collect the same debt twice. What a believer may receive is chastening. That’s the training a father gives the son he loves. Hebrews 12 says God does it for our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness. No chastening feels joyful at the time, but afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness. God disciplines his children without casting them away ( WCF 12.1 ). But not every illness, loss, or disappointment is correction for a particular sin. When the disciples asked whose sin had made a man born blind, Jesus said it was neither his nor his parents’ ( John 9:3 ). You may never learn in this life why a thing was sent. You can know it wasn’t sent in wrath. For Scripture gathered by the kind of loss, a death or a diagnosis or a broken marriage, see Grief and Hard Times .

title: Is God Punishing Me?
text: While You Endure This Tell God how it feels. Be honest. The psalms are full of believers asking why. Read Psalm 13 and pray it as your own. If a sin comes to mind, confess it and move on. Don’t dig for a hidden cause behind every hard thing. If nothing comes to mind, don’t invent one. Let people help. Tell your elders and your church what you’re facing. Say yes when someone offers a meal or a ride. Handle the practical things one at a time. Make the call, pay the bill, keep the appointment. Ask God for strength for today’s list, not next month’s.

title: Afraid of Dying
text: Christians still die, and many of them dread it. Hebrews says the Son of God took flesh and blood for this very reason.

title: Afraid of Dying
text: When Death Frightens You Call for your elders. James 5 says the sick should call for the elders of the church to pray over them. Don’t wait until the last days to ask. Tell your family where your hope is. Say it in your own words, or write it in a letter they can keep. Put your affairs in order. Make or update a will, name who should make medical decisions for you, and write down what you want for your funeral. It’s a kindness to the people you leave. Learn one passage by heart. Psalm 23 or John 14:1-3 is a good place to start. Have it ready for the hard nights.

title: Will God Keep Me to the End?
text: Underneath all these fears is the same suspicion, that in the end it all hangs on you. Paul closes Romans 8 by naming everything that could come between a believer and God. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 8:38-39 (KJV) Paul doesn’t say you're kept by your love for God. He says nothing can separate you from God’s love for you, and that love is in Christ Jesus our Lord, where no fear of yours can reach it. When Zion said the Lord had forgotten her, God answered through Isaiah. Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me. Isaiah 49:15-16 (KJV) Moses, blessing Israel before his death, told them that the eternal God was their refuge and that underneath were the everlasting arms ( Deuteronomy 33:27 ).
