On the nights you can’t hold on to anything, that’s still where you are. God preserves his people by sustaining their faith and repentance through the means he has appointed ( WCF 17.1-2 and 14.1). A believer may stumble badly, but the Lord won't leave him finally hardened and lost. His promises give strength to obey the commands to persevere. Do these things while you wait for the fear to lift. Seek counsel about the Lord’s Table. Question 172 of the Larger Catechism says the Supper was appointed for the relief even of weak and doubting Christians. One who doubts should mourn his unbelief and labor to have his doubts resolved, and as he does, he may and ought to come, so that his faith is made stronger. Take your doubts to your elders. The counsel of question 172 is for those who mourn their unbelief and sincerely seek Christ, not those persisting without repentance. Self-examination and the church's oversight still matter ( WLC 171-173 ). Keep sitting under the preached Word. The Word that first worked your faith is how God goes on strengthening it ( WCF 14.1 ). This page can’t feed you week by week. A faithful pulpit can. If you don’t yet belong to a church with a pulpit like that, find one and join it. Go even when you feel nothing. Pray Mark 9:24 honestly. Tell him you believe and ask him to help your unbelief. Ask again tomorrow. Learn a few places in Scripture you can find in the dark. Romans 8 answers the accuser. Psalm 103 speaks to shame, and John 10 to the fear that you will slip from his hand. Isaiah 40 opens with God commanding comfort for his people. A few verses on, Isaiah sees the Lord God come with a strong hand, his arm ruling for him. The next thing that arm does is gather lambs. He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young. Isaiah 40:11 (KJV)

title: Guides
text: Find help for daily Christian life. Choose a topic or search the guides below.

title: Guides
text: Before you begin About These Guides Practical teaching for things Christians have to do or decide. Some pages give a brief answer. Others take time to work through. Choose what you need today. They aren’t a new rule. Scripture is the rule, and the Westminster Confession and Catechisms are the summary of it this site holds. These guides only put that teaching into plain steps. Where a guide says more than Scripture says, trust Scripture and leave the guide. Each guide stands on its own. Browse by topic, or use the search to find one answer. None of them replaces your elders. Take hard questions to the men Christ set over you. If you have no church yet, start with How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Pray
text: What prayer is, how to pray through Christ, the Lord’s Prayer as a pattern, and the habits that keep a believer praying.

title: How to Pray
text: What Prayer Is Prayer is an offering up of our desires unto God, for things agreeable to his will, in the name of Christ, with confession of our sins, and thankful acknowledgment of his mercies. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 98 That one answer holds most of what you need. Prayer is asking. It asks for what God has said he wills. It comes through Christ, because no sinner can come to God any other way ( John 14:6 , Hebrews 4:14-16 ). And it’s honest about sin and thankful for mercy. God doesn’t need fine words. He hears through his Son, and his Spirit helps you when you don’t know what to say ( Romans 8:26 ). So pray plainly.

title: How to Pray
text: How to Pray Come in Christ’s name. To pray in Christ's name is to approach God through his sacrifice and intercession ( Hebrews 10:19-22 ). If you’ve never come to Christ, start there. The gospel tells you how. Start with God, not your list. Say who he is and thank him for what he’s done. Jesus taught us to begin, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name ( Matthew 6:9 ). Confess your sins by name. Name the sins you know of. Confess the sins you know, and come to the Father rather than delaying prayer through endless self-examination. He is faithful and just to forgive ( 1 John 1:9 ). Ask for what you need. Daily bread, help against a particular sin, wisdom for a decision, the salvation of someone you love. Ask plainly and specifically ( Philippians 4:6 ). Pray for others. Your family, your church and its elders, the persecuted church, those in authority ( 1 Timothy 2:1-2 ), and your enemies ( Matthew 5:44 ). Leave the answer with him. Ask, and then submit, as Christ did in the garden, Not my will, but thine, be done ( Luke 22:42 ).

title: How to Pray
section: Use the Lord’s Prayer as the Pattern
text: Use the Lord’s Prayer as the Pattern The Shorter Catechism says the Lord’s Prayer is given as a direction for prayer (Q&A 99). Each line teaches you what to ask. Our Father which art in heaven. Come with reverence and with a child’s confidence. Hallowed be thy name. Ask that God be honored, in you and everywhere. Thy kingdom come. Ask for the gospel to go out, for sinners to be converted, and for Christ’s return. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Ask for willing obedience, yours first. Give us this day our daily bread. Ask for what this day needs, and leave tomorrow with him ( Matthew 6:34 ). Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Ask for pardon, and forgive the people who wronged you. Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Ask to be kept from sin and from the evil one.

title: How to Pray
text: What Displeases God in Prayer Empty repetition. Jesus warned against vain repetitions, as the heathen do ( Matthew 6:7 ). Saying the same words isn’t the problem. Saying them without meaning them is. Praying to be seen. Do not pray to impress anyone ( Matthew 6:5-6 ). Holding on to a sin you mean to keep. If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me ( Psalm 66:18 ). Let go of it, then pray. Praying to anyone but God. Not to saints, not to angels, not to Mary. Prayer is part of worship, and it belongs to God alone, through the one mediator, Christ ( 1 Timothy 2:5 , WCF 21.2 ). Treating God like a vending machine. Faith asks boldly and trusts him with the answer ( James 1:5-7 , 4:3).

title: How to Pray
text: Make It a Habit Pick a time and a place. The old advice is morning, before the house wakes. Any set time is better than none ( Psalm 5:3 , Mark 1:35 ). Pray with your Bible open. Read a passage, then turn what it says into prayer. Pray with your household. Even a few minutes after supper. See How to Lead Family Worship . Pray with the church. Join the public prayers on the Lord’s Day and the prayer meeting if your church has one. Keep a short list. Names and needs, so you remember to pray and to give thanks when God answers. When you can’t pray at all, read a psalm aloud and make it your prayer. Psalm 13 , Psalm 51 , and Psalm 86 are good places to start. If God feels far away, read When God Feels Far .

title: How to Read the Bible
text: How to read Scripture with understanding, where to start, and which helps are worth having.

title: How to Read the Bible
text: Why Read It Yourself The Bible is God speaking. It's enough to make you wise unto salvation and to equip you for every good work ( 2 Timothy 3:15-17 ). Hearing it preached on the Lord’s Day comes first, but God also commands his people to read it, to know it, and to teach it at home ( Deuteronomy 6:6-7 , Acts 17:11 , WLC 156 ). See How to Lead Family Worship . Begin with a book of Scripture and read it in its context. Ask your pastor when a passage troubles you. The things you must know to be saved are set out plainly. An ordinary reader, using ordinary means, can understand them ( WCF 1.7 ).

title: How to Read the Bible
text: How to Read It The Larger Catechism says the Scriptures are to be read with a high and reverent esteem of them, with a firm persuasion that they're the very Word of God, with desire to know and obey, with diligence, and with prayer (Q&A 157). In plain steps, that comes to this. Pray before you read. Ask God to open your eyes ( Psalm 119:18 ). Read whole books. Each book was written to be read through. Don’t hop between favorite verses. Read slowly enough to notice. Ask what it says, what it means, and what it asks of you. Let clear places explain hard ones. Scripture is its own interpreter ( WCF 1.9 ). When a verse is hard, find other places that say the same thing more plainly. Look for Christ. The whole Bible points to him ( Luke 24:27 , John 5:39 ). Do what it says. Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only ( James 1:22 ). Write down one thing to obey or believe today.

title: How to Read the Bible
text: Where to Start If you’re new, start with the Gospel of Mark or John, then Acts, then Romans, then Genesis. Read a Psalm each day alongside. If you want the whole Bible, use a plan. Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s takes you through the Old Testament once and the New Testament and Psalms twice in a year. Two chapters a day will get you through in about a year and a half. If you fall behind, skip to today’s reading and keep going. A plan is a help, not a law.

title: How to Read the Bible
text: Helps Worth Having A faithful translation. This site quotes the King James Version. The ESV and the NASB are careful modern translations. A good commentary. Matthew Henry is warm and plain. Calvin is careful and deep. Read the text first and the commentary second. The Shorter Catechism. It shows you how the parts of the Bible fit together. Your pastor. Bring your questions to him. That’s part of what he is for. Sojourner , the free study program made by this ministry, puts the Bible, Henry, Calvin, and the Westminster Standards side by side on your phone or computer.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: What biblical meditation is, a simple way to think a verse through, and how a busy believer can hide God’s Word in his heart.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: What Meditation Is and Isn't But his delight is in the law of the Lord ; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. Psalm 1:2-3 (KJV) To meditate on Scripture is to fill your mind with what God has said. You think it through until it reaches your heart and hands. God told Joshua that the book of the law shouldn't depart out of his mouth, but that he should meditate therein day and night, that he might observe to do it ( Joshua 1:8 ). The psalmist said, O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day ( Psalm 119:97 ). He grew wiser than his enemies and his teachers because God’s testimonies were always on his mind ( Psalm 119:98-99 ). This differs from practices that seek to empty the mind. Eastern religion, and much of what is sold as mindfulness, aims to quiet or empty the mind. Biblical meditation gives sustained attention to what God has actually said. Paul names what to think on, whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, and lovely, and he tells you to think on these things ( Philippians 4:8 ). Nothing is truer or lovelier than the Word of God. The Shorter Catechism puts it in one phrase. We're to lay up the Word in our hearts (Q&A 90). The Larger Catechism says Scripture is to be read with meditation, and it gives Psalm 1 and Psalm 119:97 as its proof (Q&A 157). The Puritans took this seriously. Thomas Watson wrote a whole treatise on it, A Christian on the Mount, and pressed it on ordinary believers as a daily duty. Richard Baxter gave much of The Saints’ Everlasting Rest to it. He taught Christians to set their thoughts on heaven and press its truths on their own hearts.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: The Tree by the Rivers Psalm 1 uses a picture. The man isn’t a tree, but what the tree pictures is real. A tree by a river doesn’t go looking for water. Its roots already reach it, so it keeps drinking when the season is dry, and shall not be careful in the year of drought ( Jeremiah 17:8 ). So the man whose mind lives in God’s Word is fed by it when trouble comes. He bears fruit in his season, which means steady growth over years, not a show every morning. This is no promise of wealth. It promises that a life rooted in God’s Word is never wasted. Only one man ever delighted in God’s law perfectly, and that’s Christ. Those who trust him are planted in him, and his Word is the river they drink from.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
section: How to Meditate on a Verse
text: How to Meditate on a Verse Read it slowly, more than once. Read it aloud if you can. Lean on a different word each time. Ask what it says of God, and of Christ. Every verse shows something of him. Ask what it commands. Is there a duty here, or a sin to leave? Ask what it promises. What has God bound himself to do? Turn it into prayer. Give the verse back to God as thanks, confession, and asking. See How to Pray . One Verse Worked Through The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Psalm 23:1 (KJV) Of God. The Lord is his covenant name, the God who bound himself to his people by promise. A shepherd leads, feeds, and guards. And he is my shepherd, not only the church’s in general. Of Christ. Jesus took this name for himself and said, I am the good shepherd, and the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep ( John 10:11 ). The shepherd of this psalm died for his flock and rose again. The command. There’s no command in the words, but one lies under them. I am to trust him and be content with such things as I have ( Hebrews 13:5 ). The promise. I shall not want. Not every wish, but nothing that I truly need for body and soul. My God shall supply all your need ( Philippians 4:19 ). The prayer. It might run like this. Lord, you're my shepherd. Thank you that Christ laid down his life for me. Forgive me for worrying about money this week as if I had no shepherd. Give me what I need today and make me content with it. That takes a few minutes, and the verse goes with you all day.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: Why and How to Memorize Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee. Psalm 119:11 (KJV) Memory is the storehouse meditation draws from. You can’t think on a verse at a red light if it’s on a shelf at home. Paul says, Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly ( Colossians 3:16 ). When Christ was tempted in the wilderness, hungry after forty days, he answered Satan three times with It is written, each time from Deuteronomy ( Matthew 4:1-11 ). He fought with words he already carried. You'll need them too. You don’t need a great memory. You need a small amount, done often. One short verse at a time. A verse a week is plenty. One that stays beats ten that leak out. Write it out. Put it on an index card in your pocket, or make it your phone’s lock screen. Say it aloud. The mouth helps the memory. Say the reference too. Hook it to something you already do. Say it while the coffee brews or while you lace your boots. Use the Catechism’s proof texts. Learn a Shorter Catechism answer with one of the verses given to prove it. Each holds the other in place. Review the old ones. Once a week, run back through what you’ve learned. Learn it with your family. Say the week’s verse at supper or in family worship . Children learn fast and will hold you to it.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: Use the Small Moments Most days won’t give you a quiet hour. You don’t need one. God told Israel to talk of his words when thou walkest by the way ( Deuteronomy 6:7 ). For you the way may be the drive to work. Turn the radio off for five minutes and say your verse. On a break, look at the card instead of the news. On a walk, take one phrase and ask the questions above. When you lie awake, meditate on him in the night watches ( Psalm 63:6 ). Your mind will wander. That isn’t failure. Notice it and bring your thoughts back to the verse without scolding yourself. Each return is part of the work. If you miss a day or a week, don’t try to catch up. Start again today. He knoweth our frame ( Psalm 103:14 ). Meditation doesn’t earn God’s favor. It’s how a forgiven child listens to his Father. If you don’t yet know him, begin with the gospel . Meditation grows out of steady reading, so see How to Read the Bible too.

title: How to Meditate on and Memorize Scripture
text: This Week Pick one verse. Psalm 23:1 , Psalm 119:11 , or a verse from this Sunday’s sermon. Write it on a card tonight. Put it by your keys. Work through it once. Use the five steps above, ending in prayer. Choose one small moment. Pick the commute or a break, and say the verse there every day. Say it to your family. At supper on Friday, see who can say it. Start the review list. On the Lord’s Day, write the verse in a notebook. Next week, add another and say both.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Questions from Scripture and the Larger Catechism to ask yourself, how to do it each day, and how not to drown in it.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Why Examine Yourself Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? 2 Corinthians 13:5 (KJV) Scripture commands it in two places especially. Paul tells the church to examine whether they're in the faith, and he tells every communicant to examine himself before he eats of the Lord’s Supper ( 1 Corinthians 11:28 ). The aim isn’t to torment yourself. It’s to find sin and kill it, to find grace and thank God for it, and to come to Christ again.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Look at Christ First Don’t start by grading yourself. Start with the promise. God has promised everlasting life to everyone who believes on the Son ( John 3:36 ). Your standing rests on Christ and what he finished, not on how the examination turns out. Then look inward with an honest eye. The Confession grounds assurance on three things. They're the truth of God’s promises of salvation, the inward evidence of the graces those promises are made to, and the witness of the Spirit of adoption with our spirits ( WCF 18.2 ). Begin with the promises. If you begin with yourself, you'll find a reason to doubt everything. Saving faith and the assurance of it aren’t the same thing. A true believer may wait long and fight hard before he is sure. Lack of assurance doesn’t prove that faith is absent ( WCF 18.3 ). You're saved by trusting Christ, not by feeling sure that you trust him. Self-examination is a duty. Its aim is to send you back to Christ, not to keep you staring at yourself.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Questions to Ask The Larger Catechism lists what to examine before the Lord’s Supper (Q&A 171). It makes a good set of questions for any day. Am I in Christ? Am I trusting him alone, and not my own goodness, my church membership, or a prayer I once prayed? What are my sins and my needs? Name them. Where have I sinned in thought, word, and deed today? Do I know the truth? Do I understand the gospel well enough to say it plainly? Is there repentance? Do I hate my sin because it is sin, and not only because of what it costs me? Am I turning from it? Do I love God and his people? Do I love the brethren, and am I kind to all men? Have I forgiven those who wronged me? Is there a grudge I’m keeping? Do I want Christ? Is there a desire for him, and for more of him? Am I obeying? Is there new obedience, even weak and uneven, that wasn’t there before? The Ten Commandments are the best mirror for the second question. Go through them one at a time. The Ten Commandments for a Believer sets out what each one requires and forbids.

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: How to Do It Pray first. Search me, O God, and know my heart ( Psalm 139:23 ). Ask God to show you what you would rather not see. Be specific. Name the sin, the time, and the person. Vague confession leads to vague repentance ( WCF 15.5 ). Keep it short each day. A few minutes at night is enough. Look back over the day, confess, give thanks, and go to bed. Go deeper before the Lord’s Supper. Take longer in the days before communion. The Catechism directs communicants to prepare themselves before they come (Q&A 171). Make it right. If you wronged someone, confess it to them and repair what you can ( Matthew 5:23-24 ). End at the cross. Every examination should end with Christ freely offered and freely received. If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father ( 1 John 2:1 ).

title: How to Examine Yourself
text: Two Cautions Don’t skip it. A man who never looks at himself can live for years in a sin he would see in a minute if he looked. The Puritan John Owen warned that a man who finds no fight in himself against his sin is at peace with it, not dying to it. If You Have Made Peace With It speaks to that man. Don’t drown in it. Some believers turn self-examination into an endless loop of checking whether they really meant it. If that’s you, keep the searching short and the looking to Christ long. Read Am I Really Saved? If the same thoughts keep coming whether you want them or not, read thoughts you would never choose . Tell your elders too.

title: How to Repent
text: What repentance unto life is, godly and worldly sorrow, confessing sins by name, making things right, and coming home again.

title: How to Repent
text: What Repentance Is Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 87 It’s God’s gift ( Acts 11:18 ), and it’s still your own turning, which he commands of you ( Mark 1:15 ). The answer holds five things. A true sense of sin. Not only its danger but its filthiness, because it is against God’s holy nature and law ( WCF 15.2 ). A man who only fears hell is sorry about the danger. An apprehension of God’s mercy in Christ. Without it, a sight of sin drives a man to hiding or despair. There is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared ( Psalm 130:4 ). Grief and hatred of sin. You grieve that you did it, and you hate the thing itself, not only what it cost you. Turning from it unto God. Away from the sin and toward him, and from all your sins, not only the one that shamed you ( WCF 15.2 ). Full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience. You mean to obey, and you begin. The purpose is whole even when the obedience is weak. Repentance isn’t penance. It’s no satisfaction for sin and no cause of pardon. Pardon is the act of God’s free grace in Christ ( WCF 15.3 ). Your tears don’t wash you. Christ’s blood does ( 1 John 1:7 ). Yet none may expect pardon without repentance. Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish ( Luke 13:3 ). A man who says he trusts Christ while he means to keep his sin doesn’t yet know whom he is trusting.

title: How to Repent
text: Two Kinds of Sorrow For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. 2 Corinthians 7:10 (KJV) Paul was glad the Corinthians sorrowed to repentance, because it made them earnest to set things right (verses 9-11). Judas and Peter both sinned against Christ on the same night. Judas repented himself, brought back the silver, and said, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood ( Matthew 27:3-4 ). The words were true. But he took his sorrow to the priests and not to Christ, and he went out and hanged himself ( Matthew 27:5 ). Peter denied his Lord three times. Then the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter, and Peter went out, and wept bitterly ( Luke 22:61-62 ). His sorrow brought him back, and Christ restored him ( John 21:15-17 ). The difference wasn’t how much they hurt. It was where they carried the hurt. Worldly sorrow grieves over loss and shame and turns in on itself. Godly sorrow runs to God for mercy. If you’re in that darkness now, hear this carefully. Thoughts of ending your life don’t prove that your repentance is false or that you aren’t his. Deep depression is often an illness of body and mind, and true believers have been crushed by it (read When You Are Depressed ). But any voice that tells you Christ won’t have you, or that death is the way out, is lying to you about him. Christ looked at Peter to call him back, and he hasn’t stopped looking for you. Tell someone today, and if those thoughts press on you, call 988 or text 988 .

title: How to Repent
text: Repent of Sins by Name The Confession calls every man to repent of his particular sins particularly ( WCF 15.5 ). Saying “I am a sinner” costs nothing. Saying what you did costs something. David’s prayer after Bathsheba is the pattern. He begins with God’s mercy, not his record ( Psalm 51:1 ). Then he owns the sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Psalm 51:3 (KJV) He had wronged Uriah terribly, yet he says, Against thee, thee only, have I sinned (verse 4), because every sin is first against God. He asks to be washed (verse 2), for a clean heart (verse 10), and for the joy of salvation to come back (verse 12). And he knows God won't despise a broken and a contrite heart (verse 17). Confess to God first. Then confess to those you’ve wronged, who are to receive you in love ( WCF 15.6 , Matthew 5:23-24 ). Where you took something, give it back. Zacchaeus said, if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold ( Luke 19:8 ). The law asked for the thing returned and a fifth added ( Numbers 5:7 ). If you lied about someone, tell the truth to those who heard it. Some wrongs can’t be undone. Some confessions would only wound again or put someone in danger. Ask an elder how and when.

title: How to Repent
section: Coming Home, and Coming Home Again
text: Coming Home, and Coming Home Again Christ taught us to ask for forgiveness in the same prayer as our daily bread, Forgive us our debts ( Matthew 6:11-12 ). A believer keeps falling and keeps returning. That doesn’t prove you never repented. It’s what repentance looks like while sin remains ( WCF 13.2 ). If the same sin keeps winning, read When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back , and for the long fight, Struggling With Sin . Mortify can help you confess daily and fight alongside friends from your church. And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. Luke 15:20 (KJV) Jesus told the story of the prodigal son because the Pharisees murmured that he received sinners ( Luke 15:1-2 ). Jesus uses the son’s return to show the Father’s welcome for repentant sinners. The son came to himself and went home to say, Father, I've sinned (verses 17-18). He meant to ask to be a hired servant, but his father never let him finish. He called for the robe, the ring, and the feast, for this my son was dead, and is alive again (verses 19-24). That’s how the Father receives a sinner who comes home through his Son. If You Fear You've Repented Too Many Times Christ told his disciples that if a brother sins against them seven times in a day, and seven times turns again saying, I repent, they must forgive him ( Luke 17:4 ). He doesn’t ask more mercy of us than he shows. Your pardon never rested on your count. It rests on his blood, and he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him ( Hebrews 7:25 ). A heart that has hardened itself against God doesn’t usually lie awake afraid of losing him. So come again tonight. Don’t wait until you’ve stopped falling.

title: How to Repent
text: Steps for Today Come to Christ first. Repentance without him is only regret. If you’ve never trusted him, read the gospel and come today. Name the sin. Before God, say what you did and against whom. How to Examine Yourself can help you see it. Pray Psalm 51 aloud. Then believe the promise. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins ( 1 John 1:9 ). Make it right this week. Go to the person you wronged. Pay back what you took. Cut off the supply. Make not provision for the flesh ( Romans 13:14 ). Change what made the sin easy, and tell an elder or a trusted brother ( James 5:16 ). Do it again tomorrow. A few minutes each night, looking back over the day, keeps short accounts with God.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: Why a forgiven Christian still keeps God’s law, how to read it, what each commandment requires and forbids, and how to use them this week.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
section: Why a Believer Keeps the Law
text: Why a Believer Keeps the Law You aren’t saved by keeping the commandments. Christ kept them in your place, and he bore the curse for every one you broke ( Galatians 3:13 ). A believer is free from the law as a way to earn life. But he isn’t free from the law as a rule for how to live. The Confession says the moral law binds all men forever, believers included. It's a rule of life that shows them the will of God and their duty ( WCF 19.5-6 ). The law tells a forgiven man what love looks like. If ye love me, keep my commandments. John 14:15 (KJV) So you obey because you’re loved, never to become loved. And when you fail, the law sends you back to Christ. That’s one of the things it’s for.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: How to Read Them The Larger Catechism gives rules for reading the commandments (Q&A 99). Four of them do most of the work. They reach the heart. The law governs thoughts and desires, not only actions. Jesus said lust is adultery in the heart and hatred is murder in the heart ( Matthew 5:21-28 ). Every command has two sides. Where a sin is forbidden, the opposite duty is commanded. Where a duty is commanded, the opposite sin is forbidden. Thou shalt not steal also means work, and give ( Ephesians 4:28 ). One sin stands for a whole family. Murder covers anger, contempt, and reckless driving. Adultery covers lust, pornography, and immodesty. The causes and occasions are forbidden too. Whatever leads you toward the sin is part of what the command forbids.

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
text: Each Commandment in Plain Words The Shorter Catechism sets out what each one requires and forbids (Q&A 45-81). This is a short version. Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Know, worship, trust, and love the true God alone. Forbidden are atheism, false gods, and anything you love or trust more than him, including money, comfort, and approval. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image. Worship God only in the ways he has commanded in his Word. Forbidden are images of God and any worship men invent for themselves. This is where the Reformed regulative principle of worship comes from ( WCF 21.1 ). See How God Wants to Be Worshiped . Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain. Use God’s names, titles, Word, and works with reverence. Forbidden are cursing, careless use of his name, false oaths, and mocking holy things. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Set apart one whole day in seven for God, now the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Honour thy father and thy mother. Give honor and obedience to parents and to everyone God has set over you, in the home, the church, and the state. Care for those under you. Forbidden are contempt, rebellion, and abuse of authority. Thou shalt not kill. Preserve your own life and the lives of others. Forbidden are murder, abortion , suicide, unjust anger, hatred, and neglect of your body or anyone in your care. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Keep yourself and others chaste in heart, speech, and behavior. Forbidden are sex outside of marriage, pornography, lustful thoughts, and immodest dress or talk. Thou shalt not steal. Get and keep goods honestly, and work to provide for yourself and others. Forbidden are theft, cheating, laziness, waste, and gambling away what God gave you. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. Speak the truth and guard your neighbor’s good name. Forbidden are lies, slander, gossip, and flattery. Thou shalt not covet. Be content with what God gave you and glad for your neighbor’s good. Forbidden are envy, discontent, and wanting what is his. The full text is in Exodus 20:1-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21 .

title: The Ten Commandments for a Believer
section: How to Use Them This Week
text: How to Use Them This Week Learn them. Memorize the ten, then the Shorter Catechism’s questions on each. Teach them to your children. Examine yourself by them. Take one commandment each evening for ten days. Ask what it requires and what it forbids, and where you stand. See How to Examine Yourself . Pray them. Turn each one into a request for help to obey, and a confession where you haven’t. Run to Christ. No mere man since the fall is able in this life perfectly to keep the commandments of God ( WSC 82 ). When the law shows you your sin, it’s pointing you to the Savior who kept it for you. If one commandment keeps exposing the same sin, Struggling With Sin is written for that fight.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: The regulative principle in plain words. God decides how he is worshiped, what he has commanded, what that rules out, and why it matters.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: The Principle God decides how he is to be worshiped. We don’t. In worship we may do what he has commanded in Scripture, and nothing else. The Reformed churches call this the regulative principle of worship. But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture. Westminster Confession of Faith 21.1 Most churches work by a different rule. They hold that whatever Scripture doesn’t forbid may be used in worship. The Reformed rule is narrower. Whatever Scripture doesn’t command is left out. The question is never whether something is forbidden. It’s whether God asked for it.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Where Scripture Teaches It The second commandment. God forbids worshiping him by images or by any means of our own making ( Exodus 20:4-6 ). The Larger Catechism says it forbids all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and any wise approving any religious worship not instituted by God himself (Q&A 109). Nadab and Abihu. Two priests offered strange fire before the Lord , which he commanded them not, and fire from the Lord devoured them ( Leviticus 10:1-2 ). The text doesn’t say what rule they broke. It says they offered what he commanded them not, that is, what he had not commanded. Add nothing, take nothing away. God told Israel to observe what he commanded, and not to add thereto, nor diminish from it ( Deuteronomy 12:32 ). Worship that God never asked for. Through Jeremiah God condemned worship which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart ( Jeremiah 7:31 ). Jesus on the traditions of men. In vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men ( Matthew 15:9 ). Paul on will-worship. He warned against worship men devise for themselves, however humble or devout it looks ( Colossians 2:20-23 ).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What God Has Commanded The Confession lists the parts of ordinary worship, which are called its elements ( WCF 21.3-5 ). Prayer, with thanksgiving, in the name of Christ. The reading of Scripture with godly fear. Preaching of the Word, and hearing it with understanding, faith, and reverence. Singing of psalms with grace in the heart. The sacraments, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, rightly given and worthily received. On special occasions the Confession adds religious oaths, vows, solemn fastings, and thanksgivings. Giving to the Lord and the benediction belong to the service as well ( 1 Corinthians 16:1-2 , Numbers 6:24-26 , 2 Corinthians 13:14 ).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Elements and Circumstances The principle doesn’t mean Scripture must tell you what time to meet, how long the sermon runs, or whether to sit in pews. Those are circumstances, things common to any gathering of people. The Confession says they're to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word ( WCF 1.6 ). The test is simple. An element is a thing done as worship, and it needs a command. A circumstance is only how and when the commanded thing is done, and it needs good sense and good order ( 1 Corinthians 14:40 ).

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What It Means in Practice No images of God. No pictures, statues, or films of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit, in worship or out of it ( WLC 109 ). No holy days of men’s making. God appointed the Lord’s Day. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship says no other day is commanded to be kept holy. No entertainment in place of worship. No drama, dance, light shows, or performances. Worship isn’t a show for the congregation. It’s the congregation meeting God. The Word at the center. Reading and preaching aren’t a short segment between songs. They are the heart of the service. Psalms, sung without instruments. The Reformed Presbyterian churches sing only the Psalms in worship, without instruments. God gave his church a book of praise, the Psalms, and commanded it to be sung ( Colossians 3:16 , James 5:13 ). The instruments of the Old Testament were appointed for the temple and its sacrifices ( 2 Chronicles 29:25-28 ). They passed away with them when Christ fulfilled them. The New Testament church is told to sing, making melody in your heart to the Lord ( Ephesians 5:19 ). That last point is where Presbyterians who hold the same principle part ways. Many sing hymns and use instruments, and they're brothers. This site holds what the Reformed Presbyterian churches hold. It holds it as a conviction from Scripture, not as a matter of taste.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Why It Matters It honors God. He is the one being worshiped. He has the right to say how. It frees your conscience. God alone is Lord of the conscience ( WCF 20.2 ). No pastor or church can bind you to worship God in a way he never asked for. It keeps the church from drifting. Once worship is open to anything not forbidden, there’s no line. Each generation adds what the last one wouldn’t have dreamed of. It keeps Christ central. The things God commanded, the Word, the sacraments, and prayer, are the means by which Christ gives his grace ( WSC 88 ). Men’s additions crowd them out.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: Common Objections It’s legalistic. Legalism tries to earn God’s favor by works. This asks how a forgiven people should come to the God who already accepted them in Christ. Obeying his instructions for worship isn’t earning anything. It’s love ( John 14:15 ). The New Testament doesn’t give a worship manual. It gives enough. It shows the apostolic church reading, preaching, praying, singing, giving, and keeping the sacraments ( Acts 2:42 , 1 Corinthians 11 , 14, 16:1-2, 1 Timothy 4:13 ). Those are what Reformed worship does. God looks at the heart. He does, and he also told us what to do. Nadab and Abihu were priests offering incense to the true God. Sincerity doesn’t make strange fire acceptable.

title: How God Wants to Be Worshiped
text: What to Do Read WCF 21 with your Bible open. Check every proof text. Look at your church’s worship. For each part of the service, ask where God commanded it. Raise honest questions with your elders, kindly. Learn the Psalms. Sing them at home, in family worship , until you know many of them by heart. Come prepared on the Lord’s Day. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day .

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Why preaching matters, what God asks of a hearer, the four kinds of ground, and how to carry the Word home.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Why Preaching Matters The Spirit of God maketh the reading, but especially the preaching of the Word, an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners, and of building them up in holiness and comfort, through faith, unto salvation. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 89 Notice the word especially. Reading the Bible at home is a great gift. But God has made the preached Word his chief means of saving sinners and growing saints. The Larger Catechism says he uses it to drive sinners out of themselves and draw them unto Christ (Q&A 155). How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God ( Romans 10:14-17 ). A minister lawfully called is sent. Such men are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us ( 2 Corinthians 5:20 ). When he opens the Scriptures faithfully, you aren’t hearing one man’s opinions. You’re hearing God calling you to be reconciled to him. Yet the ambassador is still a man, and he must be tested. The Bereans received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so ( Acts 17:11 ).

title: How to Hear a Sermon
section: What God Asks of a Hearer
text: What God Asks of a Hearer The Larger Catechism sets out what God requires of hearers (Q&A 160). Attend with diligence, preparation, and prayer. Come ready, having asked God to bless what you will hear. Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear ( Ecclesiastes 5:1 ). Examine what you hear by the Scriptures. Keep your Bible open and ask whether the sermon says what the passage says. Receive the truth with faith, love, meekness, and readiness of mind, as the Word of God. Don’t sit as a critic waiting to grade the preacher. The Thessalonians received the word not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God ( 1 Thessalonians 2:13 ). Meditate and confer of it. Think it over afterward, and talk about it with others. Hide it in your heart. Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee ( Psalm 119:11 ). Bring forth the fruit of it in your life. The duty of hearing continues as you remember the passage and obey it through the week. It’s finished when you obey it.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Four Kinds of Hearers Jesus told of a sower whose seed fell on four kinds of ground, and then explained it himself ( Luke 8:4-15 ). The seed is the word of God ( Luke 8:11 ). The ground is the heart of the one who hears. Some hear, and the devil takes the word away. Some receive it with joy but have no root, and fall away in trouble. In some the cares and riches and pleasures of this life choke it. And some, in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience ( Luke 8:15 ). The seed, the birds, the rock, and the thorns are pictures. What they picture is real. There’s a real devil who wants you to forget the sermon before lunch. Real cares and pleasures crowd the Word out of real hearts in real pews. Jesus means you to ask which one you are. No heart is good ground by nature. God promised, A new heart also will I give you ( Ezekiel 36:26 ). The Lord opened Lydia’s heart, that she attended unto the things which were spoken ( Acts 16:14 ). If you’ve heard sermons for years and never come to Christ, read the gospel and come to him now. Take heed therefore how ye hear: for whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have. Luke 8:18 (KJV) Hearing is never neutral. The one who receives the Word is given more light. The one who lets it slide past loses even what he thought he had.

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Doers, Not Hearers Only But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed. James 1:22-25 (KJV) The glass is a mirror. It pictures what God’s Word really does. It shows you your true face, your sin and your need. The forgetful hearer glances, walks off, and is the same man on Monday. The doer keeps looking and keeps obeying, and God blesses him in it. A man can love good preaching and still never do what he hears. Ask after each sermon, What did God show me in the mirror, and what will I do about it?

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: When the Sermon Seems Dull Some Sundays the minister will be tired, or the sermon plain and weak. Don’t despise him for it. Look at your own heart first. Before blaming the preaching, examine whether you prepared to hear and prayed for understanding. Did you come prepared? Did you pray? Desire the sincere milk of the word ( 1 Peter 2:2 ), and you will find less to complain of. Remember whose power it is. We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us ( 2 Corinthians 4:7 ). Look for the bread. If the text was read and Christ was set forth, there was food for your soul. Take it home. Pray for him. Paul asked the churches to pray that utterance may be given unto me ( Ephesians 6:19 ). Keep your complaints off the table. Children who hear their parents pick apart the preacher learn to despise the Word. Dull isn’t the same as false. If a minister teaches against Scripture, go humbly to him or to your elders. Read How to Spot a False Teacher . If your church has no faithful preaching at all, read How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: How to Hear a Sermon
text: Steps for This Week Prepare on Saturday night. Get to bed in time. Set aside quarrels and grudges, laying aside all malice ( 1 Peter 2:1 ). If you know the text, read it. Pray for the minister and for all who will hear. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Listen in the pew with your Bible open. Follow the text. When your mind wanders, bring it back without fuss. Bring the children in with you. God told Israel to gather men, and women, and children, that they may hear, and that they may learn ( Deuteronomy 31:12 ). Give each child one thing to listen for, a name, a word, or a question. Don’t expect perfect stillness from little ones. Expect only that they’re there and hear something. Take notes, or do not. Some listen best with a pen, and older children often do. Others find writing pulls them away. Either is fine. The aim is to remember and obey. Talk it over at the Lord’s Day table. What did we learn about God? Where did the sermon point us to Christ? What does God call us to do this week? Let the children answer first. They that feared the Lord spake often one to another ( Malachi 3:16 ). See With Children and How to Lead Family Worship . Pick one thing to do. Name one duty, one sin to fight, or one promise to hold, and come back to it at family worship during the week.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: What the Supper is, what it means to examine yourself, whether a doubting believer may come, and what to do before, at, and after the table.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: What the Supper Is The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament, wherein, by giving and receiving bread and wine, according to Christ’s appointment, his death is showed forth; and the worthy receivers are, not after a corporal and carnal manner, but by faith, made partakers of his body and blood, with all his benefits, to their spiritual nourishment, and growth in grace. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 96 On the night he was betrayed, Jesus gave bread and the cup to his disciples and told his church to keep doing it until he comes ( 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 ). It’s his meal, not ours. The Lord's Supper gives believers spiritual communion with the crucified and risen Christ through faith. The bread and wine stay truly bread and wine, and Christ’s body isn’t in them or under them ( WCF 29.5 , 29.7). But he is present spiritually to the faith of the believer, as really as the bread is present to your hand and mouth. The believer truly feeds on Christ crucified and all the benefits of his death ( WCF 29.7 ). Nor is it a fresh sacrifice. Christ offered himself once for all on the cross, and the Supper remembers that one offering ( WCF 29.2 , Hebrews 10:10-14 ). The bread doesn’t become his body. The Confession calls that teaching, transubstantiation, contrary to Scripture and to common sense ( WCF 29.6 ). So come expecting to meet him by faith.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: Baptism and Communion Baptism is the covenant sign of admission to the visible church. The Supper nourishes communicant members who receive Christ by faith. Read Baptism and Church Membership if you're preparing to join a congregation.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: Let a Man Examine Himself Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 (KJV) Paul wrote to a church that had made the Supper an ordinary meal. Some ate their fill while the poor went hungry, and some were drunk ( 1 Corinthians 11:20-22 ). Those were Corinth’s sins at the table, but Paul’s warning reaches further. To eat unworthily is to come irreverently in any form. It's to come carelessly, or holding to a sin you mean to keep, treating the holy things of Christ as common. It doesn’t mean you must be worthy in yourself before you come. No one is. The word unworthily describes the manner of coming, not the man. A believer who comes grieved over his sin and trusting Christ’s merit alone comes worthily, though he feels himself the least of all. Notice where the command ends. Not stay away, but and so let him eat. Examination is the road to the table, not around it. Even when God disciplined the Corinthians, it was a Father’s correction, so that they shouldn't be condemned with the world (11:31-32).

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
section: If You Doubt Whether You Should Come
text: If You Doubt Whether You Should Come Many tender believers stay away because they aren’t sure they're in Christ. The Larger Catechism speaks to them. One who doubteth of his being in Christ, or of his due preparation to the sacrament of the Lord’s supper, may have true interest in Christ, though he be not yet assured thereof; and in God’s account hath it, if he be duly affected with the apprehension of the want of it, and unfeignedly desires to be found in Christ, and to depart from iniquity: in which case (because promises are made, and this sacrament is appointed, for the relief even of weak and doubting Christians) he is to bewail his unbelief, and labor to have his doubts resolved; and, so doing, he may and ought to come to the Lord’s supper, that he may be further strengthened. Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 172 You may grieve your weak assurance while sincerely seeking Christ and turning from sin. Then God counts you as having what you fear you lack. The Supper was made for weak believers too. Bring your doubts to God, ask your elders for help with them, and come, so that you may be strengthened. Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out ( John 6:37 ). If your doubts run deep, read Am I Really Saved?

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: Who Shouldn't Come The table isn’t open to everyone. Some who profess the faith and want to come are ignorant or scandalous. They may and ought to be kept from it by the power Christ left in his church, until they're taught and show that they've turned ( WLC 173 ). The scandalous are those who live in open sin and won’t leave it. Wicked men may eat the bread, but they don’t receive Christ, and they eat to their own harm ( WCF 29.8 ). That’s why Reformed churches guard the table through their elders. Before the Supper the minister usually fences the table. He warns the impenitent not to come, and he invites every sinner who mourns his sin and trusts Christ to come gladly. That’s care, not coldness. If you’re visiting a church, speak to the elders beforehand. If you trust Christ but have never professed your faith before a church, talk to the elders about joining. And if you’ve never come to Christ at all, the first thing isn’t the table but the Savior. Read the gospel and come to him.

title: How to Prepare for the Lord’s Supper
text: How to Prepare The Week Before Prepare by examining yourself, by renewing the exercise of your graces, and by serious meditation and fervent prayer ( WLC 171 ). Examine yourself. Ask whether you are in Christ, what your sins and needs are, and how you’re growing in knowledge, faith, repentance, love, and new obedience. How to Examine Yourself gives questions drawn from this same answer. Confess what you find. Name your sins before God, and turn from them. Make peace. Forgive those who wronged you. If someone has something against you, go to him first ( Matthew 5:23-24 ). Stir up your faith. Read Isaiah 53 or Matthew 27 , and think on what it cost him. Pray for the table. Ask God to meet you there, and pray for your minister. The Lord’s Day Morning Rise in time. Don’t rush in late. See How to Keep the Lord’s Day . Pray before you leave. Ask for a hungry heart and a clear eye on Christ. Hear the sermon and the fencing as meant for you. Let the warning search you and the invitation draw you. At the Table Wait on God with holy reverence. Watch the bread and wine and what is done with them. Discern the Lord’s body, and meditate on his death and sufferings ( WLC 174 ). Watch and think. The bread broken pictures his body given. The cup poured pictures his blood shed. What is pictured is real. He truly died for sinners. Mourn your sin and feed on Christ. As you eat and drink with your mouth, trust him with your heart. Receive him, rest on his merit, and rejoice in his love. Give thanks and renew your vows. Give yourself to him again, and love the brothers and sisters who eat beside you ( 1 Corinthians 10:17 ). Afterward Look back on how you came and what came of it ( WLC 175 ). If you found comfort, bless God for it. Ask him to keep it. Watch against slipping back, and keep the promises you made. If you felt nothing, don’t despair. Look again at how you prepared and came. If you were sincere, wait for the fruit in God’s time. If you were careless, be humbled, and come next time with more care. Look forward to the next time. Come often, as the Catechism urges, and keep showing forth his death till he come ( 1 Corinthians 11:26 ).

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Why God set apart one day in seven, how to keep it, what counts as necessity and mercy, and how to make it a delight for children.

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Why It Matters God set apart one whole day in seven as holy to himself. From the creation to the resurrection of Christ it was the last day of the week. Since the resurrection it has been the first day, the Lord’s Day, the Christian Sabbath ( WCF 21.7 , Acts 20:7 , Revelation 1:10 ). Christ said the Sabbath was made for man ( Mark 2:27 ). God gives us a whole day set apart for worship, rest from ordinary labor, and fellowship with his people. If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord , honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: Isaiah 58:13 (KJV)

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: How to Keep It The Shorter Catechism says the day is kept by a holy resting all that day, even from such worldly employments and recreations as are lawful on other days, and by spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God’s worship, except so much as is to be taken up in the works of necessity and mercy (Q&A 60). Prepare on Saturday. Finish the shopping, the yard, and the chores. Get to bed in time to be awake in worship. The Larger Catechism calls for this kind of foresight (Q&A 117). Worship with your church. Be at the public worship your congregation holds that day. If it meets morning and evening, the old Reformed counsel is to be at both. Public worship is the center of the day ( Hebrews 10:25 , WCF 21.6 ). Rest from your work. Leave the job, the business email, and the errands for Monday. Rest from your entertainments too. They aren’t wrong on other days. This day is set apart for better things. Fill the rest of the day. Read, pray, talk about the sermon at the table, sing psalms, visit the sick, show hospitality, and rest. See How to Lead Family Worship .

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: Works of Necessity and Mercy Jesus healed on the Sabbath and defended his disciples for picking grain when they were hungry ( Matthew 12:1-13 ). Some things must be done on any day, and some ought to be. Necessity. Feeding your family, caring for animals, and work that can’t wait, such as medicine, police, and fire. Mercy. Caring for the sick, helping someone in trouble, visiting the lonely. Your job may require Sunday work that isn’t a work of necessity or mercy. If so, talk with your elders and look for ways to change it. Don’t decide it alone.

title: How to Keep the Lord’s Day
text: With Children Make the day a delight, not just a list of things they can’t do. Keep them in worship with you. Talk about the sermon on the way home. Save special books, walks, and meals for that day. Let them see that you love it.

title: How to Fast
text: Why Christians fast, how it joins prayer, what it is not, how to begin, and when not to fast from food.

title: How to Fast
text: When Ye Fast But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly. Matthew 6:17-18 (KJV) Jesus set fasting beside giving and prayer ( Matthew 6:2 , 5, 16). He said when ye fast, not if. He took it for granted that his people would. Asked why his disciples didn’t fast, he answered with a wedding. Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast ( Matthew 9:15 ). Christ is the bridegroom, and his disciples enjoyed his presence. Fasting was out of place while he walked among them. Now he has been crucified, raised, and taken up into heaven. We live in those days. Christian fasting is the ache of the bride while the Bridegroom is away.

title: How to Fast
text: Fasting Joined to Prayer In Scripture fasting goes with prayer and with humbling the soul. Ezra proclaimed a fast that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way, and God was intreated of them ( Ezra 8:21-23 ). Nehemiah wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed ( Nehemiah 1:4 ). Daniel sought God by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and confessed the sins of his people ( Daniel 9:3-5 ). The church at Antioch fasted and prayed before sending out Barnabas and Saul ( Acts 13:2-3 ), and elders were ordained with prayer and fasting ( Acts 14:23 ). Therefore also now, saith the Lord , turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil. Joel 2:12-13 (KJV) The empty stomach serves the broken heart. Hunger reminds the body of what the soul must learn, that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God ( Matthew 4:4 ). The Confession names solemn fastings, with oaths, vows, and thanksgivings, as parts of worship upon several occasions, to be used in an holy and religious manner ( WCF 21.5 ). The Larger Catechism lists religious fasting among the duties of the second commandment (Q&A 108). Because it's worship, it's done as God directs. The Westminster Assembly gave a chapter of its Directory for Public Worship to public fasting. Scottish Presbyterians long kept a fast day in the week before the Lord’s Supper. The Covenanters kept days of public fasting and humiliation in times of trouble. If your elders call such a day, keep it with your church.

title: How to Fast
text: What Fasting Isn't Fasting can't earn God’s favor or force his hand. In Isaiah’s day the people complained, Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? ( Isaiah 58:3 ). They thought hunger put God in their debt, while they drove their workers and fasted for strife and debate (58:3-4). God answered them. Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh? Isaiah 58:6-7 (KJV) If a man fasts and stays as hard toward the poor and as harsh at home as before, that isn’t the fast God chose. Nor is it a show. The Pharisee told God, I fast twice in the week ( Luke 18:12 ), and went home unjustified. The publican had nothing to offer but God be merciful to me a sinner, and he went home justified. No fast adds anything to what Christ has done. We fast as forgiven children, not to buy forgiveness. And it isn’t a diet or a punishment of the body. Food is God’s good gift, to be received with thanksgiving ( 1 Timothy 4:4 ).

title: How to Fast
text: How to Fast Fast for something. A sin you can’t master, a hard decision, a sick friend, a child gone astray, the state of the church. Alone, as a family, or with the church. Keep a private fast quietly ( Matthew 6:17-18 ). A husband and wife may agree to fast together ( 1 Corinthians 7:5 ). Older children may join by giving up one meal. Start small. Scripture shows a fast of one day until evening ( Judges 20:26 ), and in great danger, three days ( Esther 4:16 ). The forty days of Moses, Elijah, and our Lord were extraordinary, not a pattern. Begin with one meal, or from one supper to the next. Keep drinking water. Give the time to God. Spend the mealtime with your Bible open, in a prayer of humbling such as Psalm 51 or Daniel 9 . Confess your sins by name, then pray for what you’re fasting about. When hunger comes, let it send you back to prayer. See How to Pray . Break the fast gently. Eat something light and give thanks.

title: How to Fast
section: When Not to Fast From Food
text: When Not to Fast From Food The sixth commandment requires a sober use of meat and drink to keep the life God gave you (Larger Catechism Q&A 135). If you have diabetes, are pregnant or nursing, take medication, or have any serious illness, see your doctor before you fast from food. If the answer is no, fast another way. Give up one meal if your doctor allows it, or the phone and the news for a day, or a comfort you lean on. Hunger isn’t the point. Humbling yourself before God is the point, and he sees the heart. If you’ve lived with an eating disorder, hear this gently. Going without food can feed the very thing that has hurt you and dress it up as holiness. For you the faithful path may be not to fast from food at all, and that’s no lesser obedience. Set aside an evening for prayer instead, and eat as your doctor tells you. Struggling With Sin has a short word on getting help. If you’re starving or purging now, see a doctor this week. If you feel driven to hurt yourself, call 988 or text 988 .

title: How to Fast
text: Your First Fast Christ fasted forty days and would not turn stones into bread ( Matthew 4:2-4 ). Where Adam fell over food, he stood for his people. Fasting can't bring you to God, but he can ( the gospel ). If you’re his, fast as one waiting for the marriage supper of the Lamb ( Revelation 19:9 ), when no one will fast again. Choose one meal this week, and write down why you’re fasting. Check your health first. If a caution above is yours, ask your doctor, or fast from something other than food. Spend that mealtime with God. Read Psalm 51 , confess, and pray for what you wrote down. Do a mercy. Give what the meal would have cost to someone in need ( Isaiah 58:7 ). Break the fast gently and give thanks. Leave the answer with God, and look to Christ, the bread of life ( John 6:35 ).

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: Read, sing, and pray. A few minutes a day, the way Reformed households have done it for centuries.

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: Why a Household Worships God commanded parents to teach his words to their children at home, when they sit, walk, lie down, and rise up ( Deuteronomy 6:6-7 ). The Confession says God is to be worshiped in private families daily, as well as in secret and in public ( WCF 21.6 ). The Church of Scotland wrote a whole Directory for Family-Worship in 1647 to help households do it. Fathers, this is your charge first ( Ephesians 6:4 ). But a mother with children, a single believer with roommates, or a couple with no children can keep it too. Parents who want to understand their children's place in the covenant can read Baptism and Church Membership .

title: How to Lead Family Worship
text: What to Do It doesn’t need to be long. Ten or fifteen minutes is enough. The old pattern has three parts. Read. Read a short passage, going straight through the Bible a chapter or part of a chapter at a time. Ask one or two simple questions about it. What does this teach us about God? What does it tell us to do? Sing. A psalm, or part of one. Learn a few tunes and use them often. Pray. Thank God, confess sin, and ask for the needs of the family, the church, and the world. Let older children pray too. Many households add a question or two from the Shorter Catechism, or the Catechism for Young Children with little ones.

title: How to Lead Family Worship
section: How to Start and Keep Going
text: How to Start and Keep Going Pick a time you already share. Right after supper works for many families, because everyone is already at the table. Start small. One passage, one psalm, one prayer. Do it tonight. Do not wait until you feel ready. Read the passage, sing a psalm, and pray together. A short, faithful gathering is enough to begin. Miss a night, pick it up the next. If you miss a night, resume the next day without turning family worship into a contest. Ask your elders for help. Ask them what other families in your church do. Sojourner’s family worship page walks through the reading, a psalm with its tune, a catechism question, and prayer, step by step.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: Forgiven people forgive. How to confess a wrong, go to a brother, cover an offense, and what forgiveness does not require.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: Forgiven People Forgive And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. Ephesians 4:32 (KJV) Christ taught us to pray, Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Then he added a warning, If ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses ( Matthew 6:12 , 15). He told a parable to show why ( Matthew 18:21-35 ). A king forgave his servant ten thousand talents, a debt no servant could ever repay. That servant then grabbed a fellow servant by the throat over a hundred pence and threw him into prison. So the king handed him over to the tormentors. Christ told this parable to expose the wickedness of receiving mercy while withholding it from another. Your debt to God is beyond counting, and God really does forgive it in Christ. A heart that won’t forgive the small debts owed to it's in real danger. Jesus ends, So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses (18:35). You don’t earn God’s pardon by forgiving others. Christ alone paid for sin. But a heart that has received mercy learns to show it, and God gives the grace to do so. In the fifth petition, which is, And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors, we pray that God, for Christ’s sake, would freely pardon all our sins; which we are the rather encouraged to ask, because by his grace we are enabled from the heart to forgive others. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 105

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: When You've Wronged Someone If you remember that thy brother hath ought against thee, Jesus says, leave your gift at the altar, first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift ( Matthew 5:23-24 ). Name it plainly. Say what you did and call it sin. I lied to you. I spoke against you behind your back. Not “if I hurt you” or “mistakes were made.” The one who offends his brother is to declare his repentance to those that are offended ( WCF 15.6 ). Leave off the “but.” “I was wrong, but you provoked me” shifts the blame back to the person you hurt. Ask, Will you forgive me? Then let them answer in their own time. Make it right where you can. Under the law a man who wronged his neighbor was to confess, repay what he took, and add unto it the fifth part thereof ( Numbers 5:7 ). Zacchaeus promised to restore fourfold whatever he had taken by false accusation ( Luke 19:8 ). Pay back what you took. Correct the lie you told. If you’ve been violent at home or made your family afraid, don't press them to forgive you or to let you come back. Read My anger frightens my family . If you broke faith in marriage, read If you are the one who broke faith .

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: When Someone Has Wronged You Most offenses should simply be covered. The discretion of a man deferreth his anger, and it is his glory to pass over a transgression ( Proverbs 19:11 ), and charity shall cover the multitude of sins ( 1 Peter 4:8 ). The careless word and the small slight can be forgiven in your heart and never mentioned again. Some sins are too serious to pass over, or they keep standing between you. Then Jesus says, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone ( Matthew 18:15 ). Go gently, to win your brother, not the argument. If he won’t hear, take one or two others, and then tell it to the church (18:16-17). If he repents, forgive him, even seven times in a day ( Luke 17:3-4 ). That pattern is for ordinary sins between believers. It isn’t for abuse or crime. Don't go alone to face someone who has hurt you or a child. Go to the police and to your elders.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: What Forgiveness Is and Isn't To forgive is to make a promise. You won’t hold the sin against them, bring it up to wound them, or pay them back. Recompense to no man evil for evil, and avenge not yourselves, Paul says. Instead, if thine enemy hunger, feed him ( Romans 12:17-21 ). It isn’t first a feeling. It’s a choice made before God, and you may have to make it again each time the memory comes back. Forgiveness doesn’t mean these things. Pretending it didn’t happen. Joseph forgave his brothers, and still told them, ye thought evil against me ( Genesis 50:20 ). Trusting at once. Forgiveness is given. Trust is earned back over time. Staying in danger. Never. Getting safe isn’t a failure to forgive. Keeping a crime from the police. God gave the ruler the sword against evildoers ( Romans 13:4 ). Reporting a crime isn’t revenge. Reconciliation takes two, and it may take a long time. Paul says, If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men ( Romans 12:18 ). Some of it doesn’t lie in you. If the other won’t repent or make peace, you’ve done your part. You've forgiven, and you’ve kept the door open as far as it’s safe.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
section: When They Never Make It Right
text: When They Never Make It Right Some who wronged you'll never say they’re sorry. Some have died. Reformed teachers differ on how to speak of this. Some say full forgiveness waits for repentance, for Jesus said, if he repent, forgive him ( Luke 17:3 ). Others stress that we are to forgive whenever we stand praying ( Mark 11:25 ). Both agree on what you must do. Put away bitterness and revenge, and give the wrong to God. Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord ( Hebrews 10:30 ). He will judge rightly. Look at Christ. While they crucified him, he prayed, Father, forgive them ( Luke 23:34 ). He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously ( 1 Peter 2:23 ). That prayer was heard. Weeks later, in the city that crucified him, about three thousand repented and were baptized for the remission of sins ( Acts 2:36-41 ). He died for sinners and rose again. If you’ve never come to him for your own pardon, start there . Then search your heart. Feeling the pain again isn’t the same as refusing to forgive. But if you nurse the grudge and want them to suffer, that’s bitterness, and God says to put it away ( Ephesians 4:31 ). A heart that flatly refuses to forgive is the servant in the parable, and it should be afraid. Don’t despair. Bring it to Christ and ask him to make you willing.

title: How to Forgive and Seek Forgiveness
text: When You Need to Forgive Pray the fifth petition slowly. Ask God to forgive you, and name before him the people you need to forgive. See the Lord’s Prayer as the pattern . Go to one person you’ve wronged. Confess it plainly with no “but,” and make right what you can. Let one small offense go. Don’t bring it up again, to them or to anyone. If a serious sin stands between you and a brother, go to him alone and gently. If it’s abuse or a crime, go to the police and your elders instead. Pray for someone who wronged you. Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you ( Luke 6:28 ).

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Know the message, pray for people by name, tell the bad news and the good, call for repentance and faith, and bring them to church.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Why Every Christian Tells Others Christ sent his church to every nation ( Matthew 28:19-20 ). Preaching belongs to ministers, but every Christian can tell what he knows and invite others to hear it. People can’t call on one they haven’t heard of ( Romans 10:14 ). You don’t save anyone. You tell, and God gives the increase ( 1 Corinthians 3:6-7 ). That takes the pressure off. It also takes away the excuse. God uses the plain words of ordinary believers.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: Know the Message You can’t give what you don’t have. Be able to tell the gospel in a few minutes. God. He made us, he is holy, and we owe him everything. Sin. We have all broken his law, and his judgment on sin is just and real. Christ. The Son of God became man, lived without sin, died in the place of sinners, and rose bodily on the third day. Response. Repent of your sin and trust Christ alone. Everyone who comes to him he will in no wise cast out ( John 6:37 ). The gospel page sets this out in full. Read it until you could explain it to a friend.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: How to Do It Pray for people by name. Ask God to open their hearts and to give you a chance to speak. Live so your words are believed. Be honest at work, keep your word, and be kind. Hypocrisy closes ears. Ask questions. What do you think happens when you die? What do you think of Jesus? Then listen. Tell the bad news and the good news. Don’t skip sin and judgment. Without them the cross makes no sense. Don’t stop at sin either. End with Christ. Call for a response. Tell them to repent and believe, as Jesus did ( Mark 1:15 ). Don’t pressure them into a prayer or a decision. Faith is God’s gift. You can’t manufacture it. Invite them to church. Bring them to hear the Word preached, and sit with them. That’s God’s ordinary way of making disciples. Give them something to read. The Gospel of John, or the gospel page .

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: When They Object Answer with meekness and fear ( 1 Peter 3:15 ). You don’t have to win an argument or know every answer. Say you’ll find out, and then do. The answers to objections on this site take the common ones one at a time. Jesus says men love darkness rather than light because their deeds are evil ( John 3:19 ). That warns us that unbelief is a matter of the heart as well as the mind. But don't use that verse to dismiss a person's actual question. Answer what he asks as faithfully as you can, admit what you don't know, and return to Christ and his gospel. You're a witness, not the Holy Spirit.

title: How to Share the Gospel
text: What to Avoid Tricks and pressure. No false urgency, no manipulation, no promises God didn’t make. A gospel without repentance. Christ calls sinners to turn from sin, not only to accept a gift. A gospel of health and wealth. Christ didn’t promise comfort in this life. He promised himself. Silence out of fear. The fear of man bringeth a snare ( Proverbs 29:25 ). Ask God for courage, and speak.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: All of it is true. What reading literally means, the kinds of writing in Scripture, how to tell a figure of speech, and Christ at the center.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: All of It's True All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: 2 Timothy 3:16 (KJV) Given by inspiration means breathed out by God. The Bible doesn’t merely contain the Word of God. It is the Word of God, and Jesus said to his Father, thy word is truth ( John 17:17 ). The Confession says we believe it not because a man or a church vouches for it. We believe it because God, who is truth itself, is its Author ( WCF 1.4 ). And his Spirit bears witness by and with the Word in our hearts ( WCF 1.5 ). You don’t sit over the Bible as its judge. You sit under it as a child before his Father. For many of us the hard part isn’t believing it’s true. It’s knowing what each part means. This page is for that.

title: How to Read the Bible Rightly
text: What Reading Literally Means Taking the Bible literally means taking each part as it was meant to be taken. A psalm is a song, a law is a law, and a proverb is a proverb. The meaning of a passage is the sense its author intended. Behind every human author stands God, who meant it first. That guards against two errors. A wooden reading makes the words say what no writer meant, as if the floods must grow hands because the psalm tells them to clap ( Psalm 98:8 ). A loose reading turns plain statements into pictures whenever they become uncomfortable. The first mistakes the form. The second refuses the content. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly.
