Paul warned of men supposing that gain is godliness ( 1 Timothy 6:5 ). That teaching crushes the poor saint by telling him his want proves weak faith. Yet Christ was poor. It isn’t a different emphasis. It’s another gospel. See Where Heresy Shows Up .

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Honoring God With Your Substance Honour the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: Proverbs 3:9 (KJV) The firstfruits were the first of the harvest, brought to God before the farmer knew how the rest would turn out. Faithful giving still has that shape. It comes off the top, not out of what’s left. The best picture of giving comes from the poor churches of Macedonia, whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality ( 2 Corinthians 8:2 ). They first gave their own selves to the Lord (8:5), and the money followed. Then Paul gives the root of all giving. For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. 2 Corinthians 8:9 (KJV) The Son of God left heaven’s glory, was laid in a manger, and gave himself on the cross. We don’t give to earn his love. We give because we have it. So give regularly and in proportion. Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him ( 1 Corinthians 16:2 ). Give gladly, for God loveth a cheerful giver ( 2 Corinthians 9:7 ). And give in trust. He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully (9:6). Sowing is a picture of seed thrown into the dirt in hope. The harvest is real, though not always paid in money, for God is able to make all grace abound toward you (9:8). If your gift seems too small, remember the widow and her two mites. Jesus said she gave more than all the rich, for she gave of her want ( Mark 12:41-44 ). Does the Tithe Still Bind? Faithful Reformed teachers differ here. Some hold that the tithe, a tenth, binds Christians still. Abraham gave tithes long before Moses ( Genesis 14:20 ), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to leave it undone ( Matthew 23:23 ). Others answer that the tithe supported Israel’s Levites and temple, which Christ fulfilled. They add that the New Testament names no percentage. Both sides agree on far more. Giving should be regular, generous, proportionate, and first. The church that feeds you with the Word should be supported by you ( Galatians 6:6 ). Many who don’t hold it binding still start with a tenth, as a floor and not a ceiling. If a tenth feels impossible right now, don’t give nothing. Set an amount, give it first, and ask God to grow it.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Borrowing and Debt The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Proverbs 22:7 (KJV) When you owe, part of next month’s paycheck is spent before you earn it. Debt promises freedom and delivers a kind of servitude. Scripture is just as plain about failing to pay. The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again ( Psalm 37:21 ). A debt is a promise, and a Christian keeps it even when it costs him. Owe No Man Any Thing Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law. Romans 13:8 (KJV) Some read this as a ban on every loan. Many Reformed teachers read it with the verse before, Render therefore to all their dues (13:7). They take it as a command to pay what is due when it’s due, and not to stay in debt. The same Bible that warns about debt regulates lending. God forbade charging interest to a poor brother ( Exodus 22:25 ), and Jesus said, from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away ( Matthew 5:42 ). He wouldn’t command his people to lend if every loan were sin. Other faithful Christians hold that a believer should avoid borrowing almost entirely, and they deserve respect. Both agree that debt is dangerous, that a promised payment must be made, and that the one debt never paid off is love. Cards, Payday Loans, and Car Notes Credit cards. A card paid in full every month is a tool. A balance carried over grows while you sleep. If you can’t stop carrying one, cut the card up. Payday and title loans. The Larger Catechism names usury and extortion as sins ( WLC 142 ). Calvin and many after him allowed fair interest in trade, but lending that preys on the desperate is what Scripture condemns. Go to your deacons first. Buy now, pay later. Several small payments at once can quietly eat a paycheck. If you couldn’t buy it today, ask whether you should buy it at all. Car loans. A working man needs a car that runs. A plain used car you can afford beats a new one you’ll pay on for years. Cosigning The old word for cosigning is surety. It means promising to pay another man’s debt if he doesn’t. Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts. If thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? ( Proverbs 22:26-27 ). If you’ve already done it, Solomon says to go humbly and press the man to release you. Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids ( Proverbs 6:3-4 ). He pictures a roe and a bird slipping out of a trap (6:5), and the trap is real. When a son or friend needs help, it’s often kinder to give what you can afford to lose than to sign for what you can’t ( WLC 141 ).

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Thou Shalt Not Steal The eighth commandment reaches much further than shoplifting. The eighth commandment requireth the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 74 The Larger Catechism fills it out ( WLC 141-142 ). It requires honest dealing, paying each his due, restoring what we wrongly kept, and giving and lending freely as we're able. It requires a lawful calling worked hard, careful provision, and frugality. It forbids theft, fraud, extortion, and usury, and also covetousness, anxious care, envy, idleness, waste, and wasteful gaming (see What the Bible Says About Gambling ). It even forbids robbing yourself and your family of the right use and comfort of what God gave. No one keeps that list. It should send us all to Christ. Working and Saving God’s first plan for a family’s needs is work. If any provide not for his own, he hath denied the faith ( 1 Timothy 5:8 ). A modest wage faithfully earned is a holy thing. See Diligence, Honesty, and Providing for Your Own . Solomon sends the sluggard to the ant, who gathers her food in the harvest ( Proverbs 6:6-8 ). There's treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spendeth it up ( Proverbs 21:20 ). Jesus asked which man would build a tower without first sitting down to count the cost ( Luke 14:28 ). A budget is just counting the cost. Yet the rich fool saved too. Saving for the broken water heater or the lean months is faithfulness. Saving so that you’ll never need to trust God is hoarding. Plan, and then sleep. Paying Taxes Taxes are part of what is due. For for this cause pay ye tribute also, Paul wrote, for they are God’s ministers ( Romans 13:6 ). He wrote under Nero. Jesus said, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s ( Matthew 22:21 ). That holds when taxes are high and rulers waste them ( WCF 23.4 ). It means an honest return, cash jobs included. Don’t cheat. See What the Bible Says About Government . Remembering the Poor He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord ; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. Proverbs 19:17 (KJV) Here’s a loan Scripture urges on you, and it’s made to God. The apostles asked Paul for one thing, that we should remember the poor ( Galatians 2:10 ). John asks, whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? ( 1 John 3:17 ). Bowels was the old word for the deep inward feelings. Christ gave his church an office for this work. When widows were neglected, the church chose seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to see to it ( Acts 6:1-3 ). Reformed churches see the deacon’s office there. Give to the deacons’ fund, and tell them when you see a need. If the need is yours, let them help. Saints are bound to relieve each other in outward things, according to their several abilities and necessities ( WCF 26.2 ).

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: When Debt Has You Under Maybe the bills are stacked on the counter unopened. Maybe you’ve hidden them from your husband or wife, or from your church, because the shame is heavy. Maybe it’s your own fault, or partly, or it came through sickness or a layoff. Hear this. Your worth isn’t your credit score, and God hasn’t turned his face away. Scripture tells of a widow whose husband had feared the Lord and still left debts. The creditor was coming to take her two sons as bondmen. God filled her empty vessels with oil, and Elisha told her, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest ( 2 Kings 4:1-7 ). That happened. God didn’t shame her. He provided so that she could pay. He may not fill your jars that way, but his ordinary way of helping is through his people. Tell the truth. If you’re married, tell your spouse all of it, if it’s safe to. Then tell your deacons. Stop digging. No new debt, even if it means hard cuts for a season. Write it all down. Every debt, its amount, rate, and due date. Talk to those you owe. Many will work out a plan with an honest debtor. Beware anyone who promises to make debt vanish for a fee. Pay something, faithfully. A small payment kept every month is the righteous man of Psalm 37 at work. If you’re weighing bankruptcy, don’t decide it alone. Talk with your elders. The law may release a debt that love would still move you to repay if God later prospers you. If some of this is sin, the overspending, the hiding, the envy, confess it plainly. Jesus taught us to pray, forgive us our debts ( Matthew 6:12 ). Debt there's a picture of sin, and the debt it pictures is real and far larger than any bill. Christ paid it, blotting out the handwriting that was against us, nailing it to his cross ( Colossians 2:14 ). If he paid the debt you never could, he won’t leave you alone with the one you can.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
text: Christ Our Treasure Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Matthew 6:19-21 (KJV) Moths in the closet and rust on the truck are real, and everything you can hold will wear out or be taken. Treasure in heaven is just as real, and nothing touches it. The true treasure is Christ himself. He was sold for thirty pieces of silver, and he died under God’s wrath for sinners who loved money more than God. On the third day he rose. Now he offers himself freely. He that hath no money, come ye, buy, and eat ( Isaiah 55:1 ). If you've loved money, or feared its lack more than you trusted God, turn from that and trust Christ alone. If you don’t know him yet, read the gospel . Whoever has him is rich, whatever the bank says.

title: What the Bible Says About Money and Debt
section: A Few Financial Duties to Begin With
text: A Few Financial Duties to Begin With Give thanks. Name ten things God has given you, starting with the plain ones. Count the cost. Write down what comes in and goes out this month, with your spouse if you’re married. Pray over it. Set your giving first. Decide what you will give on the Lord’s Day, and set it aside before anything else is paid. Start a small reserve. Put by a few dollars a week for the breakdown you know will come. Make things right. If you owe money you’ve been avoiding, or kept what isn’t yours, begin to pay it back ( WLC 141 ). Remember the poor. Give to your deacons’ fund, or meet one need you know of. Pray for daily bread. Ask for a competent portion, enough, as God’s fatherly wisdom sees best ( WLC 193 ). Then rest. He hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: No verse says thou shalt not gamble. What the commandments do say, about lotteries, betting apps, lots, and the way out.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: Where Scripture Speaks and Where It's Silent
text: Where Scripture Speaks and Where It's Silent Let’s be honest from the start. No verse in the Bible says, Thou shalt not gamble. Anyone who tells you otherwise is saying more than God said. But Scripture isn’t silent about money, about the heart that craves it, or about the neighbor whose loss becomes our gain. The Confession says the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in Scripture or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from it ( WCF 1.6 ). So we answer this the way we answer most questions of daily life. We ask what the commandments require and forbid, and we apply them with care. The Larger Catechism did exactly that. In its long list of sins against the eighth commandment, Thou shalt not steal, it names gaming among them. covetousness; inordinate prizing and affecting worldly goods; distrustful and distracting cares and studies in getting, keeping, and using them; envying at the prosperity of others; as likewise idleness, prodigality, wasteful gaming; and all other ways whereby we do unduly prejudice our own outward estate, and defrauding ourselves of the due use and comfort of that estate which God hath given us. Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 142 Notice the word wasteful. The Catechism doesn’t say every game is a sin. It sets wasteful gaming beside idleness and prodigality, which means throwing money away. It counts them as ways of robbing ourselves and our households of what God gave us. That’s theft too, even if no one else’s wallet is touched. For the whole commandment in plain words, see the Ten Commandments .

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: The Heart That Hastes to Be Rich
text: The Heart That Hastes to Be Rich The tenth commandment goes beneath our hands to our desires. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s. Exodus 20:17 (KJV) Gambling feeds on the wish to have much without waiting and without working. Solomon warned against that wish. A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent. Proverbs 28:20 (KJV) He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him ( Proverbs 28:22 ). Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished, but he that gathereth by labour shall increase ( Proverbs 13:11 ). Vanity there means emptiness, gain that comes from nothing. God’s way is slower, and it runs through labor. But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. 1 Timothy 6:9-10 (KJV) A snare is a hunter’s trap, set with bait. The trap it pictures is real. Men are drowned by it, and their families with them. What Is in Your Hand Is God’s The earth is the Lord ’s, and the fulness thereof ( Psalm 24:1 ). Your paycheck is his, and you hold it as a steward. And it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful ( 1 Corinthians 4:2 ). He gives it to feed your family, to pay what you owe, and to give to him that needeth ( Ephesians 4:28 ). Staking it on a roll or a game hands what belongs to him over to chance. For more, read What the Bible Says About Money and Debt . Gain From Your Neighbor’s Loss God’s law knows a few honest ways for goods to pass from one man to another. You may work for them, trade something of worth for them, or receive them as a gift. Gambling is none of these. The winner does no work and gives nothing in exchange. In a lottery, the prize is simply the other players’ losses gathered up. He gets it only because others lost, and he wanted them to. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. Romans 13:10 (KJV) Hoping another man loses his rent so you can have it isn’t love, even if he played freely. The Catechism asks us to further the wealth and outward estate of others, as well as our own ( WLC 141 ). Gambling turns that upside down.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Lotteries, Apps, and the House Most gambling today isn’t a game between friends. It’s a business. Every casino, lottery, and betting site sets its odds so that, over time, the players as a whole lose more than they win. The house profits because the odds favor it over time. Look at who buys lottery tickets. The lottery draws hardest on those who have the least. It sells the hope of a way out to people who feel they have none. A government that lives off that hope is feeding on its weakest citizens. Rob not the poor, because he is poor ( Proverbs 22:22 ). He that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches shall surely come to want ( Proverbs 22:16 ). Sports betting apps and online casinos never close. They live in your pocket. They offer free bets to start, so you learn the habit before you spend your own money. They make losing feel like nearly winning. They send offers during the game and at midnight. They aren’t built to entertain you. They’re built to keep you.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Lots, Raffles, and Friendly Bets Casting Lots in Scripture Some say the Bible approves of gambling because God’s people cast lots. But look at what they were doing. The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord . Proverbs 16:33 (KJV) The lot was a way of asking God to decide what men couldn't settle. When the apostles needed a man to take Judas’s place, they prayed, Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen, and the lot fell upon Matthias ( Acts 1:24-26 ). Even the heathen sailors in Jonah’s ship cast lots to learn who had brought the storm ( Jonah 1:7 ). No one staked money. They were seeking an answer, not a prize. So the lot is no defense of gambling. Scripture does show one group casting lots for gain. At the foot of the cross the soldiers gambled for the coat of the dying Christ ( John 19:23-24 ). They wanted a prize. He was giving his life. The Larger Catechism says lots are to be used holily and reverently, and it lists sinful lots among the sins of the third commandment ( WLC 112-113 ). Some Puritans warned that to play at lots is to treat God’s providence lightly. Others disagreed. Thomas Gataker, who later sat in the Westminster Assembly, held that a lot used in play is no such appeal to God. Faithful men differed on that point. Small Bets and Raffles What about a dollar bet with a friend on a ballgame, or a raffle ticket at a school fundraiser? Here we mustn't invent rules God hasn’t given. Rolling dice in a board game where nothing changes hands isn’t gambling at all. Beyond that, faithful Christians differ. Some will stake nothing, however small, because they see the same root in a dollar as in a thousand. Others think a friendly wager, with no one hurt and nothing coveted, isn’t the wasteful gaming the Catechism means. Some churches won’t hold raffles. They want gifts given freely, not bought with a chance to win. Others see a raffle as a gift with a small token attached. Where Scripture isn’t plain, ask honest questions before God. Am I hoping to get something for nothing? Would I be glad to see my friend lose? Could this be a first step for someone weaker, or for me? Whatsoever is not of faith is sin ( Romans 14:23 ). Paul said, All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any ( 1 Corinthians 6:12 ). If even a small bet stirs a hunger you can’t easily put down, leave it alone entirely.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: When Gambling Has Hold of You
text: When Gambling Has Hold of You For some, gambling isn’t a question of liberty. It’s a chain. You tell yourself one more bet will win it back. You hide the statements. You borrow, then lie about why. Maybe the rent is gone, or the savings. This ruins families. Trust breaks, and honest men become liars. Christ came for people exactly where you are. God is faithful, Paul says, and with the temptation he will also make a way to escape ( 1 Corinthians 10:13 ). But you won’t get out alone, or by trying harder in secret. Confess it. He that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy ( Proverbs 28:13 ). Tell God, then your husband or wife and your pastor or an elder, the whole truth, including how much. Cut off access. Jesus said, If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out ( Matthew 5:29 ). The eye is a figure. Christ commands you to remove whatever feeds the temptation, even when giving it up costs you. Delete the apps today and close the accounts. Many states and betting sites let you ban yourself. Ask your bank whether it can block gambling payments. Give someone else control of the money. Hand your cards and accounts to your spouse or a trusted friend from church for a season. This isn’t shame. It’s wisdom. Find accountability. Ask a few believers to ask you plainly and often whether you’ve gambled. Mortify lets you link with fellow believers from your church and fight covetousness and the love of money together. For the long fight itself, read Struggling With Sin . See a doctor. God works through means. A doctor can treat the depression and anxiety that so often come with this, and can point you to further help. Lean on the church. Tell the deacons if your family needs help with food or rent. Let the elders help you make a plan for your debts, and read When Debt Has You Under . Don’t borrow to chase what you lost. If the debts and the shame have you thinking your family would be better off without you, that’s a lie. They wouldn’t. Call 988 or text 988 now, and tell someone near you tonight.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
text: Pardon for What You Lost Maybe what you lost wasn’t yours. It was the family’s savings, or money from an employer, a client, or a church. The guilt is heavy because the wrong is real, and this page won’t tell you it was nothing. But your sin isn’t bigger than the blood of Christ. Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot: 1 Peter 1:18-19 (KJV) You could never buy back your soul with money, and you don’t have to. Christ paid with his own blood, and he rose again on the third day. Turn from your sin to him. Let him return unto the Lord , and he will have mercy upon him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon ( Isaiah 55:7 ). If you don’t know him yet, read the gospel , and come. Pardon from God doesn’t end your duty to those you wronged. When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he said, If I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold ( Luke 19:8 ). He didn’t pay to be forgiven. He paid back because he had been. God’s law required the guilty man to restore what he took and add a fifth part ( Numbers 5:7 ). The Catechism names restitution among the duties of the eighth commandment ( WLC 141 ). If you took from an employer, confess it, even if it costs you the job. Make a plan with your elders to repay, little by little if you must. Some of what was lost may never be repaid. God knows that, and his pardon is no less full.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: Contentment and the Treasure No Wager Can Buy
text: Contentment and the Treasure No Wager Can Buy The cure for the gambler’s hunger isn’t a smaller hunger. It’s a better treasure. Paul wrote from prison. Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. Philippians 4:11-13 (KJV) Contentment is learned. It doesn’t come in a jackpot. It rests on a promise. Your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you ( Matthew 6:32-33 ). The gambler is always trying to secure tomorrow by luck. The believer has a Father who has already promised it. He has said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee ( Hebrews 13:5 ). Jesus told of a man who found treasure hid in a field. For joy thereof he goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field ( Matthew 13:44 ). Jesus compares the kingdom to treasure worth everything a man has. Christ and his kingdom are worth more than everything you own. Yet no wager can win him, and no money can buy him. He gives himself freely. Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money ( Isaiah 55:1 ). Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich ( 2 Corinthians 8:9 ). Whoever has him has already gained what the whole world can't give.

title: What the Bible Says About Gambling
section: If Gambling Has a Hold on You
text: If Gambling Has a Hold on You Look honestly at your own money. Add up what went to tickets, apps, and bets in the last year, and bring the number to God. If it has a hold on you, act today. Follow the steps above . Don’t wait for Monday. Pray for contentment. Pray Agur’s prayer, Give me neither poverty nor riches, feed me with food convenient for me ( Proverbs 30:8 ). Give. Put something in the offering this Lord’s Day, or into a needy hand. Giving loosens money’s grip on the heart. A word to husbands and wives. If your spouse gambles, it isn’t your fault, and covering for it won’t fix it. Don’t quietly pay the debts and keep the secret. Protect what your household needs to live on, in a separate account if you must. Go to your elders together, or alone if he won’t come. If the lying has turned to threats or violence, get safe first . Love him enough to let him face what he has done. A word to parents. Your children are being taught to bet before they can drive. The ads come with every game, and some video games sell paid chances at prizes that work much the same way. Talk about it plainly, and show them how the house wins. Let them see you content with what God gives, and see you give. For more, read What the Bible Says About Raising Children . In the church, welcome the one who is fighting. Someone near you may be hiding this. Let him hear that there’s mercy in Christ and help in his people.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Wine is a gift and drunkenness is sin. Christian liberty, the weaker brother, when to abstain, drugs, and help when drink has hold.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: A Good Gift From God Scripture doesn’t begin with wine as an enemy. It names wine among the good things God brings out of the earth. He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth; And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man’s heart. Psalm 104:14-15 (KJV) The psalm praises God the Creator, and the gladness it names is real. The Preacher says the same. Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart ( Ecclesiastes 9:7 ). The Wine at Cana and at the Table The Lord Jesus did his first sign at a wedding in Cana when the wine ran out ( John 2:1-11 ). He had six stone waterpots filled to the brim, and the water became wine, well over a hundred gallons of it. And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now. This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him. John 2:10-11 (KJV) The wine was real, and so was the joy he gave that couple. The sign also pointed past itself. Isaiah foretold a feast of wines on the lees well refined that God would spread for all people ( Isaiah 25:6 ). Christ is the Bridegroom who brings that feast, and he has kept the good wine until now. On the night he was betrayed, he took the cup and said, Drink ye all of it, for this is my blood of the new testament ( Matthew 26:27-28 ). He called what was in it this fruit of the vine (26:29), and the Confession speaks of the elements of bread and wine ( WCF 29.3 ). Reformed churches today differ in what they pour. Many use wine, many use grape juice, and some offer both so that no one who must abstain is kept from the table. Was It Only Grape Juice? Some sincere Christians have seen what drink did to the homes around them. They've taught that the good wine of the Bible was unfermented juice. But the case doesn’t hold. Noah drank of the wine, and was drunken ( Genesis 9:21 ). Paul says, be not drunk with wine, and no one needs that warning about juice. At Corinth some left the Lord’s Supper drunken ( 1 Corinthians 11:21 ). Jesus was slandered as a winebibber because he drank wine where John the Baptist did not ( Luke 7:33-34 ). Juice that would keep without turning to wine came only in the 1800s. The wine of Scripture was wine. That’s why the Bible both praises it and warns about it.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Drunkenness Is Sin The Bible that calls wine a gift calls drunkenness a sin. And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; Ephesians 5:18 (KJV) Excess means a wasted, unruly life. Paul sets two fillings side by side. The drunkard lets something outside him take over his mind and lift his heart for a few hours. God fills his people with his own Spirit, and the fruit is singing and thanksgiving (5:19-20). Many drink to feel brave or to get through the night. The Spirit gives what the bottle only promises, and he leaves no ruin in the morning. Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise ( Proverbs 20:1 ). It mocks the one who trusts it. Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. Proverbs 23:29-32 (KJV) The serpent is a picture, and the harm it pictures is real. The drunk man says what he never would sober. His world reels like a ship’s mast, and he wakes up beaten without having felt it (23:33-35). Then comes the saddest line of all. When shall I awake? I'll seek it yet again. A person who can't stop drinking is already being mastered by it. Drunkenness includes the loss of sober judgment long before a person falls down in the street. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh, and says that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God ( Galatians 5:21 ). Drunkards stand beside thieves and adulterers in 1 Corinthians 6:10 . Scripture also pronounces a woe on him that makes his neighbour drunken ( Habakkuk 2:15 ). The host who keeps pouring for a friend who has had enough shares the sin.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: Free to Drink, Free to Abstain
text: Free to Drink, Free to Abstain Scripture allows wine and forbids drunkenness. So a believer may drink in moderation with thanks, or he may abstain, and either may do it to the Lord. No man and no church may add a rule to God’s Word and bind a conscience with it. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 Beside it means added to it. But the Confession guards the other side just as firmly. They who, upon pretense of Christian liberty, do practice any sin, or cherish any lust, do thereby destroy the end of Christian liberty; which is, that, being delivered out of the hands of our enemies, we might serve the Lord without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.3 Upon pretense means using liberty as an excuse. Christ didn’t free you from sin so that you could drink your way back into it. Paul’s word about food fits the cup as well. Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him. Romans 14:3 (KJV) The one who drinks mustn't despise the one who abstains as narrow. The one who abstains mustn't judge the one who drinks as worldly. Both give God thanks, and both do it to the Lord (14:6). Faithful Reformed people have differed here. In the 1800s many Presbyterian ministers had watched drink ruin families, and they urged total abstinence on every Christian. Others held moderate drinking free. A church may wisely counsel abstinence in a hard age. But it may not call wine itself a sin, because God doesn’t. The Reformed Presbyterian Church once required total abstinence of every member and officer. In the 1980s its Synod ruled that the Testimony strongly recommends abstinence but doesn’t demand it. In 1998 the promise to abstain was taken out of the vows of its officers. The Testimony still teaches that, to avoid harming our neighbor and to help one another live a disciplined life, it's altogether wise and right for Christians to abstain from the use, sale, and making of alcoholic drinks (RP Testimony 26.6). If you belong to a Reformed Presbyterian congregation, give that counsel real weight, and talk with your elders. For the Sake of Your Brother It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. Romans 14:21 (KJV) The weaker brother isn’t merely someone who disapproves. Your example may lead him against his conscience, or back into a sin that once ruled him. Take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak, Paul says. To wound such a conscience is to sin against Christ, who died for that brother ( 1 Corinthians 8:9-13 ). If a friend at your table is fighting to stay sober, leave the bottle in the cupboard. Liberty is never the last word. Love is.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: When It's Wise to Abstain A Christian who may drink isn’t bound to, and Scripture honors some who didn’t. He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried. Numbers 6:3 (KJV) The Nazarite vow was taken freely by one who wished to be set apart to the Lord for a season ( Numbers 6:2 ). The Rechabites drank no wine for generations at their father’s charge. God held up their faithfulness as a rebuke to Judah, which would not keep his word ( Jeremiah 35:6 , 14). The lesson there was obedience. God never made either path a law for all his people. They're examples for those who choose to abstain, and some have good reason to. A family history of addiction. If drink ruined a parent or grandparent, you may be wise to leave it alone. All things are lawful unto me, Paul said, but I will not be brought under the power of any ( 1 Corinthians 6:12 ). Recovery. If drink once ruled you, the cup is a door back into the old bondage. Keep it shut, and let no one shame you for it. A calling. Kings were warned against wine lest they forget the law ( Proverbs 31:4-5 ). A pastor, or anyone who works among those who struggle, may abstain so nothing he does becomes their excuse. An unsettled conscience. Whatsoever is not of faith is sin ( Romans 14:23 ). If you aren’t sure before God that you may, don’t.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: The Law of the Land and the Life of Your Neighbor
text: The Law of the Land and the Life of Your Neighbor Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Romans 13:1 (KJV) Where the law sets an age for drinking, a Christian under that age keeps it, because God set that ruler over him. A teenager who drinks behind his parents’ backs disobeys both. An adult who buys drink for other people’s children sins with them. For more, read What the Bible Says About Government . Drunk Driving Thou shalt not kill reaches further than murder. The Larger Catechism says the sixth commandment forbids the immoderate use of drink, and whatever else tends to destroy anyone’s life ( WLC 136 ). Driving after drinking gambles with your neighbor’s life. Moses’ law made a man build a wall around his flat roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence ( Deuteronomy 22:8 ). God holds a man guilty for the danger he could have prevented. Don’t drive when you’ve been drinking, and don’t ride with anyone who has. Marijuana and Other Drugs Scripture doesn’t name marijuana or pills, but it says plainly what a Christian’s mind is to be. Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: 1 Peter 5:8 (KJV) The lion is a picture, and the enemy it pictures is real. To be sober is to keep a clear and watchful mind, for they that be drunken are drunken in the night, and we are of the day ( 1 Thessalonians 5:6-8 ). A man can drink a glass of wine with supper and keep his head. But a drug taken to get high is taken for the altered mind itself. That's drunkenness by another road. Where the law now allows it, the call to be sober hasn’t changed. Medicine prescribed by a doctor is a different thing. The Larger Catechism counts a sober use of physic, the old word for medicine, among the duties of the sixth commandment ( WLC 135 ). Pain medicine after surgery, or medicine for anxiety or depression, taken as directed, is a lawful means of preserving life. Scripture even says, Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish ( Proverbs 31:6 ). Taking more than you were told, or taking it for the feeling, is another matter.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
section: If Drink Has Hold of You
text: If Drink Has Hold of You Maybe you hide how much you drink, or you’ve promised to cut back and couldn’t. Then you’re in bondage, and you need a deliverer. First, hear this. If you drink heavily every day, don’t stop all at once on your own. Stopping suddenly can bring seizures and can kill. See a doctor this week, and tell him the whole truth about how much you drink. Let someone go with you. The same is true of daily pills like Xanax or Valium. God works through means, and a doctor and treatment are among them. Then tell your pastor or an elder. You weren’t meant to fight this in secret. Read Drink or drugs have hold of me , and for the daily fight, Mortify . Get the bottles out of the house, and stay away from the friends who pull you back. Make not provision for the flesh ( Romans 13:14 ). You aren’t only giving something up. You’re being filled with the Spirit, whose joy doesn’t end in shame. If you love someone who drinks, his choices aren’t your fault, and you can’t stop him by your own effort. Pray, speak the truth in love, and lean on your church. If he is a danger to you or your children, your safety comes first.

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Washed and Justified Paul wrote this to a church that had drunkards in it. Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. 1 Corinthians 6:10-11 (KJV) They had been drunkards, and now they were washed, set apart for God, and declared righteous. That pardon is held out to you. Look at the Lord Jesus on the cross. They gave him to drink wine mingled with myrrh, and he received it not ( Mark 15:23 ). Many take it to have been a drink to dull the pain. In the garden he had prayed about another cup, the cup of his Father’s wrath against sin ( Matthew 26:39 ). He drank that one to the bottom with a clear mind, for drunkards and for all who come to him, and he rose again. If you’ve never come to him, read The Gospel , and come today. Confess the sin by name, and the things you did while drunk. Make right what you can. If someone was hurt or killed because of your drinking, Christ forgives that too. But pardon with God doesn’t cancel earthly justice. If you fall again, don’t hide from him. If old guilt keeps returning after you’ve confessed it, read What I did is too great to forgive .

title: What the Bible Says About Alcohol
text: Practicing Christian Freedom With Care If you drink, give thanks. Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God ( 1 Corinthians 10:31 ). Ask yourself whether you could gladly go a month without it. If not, put it down and talk to someone. If you abstain, keep it free of pride. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost ( Romans 14:17 ). If you host, host with love. Have something good for those who don’t drink, and never press a glass on anyone. If You're a Parent In Proverbs 23 a father says, My son, give me thine heart (23:26). A few verses later he warns his son about the wine that bites like a serpent. Talk to your teens about drink before the world does. Teach both halves. Wine is God’s gift and drunkenness is sin. Tell them the family history. If addiction runs in your family, say so plainly and early. Teach them to keep the law. Underage drinking isn’t a rite of passage. It is disobedience to rulers God set over them, and to you. Let your example speak. If you drink, let them never see you drunk or see you need it. If you abstain, don’t teach them that Christians who drink are lesser Christians. Give them a way out. If they ever need to leave a place where there is drink, or the driver has been drinking, they can call you and you will come. Get them home safe first, and talk the next day. For more, read The Teen Years .

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What Leviticus 19:28 meant, how Old Testament laws bind now, Christian liberty, and a word for those who already have them.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What Leviticus 19:28 Says One verse in the Bible speaks to marks on the skin. Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the Lord . Leviticus 19:28 (KJV) A verse must be read where God put it. Just before it, Israel is told not to use enchantment or observe times, and not to round the corners of the head or mar the corners of the beard ( Leviticus 19:26-27 ). These were the ways of the nations around Israel, in their sorcery and in their grief. Moses gives the reason in Deuteronomy. Ye are the children of the Lord your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. For thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God, and the Lord hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations that are upon the earth. Deuteronomy 14:1-2 (KJV) The heathen cut themselves for their dead, and the prophets of Baal cut themselves till the blood gushed out upon them ( 1 Kings 18:28 ). Israel wasn’t to grieve or worship like that. The word translated marks is found nowhere else in the Old Testament, so its exact sense isn’t certain. Whether for the dead reaches to the marks as well as the cuttings is debated. What is plain is the reason God gives. I'm the Lord . Israel belonged to him, and wasn’t to carry the signs of other gods or of hopeless grief.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: Which Kind of Law Is It?
text: Which Kind of Law Is It? Leviticus 19 holds very different laws side by side. It says, thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (19:18), and a line later forbids a garment mingled of linen and woollen (19:19). No one thinks those bind us in the same way. The Confession says the moral law, summed up in the ten commandments, binds all men forever ( WCF 19.5 ). Then it names two other kinds. Beside this law, commonly called moral, God was pleased to give to the people of Israel, as a Church under age, ceremonial laws, containing several typical ordinances, partly of worship, prefiguring Christ, his graces, actions, sufferings, and benefits; and partly holding forth divers instructions of moral duties. All which ceremonial laws are now abrogated under the New Testament. Westminster Confession of Faith 19.3 Israel’s judicial laws, the civil laws of her nation, expired with that state. They bind others now only as far as their general equity requires ( WCF 19.4 ). So which is Leviticus 19:28 ? Reformed teachers ask whether a law is rooted in creation and the ten commandments. Or does its reason lie in Israel’s being set apart from the nations, as a picture of the holiness Christ would bring? Many answer that this law belongs with the beard and the mingled cloth. It marked Israel off from her neighbors, and that wall came down in Christ. But they see a moral duty folded inside it. Don't take on the marks of false gods. Do not sorrow as others which have no hope ( 1 Thessalonians 4:13 ). God’s people are still a peculiar people ( 1 Peter 2:9 ), but now by holiness of life and not by the cut of the beard. Other faithful teachers hold that the ban on marks still binds, as a moral law guarding the body God made. They counsel every Christian never to be tattooed. Still others call it ceremonial but think its general equity weighs so heavily against tattoos that a believer shouldn't get one. These are godly men, and they don’t all land in the same place. This page won’t settle more than Scripture settles. No one may bind you where God’s Word hasn't, or loosen you where it has. The questions below bind every believer, whichever view he holds. Pictures Aren't Permits Some say God approves of tattoos because he said, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands ( Isaiah 49:16 ). That’s a picture. God is saying he can’t forget his people, any more than a man could forget what is cut into his own palm. What it shows is real and very sweet, but it isn’t a ruling on tattoos. When Paul says, I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus ( Galatians 6:17 ), he means the scars of his beatings for Christ ( 2 Corinthians 11:24-25 ). Reading a figure as a permit is as careless as reading Leviticus 19:28 without its setting.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: Your Body Belongs to God What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 (KJV) Paul wrote this about sexual sin, but it reaches every use of the body. Paul calls the believer’s body a temple because the Holy Spirit dwells within him. Christ purchased that body with his blood. You’re a steward, not an owner. No Christian may say, “It’s my body, so it’s my business.” But the verse doesn’t by itself forbid every change to the body. Christians cut their hair and have surgery, and the verse doesn’t say which changes honor God. It tells you whom you must ask, and that the answer matters.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: Christian Liberty and Its Limits God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 Where Scripture hasn’t forbidden a thing, the church may not make a new law and lay it on your neck. But the Confession says at once that those who, under pretense of liberty, practice any sin or cherish any lust destroy the very end of liberty, which is to serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness ( WCF 20.3 ). Paul said, Ye have been called unto liberty, only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another ( Galatians 5:13 ). All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not. 1 Corinthians 10:23 (KJV) Expedient means helpful. Whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God ( 1 Corinthians 10:31 ). And whatsoever is not of faith is sin ( Romans 14:23 ). If you can’t get a tattoo with a clear conscience, you mustn't get one. Questions to Ask First Why do I want it? To be admired, or to fit in? Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain ( Proverbs 31:30 ). Is it rebellion? If part of the pleasure is that it will upset your parents, the motive is already sin. Will I want it when I’m old? What seems deep at twenty may shame you at sixty. Where will it go? A mark placed to draw eyes to what should be covered is immodest ( WLC 139 ). What does it say? Nothing occult, obscene, cruel, or mocking of holy things belongs on a Christian ( Philippians 4:8 ). What does it tie me to? A believer may not wear the badge of a gang, a false religion, or a sinful way of life. What will it say to others? Think of your witness and of the weaker believer ( 1 Corinthians 8:9 ). Love sometimes gives up what liberty allows.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: If You're Young and Living at Home
text: If You're Young and Living at Home Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right. Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth. Ephesians 6:1-3 (KJV) In the Lord means in all things lawful. A parent who says no to a tattoo isn’t commanding sin. Children owe willing obedience to their parents’ lawful commands and counsels ( WLC 127 ). While you live under your parents’ roof, their decision is your answer, even if the law of the land would let you go ahead. Getting one in secret breaks the fifth commandment. A tattoo will still be possible in five years. Broken trust is harder to mend. Parents, give your reasons, and be honest about which are God’s law and which are your own judgment. Provoke not your children to wrath ( Ephesians 6:4 ). See also The Teen Years .

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What About Piercings? Abraham’s servant put the earring upon Rebekah’s face as a gift for a bride ( Genesis 24:47 ). When God pictures his rich grace to Jerusalem, he says he put earrings in her ears ( Ezekiel 16:12 ), He would hardly use what is wicked in itself to picture his own kindness. But earrings were also bound up with idols. Jacob’s household buried theirs with their strange gods ( Genesis 35:4 ). So jewelry isn’t sin in itself. Ask the same questions of it. A plain earring and a face full of metal meant to shock don’t say the same thing. Some piercings leave lasting marks and deserve the same care as a tattoo. Young people at home should again honor their parents’ decision.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: If You Already Have Tattoos Maybe you got them before you knew Christ, or as a believer and now wish you hadn’t. Hear this plainly. You aren’t a second-class Christian. Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV) The ink is still in your skin, but you aren’t who you were. Whatever your old life held, such were some of you, but ye are washed ( 1 Corinthians 6:11 ). The blood of Christ purges the conscience from dead works to serve the living God ( Hebrews 9:14 ). Ink can’t reach where that blood has washed. If your tattoo was a matter of liberty, there’s nothing to repent of. If you got it in sin, out of rebellion or vanity, confess that sin to God by name. The sin was in the heart, and the heart is what Christ forgives. If you don’t yet know him, read The Gospel . He receives sinners as they are. If a tattoo shows something sinful or obscene, love for God and your neighbor will want it out of sight. Cover it with clothing, have an artist work it into something clean, or have it removed if you can. But removal is never a condition of grace. Christ doesn’t wait for clear skin before he receives you, and no church should either. If you’re unsure, talk with your pastor.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
section: How the Church Should Receive Them
text: How the Church Should Receive Them James warns the church that seats the man with a gold ring in a good place. It tells the poor man in vile raiment to stand. Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? ( James 2:1-4 ). Skin is no different from clothing here. Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart ( 1 Samuel 16:7 ). The tattooed man who walks into your church may be a new believer, or a sinner God is drawing, or a brother of forty years in Christ. You can’t tell by looking. Don’t stare or lecture. Learn his name and sit with him. Many have known years of scorn from Christians. Let your church be where that ends.

title: What the Bible Says About Tattoos
text: What to Do If you want a tattoo, wait. Give it a long season, and pray through the questions above. Ask the right people. If you live at home, abide by your parents’ answer. If you’re married, decide it with your husband or wife. Keep your conviction without binding others. If you think tattoos are forbidden, don’t treat believers who differ as rebels. If you think they’re allowed, don’t press your liberty on the weak or the young. Deal honestly with what you have. If a tattoo you have is sinful in its message, cover it this week. Then stop carrying shame that Christ has already carried. Welcome the stranger. Next Lord’s Day, look for the person who looks least like your church, and greet him first. One risen body still bore marks. Thomas said he would not believe unless he saw in his hands the print of the nails ( John 20:25 ), and the risen Christ showed him. He was wounded for our transgressions ( Isaiah 53:5 ). Every mark of shame we carry, on the skin or in the conscience, he carried to the cross. And he will finish his work in our bodies too. Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself. Philippians 3:21 (KJV) Vile here means lowly and weak. Whatever your skin carries today, if you’re his, he will raise your body and make it glorious, to stand with him forever.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Rulers are ordained of God and owe allegiance to his Son. Obeying, praying, paying taxes, and when to obey God rather than men.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Government Is God’s Ordinance Government wasn’t invented by kings or voted into being by the people. God made it. Paul wrote this to Christians living under Rome, a pagan empire that would later put many of them to death. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. Romans 13:1-2 (KJV) God, the Supreme Lord and King of all the world, hath ordained civil magistrates to be under him, over the people, for his own glory and the public good, and to this end hath armed them with the power of the sword, for the defense and encouragement of them that are good, and for the punishment of evil-doers. Westminster Confession of Faith 23.1 Rulers are over the people, and they're under God. The proudest king on earth had to learn that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men ( Daniel 4:17 ). The Minister of God With the Sword Peter says governors are sent for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well ( 1 Peter 2:14 ). Paul says it more sharply. For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Romans 13:4 (KJV) Minister means servant. The magistrate serves God as truly as a pastor does, though in a different work. The sword signifies lawful authority to use force and punish evildoers, even with death. God gave it after the flood. Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man ( Genesis 9:6 ). Private men may not avenge themselves ( Romans 12:19 ). God repays by the hand of the ruler. So a Christian may hold the sword. The Confession teaches that Christians may accept the office of a magistrate when called to it. It also teaches that rulers may wage war upon just and necessary occasion ( WCF 23.2 ). John the Baptist didn’t tell soldiers to leave the army. He told them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely ( Luke 3:14 ). Cornelius was a centurion who feared God with all his house ( Acts 10:1-2 ). A believer may serve as a judge, a soldier, or a police officer to the glory of God. If You Have Borne the Sword Some who read this have used force in war or in the line of duty, and some have taken a life. Lawful force used for justice and in defense of others isn’t murder. Yet many carry it for years. The weight may come from grief over what sin has done, even where the use of force was lawful. If there was real sin in it, cruelty or rage or harm to the innocent, Christ’s blood is enough for that too. Confess it to him plainly, and tell your pastor. If the weight has brought you to thoughts of ending your life, call 988 or text 988 now, and read the page on getting safe .

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Christ Is King of Kings Above every ruler stands a King. In the second psalm the nations rage against the Lord and his anointed, and God laughs, for he has set his King on his holy hill ( Psalm 2:1-6 ). Then he speaks to the rulers. Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him. Psalm 2:10-12 (KJV) A subject kissed his king as a sign of homage, and a worshiper kissed his idol ( 1 Kings 19:18 ). The kiss signifies allegiance. God commands kings and judges, as kings and judges, to bow to his Son. That Son is Jesus Christ. After he rose he said, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth ( Matthew 28:18 ). As the eternal Son he always ruled with the Father. This is power given to him as Mediator. He is the God-man who died and rose again, crowned and set over everything for his people’s sake. Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Ephesians 1:20-22 (KJV) Under his feet is a picture of a conquering king, and the rule it pictures is real. Every court and congress is beneath him now. John calls him the prince of the kings of the earth ( Revelation 1:5 ). In John’s vision he rides out with a name written on his robe, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS ( Revelation 19:16 ). The vision is full of pictures, but that name is the plain truth about him. So a nation isn’t neutral ground. Its rulers owe Christ their allegiance, and its laws ought to honor his law. The original 1647 Confession expressly gives civil magistrates duties concerning the truth of God, his worship, and the peace of the church ( WCF 23.1-3 ). The Hope for the Nations Scripture promises, Yea, all kings shall fall down before him, all nations shall serve him ( Psalm 72:11 ). Reformed believers differ on how much of that we'll see before Christ returns. Some believe the gospel will so prevail in this age that nations as nations will confess Christ before he comes. They point to the leaven that worked till the whole was leavened ( Matthew 13:33 ), and the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord ( Habakkuk 2:14 ). Others believe Christ gathers his people out of every nation while this age stays mixed, wheat and tares growing together until the harvest ( Matthew 13:30 ). In this view the church is often small and suffering, and every knee will bow on the day he appears ( Philippians 2:10-11 ). Both hold that Christ reigns now, that the nations owe him obedience now, and that he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet ( 1 Corinthians 15:25 ). Both pray, Thy kingdom come. We see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus ( Hebrews 2:8-9 ).

title: What the Bible Says About Government
section: The Magistrate's Duty Toward True Religion
text: The Magistrate's Duty Toward True Religion The original Westminster Confession of 1647 teaches more than the duty of rulers to keep public order. It also says they must protect true religion and oppose public corruption in the church. We mustn't quote only the first sentence of chapter 23.3 and leave out what follows. The civil magistrate may not assume to himself the administration of the Word and sacraments; or the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven: yet he hath authority, and it is his duty, to take order, that unity and peace be preserved in the Church, that the truth of God be kept pure and entire; that all blasphemies and heresies be suppressed; all corruptions and abuses in worship and discipline prevented or reformed; and all the ordinances of God duly settled, administered, and observed. For the better effecting whereof, he hath power to call synods, to be present at them, and to provide that whatsoever is transacted in them be according to the mind of God. Westminster Confession of Faith 23.3 (1647) This is the establishment teaching of the original Confession. It doesn't treat the civil ruler as religiously neutral. The magistrate is answerable to Christ for public justice and for the protection of true religion. The language about suppressing blasphemy and heresy is part of the original doctrine. It mustn't be hidden or exchanged for the later American revision. Chapter 20.4 goes further. It says that certain teachings and practices contrary to the known principles of Christianity or destructive of the church's peace may be proceeded against by church censures and by the power of the civil magistrate. That's what the 1647 text teaches. It doesn't follow that every personal disagreement is heresy, or that a private person may take the sword into his own hands. Romans 13 places the sword in lawful public office, and rulers themselves remain accountable to God's Word. The Ruler Isn't a Minister of Word and Sacrament The same paragraph that gives the magistrate these duties forbids him to preach by virtue of his civil office, administer baptism or the Supper, or exercise the keys of the kingdom. Christ gave church government and discipline to church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate ( WCF 30.1-4 ). A ruler's duty to uphold true religion doesn't make him a pastor or an elder. Chapter 31.2 permits magistrates to call synods. It also says that when magistrates are open enemies to the church, ministers may assemble by virtue of their office. And chapter 31.3 gives synods their own ministerial responsibility to decide controversies and matters of church government according to Scripture. The church isn't merely a department of the state. God Alone Is Lord of the Conscience God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship. Westminster Confession of Faith 20.2 (1647) The magistrate may require lawful outward obedience. He can't make a sinner believe, declare a human invention to be God's command, or take Christ's place as Lord of the conscience. Yet chapter 20.2 must be read alongside chapter 20.4. In the original Confession, liberty of conscience never meant a civil government had no duty concerning religion. Read the full text and its Scripture proofs at The Westminster Standard . These paragraphs are the original Westminster position, not the altered teaching of the 1788 American revision.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: Honor, Pray, Pay, and Obey The fifth commandment reaches to all who are over us by God’s ordinance, whether in family, church, or commonwealth ( WLC 124 ). It is the duty of people to pray for magistrates, to honor their persons, to pay them tribute and other dues, to obey their lawful commands, and to be subject to their authority, for conscience’ sake. Infidelity or difference in religion doth not make void the magistrate’s just and legal authority, nor free the people from their due obedience to him Westminster Confession of Faith 23.4 A ruler who doesn’t believe, or believes falsely, is still a ruler. Peter wrote under a pagan emperor, Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king ( 1 Peter 2:17 ). I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. 1 Timothy 2:1-2 (KJV) First of all. Before we complain about rulers, we pray for them, and even give thanks. If a ruler seems foolish or wicked, pray for him anyway. Ask God to give him wisdom and to save his soul. Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon, the city that had burned Jerusalem, and pray unto the Lord for it ( Jeremiah 29:7 ). Render therefore to all their dues, tribute to whom tribute is due ( Romans 13:7 ). Cheating on taxes is stealing, even when the money will be spent badly. Obey the laws, not only for fear of being caught but for conscience sake ( Romans 13:5 ). And Paul says to speak evil of no man ( Titus 3:2 ). That includes the man in office you didn’t vote for.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
section: When We Must Obey God Rather Than Men
text: When We Must Obey God Rather Than Men Our obedience to rulers has a limit, and the limit is God. When the council commanded the apostles to stop preaching Jesus, Peter and John answered, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard ( Acts 4:19-20 ). Brought back again, they answered in fewer words. Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. Acts 5:29 (KJV) The Hebrew midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive ( Exodus 1:17 ), and God dealt well with them. Daniel kept praying three times a day, as he did aforetime, after a law forbade it ( Daniel 6:10 ). And three young men wouldn't bow to a golden image. If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. Daniel 3:17-18 (KJV) Look at how they disobeyed. They refused only what would have been sin, and they did it openly. Daniel still said, O king, live for ever ( Daniel 6:21 ). They took up no sword. They left the outcome with God. If a ruler commands you to deny Christ, to worship falsely, or to take part in killing the innocent, you must refuse. Refuse humbly, and refuse firmly. What about rulers who become tyrants? Calvin, at the close of his Institutes, taught that private persons aren't to rise up against their rulers on their own. But lesser magistrates, those who also hold lawful office, ought to restrain a ruler who oppresses the people. The Reformed tradition after him has held that resistance to tyranny belongs first to such lawful authorities and to lawful means. Paul, denied justice, used the law and said, I appeal unto Caesar ( Acts 25:11 ). Bring hard questions of this kind to your elders before you act.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: The Christian Citizen Most of us are citizens, not rulers. Where the law gives us a voice, a Christian may vote, petition, and speak in public with a conscience shaped by Scripture. Our rulers are to maintain piety, justice, and peace ( WCF 23.2 ). They're subject to God's law even when they don't acknowledge him. When choosing a magistrate, consider his duties before God, what his office requires, and whether your own participation would compromise obedience to Christ. Don't let party loyalty settle a matter that belongs to conscience. Ask your elders for counsel where you're unsure. The 1647 Confession sets out the underlying duties, though it doesn't prescribe the voting rules of any modern republic. Righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people ( Proverbs 14:34 ). It’s right to ask rulers to protect life and punish evil. See What Christians Should Do about abortion for one plain case. Put Not Your Trust in Princes Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish. Psalm 146:3-4 (KJV) Every leader you hope in will die. If your peace rises and falls with an election, your trust is in a prince. Ask yourself. Do I feel more joy when my side wins than when a sinner repents? Do I despise the people who vote the other way? The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God ( James 1:20 ). Rage at the news and contempt for opponents are sins, not zeal. Your political opponent is a neighbor made in God’s image, and perhaps a brother in Christ. Love him. Keep the church above party. She must preach the whole Word, including what God says to rulers. And the Confession keeps her assemblies from meddling in civil affairs beyond humble petition and advice ( WCF 31.5 ). Her message is, Be ye reconciled to God ( 2 Corinthians 5:20 ). When she becomes the chaplain of a party, she trades it for a smaller one.

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: The Throne That Matters Most On the morning of the day he died, Jesus stood before a Roman governor who asked whether he was a king. Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence. John 18:36 (KJV) Not of this world means his kingdom doesn’t come from here. It isn’t won by votes or held by soldiers. It spreads by the Word and the Spirit. Yet he rules over all. He told Pilate, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above ( John 19:11 ). Then the soldiers crowned him with thorns and mocked him, Hail, King of the Jews ( Matthew 27:29 ). Pilate put a title on the cross, THE KING OF THE JEWS ( John 19:19 ). They meant it as a joke, but it was true. The King was lifted up on a cross, bearing the wrath of God for rebels. He won his kingdom not by taking his enemies’ lives but by giving his own for them. On the third day he rose, and now he sits at the right hand of God. Every one of us has been a rebel against this King. The command to kiss the Son is spoken to you before any president. Turn from your sin and trust him. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him ( Psalm 2:12 ). He is the prince of the kings of the earth, and in the same breath John says he loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood ( Revelation 1:5 ). If you don’t know him yet, read the gospel . The throne that matters most isn’t in any capital. It’s the one Christ sits on now, where he gathers and defends his church, subdues her enemies, and makes intercession for his people ( WLC 54 ). He removeth kings, and setteth up kings ( Daniel 2:21 ). But of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end ( Isaiah 9:7 ). We have received a kingdom which cannot be moved ( Hebrews 12:28 ).

title: What the Bible Says About Government
text: What Christians Should Do Kiss the Son yourself. Before you ask anything of your rulers, bow to Christ. Confess where politics has ruled your heart more than he has. Pray for your rulers by name. Pray this week for the president, your governor, and one local official, and give thanks for them. See How to Pray . Pay and obey with a clean conscience. If you’ve cheated on taxes or broken a just law, confess it and set it right. Watch your mouth. Speak of officials with respect, even in disagreement. Stop passing on what mocks or slanders. Take part with care. Vote, write, and speak as a servant of Christ, with the counsel of your elders. Know your line. Settle now what you will not do, whatever a ruler commands. Ask God for Daniel’s courage and Daniel’s respect. Turn off the noise. If the news feeds fear or rage, put it down and read Psalm 2 instead.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: Death is an enemy Christ has beaten. What happens when we die, the resurrection, burial and cremation, and the end of life.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What Death Is People call death a natural part of life, but Scripture names it an enemy ( 1 Corinthians 15:26 ). God made man to live. He warned Adam about the forbidden tree, In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die ( Genesis 2:17 ). Adam ate, and God said, Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return ( Genesis 3:19 ). By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned ( Romans 5:12 ). For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans 6:23 (KJV) Wages are what a man has earned, and death is what sin has earned. It wasn’t part of God’s first creation. That’s why it feels so wrong to us. It's wrong. So the Bible calls death an enemy, the last enemy that shall be destroyed ( 1 Corinthians 15:26 ). Jesus stood at his friend’s grave and groaned in the spirit ( John 11:33 ). Yet death isn’t loose in the world on its own. God says, I kill, and I make alive ( Deuteronomy 32:39 ). No one dies outside his hand. For those in Christ the enemy is already beaten. The sting is gone, though the wound is still felt.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What Happens When We Die At death body and soul are torn apart for a time. The body goes to the grave, and the soul goes on, awake, to God. The bodies of men, after death, return to dust, and see corruption; but their souls (which neither die nor sleep), having an immortal subsistence, immediately return to God who gave them. The souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies: and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, reserved to the judgment of the great day. Besides these two places for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none. Westminster Confession of Faith 32.1 So the soul doesn’t sleep until the last day. There's no purgatory where believers pay what Christ left unpaid. The Shorter Catechism gives the believer’s part. Their souls are made perfect in holiness and immediately pass into glory, and their bodies, still united to Christ, rest in their graves till the resurrection ( WSC 37 ). The Believer Goes to Be with Christ For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Philippians 1:21 (KJV) Paul had a desire to depart, and to be with Christ, which is far better ( Philippians 1:23 ). He was willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord ( 2 Corinthians 5:8 ). Jesus told the dying thief, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise ( Luke 23:43 ). Paradise recalls Eden. Christ promised the dying thief that he would be with him that very day. The Unbeliever Is Kept for Judgment This must be said soberly, and never with pleasure. Jesus told of a rich man who lived for himself and died. In hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments ( Luke 16:23 ). Jesus speaks of his tongue and of a flame, though the man’s body lay in its grave. Those words picture the torment of a soul without its body, and the torment is real. Between that place and Abraham’s side there's a great gulf fixed (16:26). It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment ( Hebrews 9:27 ). No one repents after death. That’s why the gospel always says today. Yet we may not pronounce on any particular person who has died. We don’t know what passed between a soul and God at the end. If that fear presses on you, read When You Fear They Did Not Know Christ . But it’s our place to warn the living, ourselves first.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: The Resurrection of the Body God made us body and soul, and he won’t leave half his work in the dust. Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation. John 5:28-29 (KJV) All will rise, the just and the unjust, each in the same body that was laid down. At the last day, such as are found alive shall not die, but be changed; and all the dead shall be raised up with the self-same bodies, and none other, although with different qualities, which shall be united again to their souls forever. Westminster Confession of Faith 32.2 Job knew it long before Christ came. Though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God ( Job 19:26 ). The pattern is Christ’s own body. After he rose he said, Handle me, and see, for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have ( Luke 24:39 ). The risen body isn’t a new creature in place of the old one. It's the old one made new. The Confession adds that the bodies of the unjust are raised by Christ’s power to dishonor, and the bodies of the just by his Spirit to honor, made like his own glorious body ( WCF 32.3 ). He shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body ( Philippians 3:21 ). Vile here means lowly and weak.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
