text: Burial in Scripture Because the body will rise, God’s people have always honored it in death. In Scripture burial is often an act of faith. I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight. Genesis 23:4 (KJV) When Sarah died, Abraham owned no land in Canaan. God had promised him all of it, but he still lived in tents. The first piece of the promised land he ever owned was a grave, bought at full price ( Genesis 23:16-20 ). He laid his wife in the promised land because he believed the promise. Joseph died a ruler in Egypt, but he made his brothers swear to carry his bones up out of it ( Genesis 50:24-25 ). Centuries later Moses carried that coffin out in the exodus, and Israel buried it at Shechem ( Exodus 13:19 , Joshua 24:32 ). The Holy Spirit counts the request among the great acts of faith. By faith Joseph, when he died, gave commandment concerning his bones ( Hebrews 11:22 ). Most of all, Christ himself was buried. Paul counts it part of the gospel, that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day ( 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 ). Faithful hands wound his body in linen with spices and laid it in a new tomb in a garden ( John 19:40-41 ). Because he lay in a grave, the grave of a believer is no longer a prison. Their bodies rest in their graves as in their beds ( WLC 86 ). So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 (KJV) Paul pictures burial as sowing. A farmer drops a seed into the ground, and it rots there and seems lost. Then up comes a living plant, far more glorious than the bare grain, yet grown from that very seed (15:36-38). The body laid in the grave is the seed. The sowing is the picture. The rising isn’t a picture. It's as real as the resurrection of Jesus, and the same God promises it. A spiritual body doesn’t mean a body made of spirit. Christ’s risen body had flesh and bones. It means a body wholly ruled and filled by the Holy Spirit, never again weak or dying or able to sin. A Christian standing at a grave is standing in a field God has sown, waiting for the harvest.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: What About Cremation Christians have historically buried their dead, as a testimony that the body will rise. Many Reformed teachers still counsel burial today. Burial says with the body what the creed says with the mouth. In Scripture the burning of a body is mostly tied to judgment. Achan was stoned and then burned for his sin ( Joshua 7:25 ). God also judged Moab for an act of contempt toward the dead. Thus saith the Lord ; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime: Amos 2:1 (KJV) There's one case to weigh honestly. When the Philistines killed King Saul, they cut off his head and fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan ( 1 Samuel 31:9-10 ). The men of Jabeshgilead went all night, took down the bodies of Saul and his sons, and burnt them. Then they took their bones, and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days (31:12-13). David blessed them for this kindness ( 2 Samuel 2:5 ). So burning wasn’t always contempt. Here it seems meant to spare bodies already shamed by enemies, and even then they buried the bones. It was a hard measure in a hard time, not a new custom. But hear this just as plainly. Cremation doesn’t hinder God from raising anyone. Every body returns to dust in the end, whether in a grave or a fire or the sea, and the sea gave up the dead which were in it ( Revelation 20:13 ). Many martyrs were burned and their ashes scattered, and they'll rise in glory. Scripture gives no direct command about how the dead must be laid to rest. So faithful Christians differ. Some believe cremation should never be chosen. Many more hold that it isn’t forbidden, but that burial is the clearer testimony. They counsel it whenever it can be done. God alone is Lord of the conscience ( WCF 20.2 ), and no church may bind where Scripture hasn’t. Where cremation is chosen, many counsel burying the ashes under a stone with a name, rather than scattering them. If someone you love was cremated, hear this gently. You didn’t shut them out of the resurrection. If they were in Christ, their body is still united to him, whatever has become of it, and he will raise it. If you must choose cremation because of cost, you’re not sinning against your loved one or against God. Before you decide, tell your pastor or your deacons. The church may be able to help with a simple burial. But if cremation is the only way you can bear the cost, choose it without shame, and trust God with the last day.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
section: Choices at the End of Life
text: Choices at the End of Life Thou shalt not kill ( Exodus 20:13 ). The Larger Catechism says the sixth commandment forbids taking away our own life or anyone else’s, except in public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense. It also forbids neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of keeping life ( WLC 136 ). That rules out euthanasia and assisted suicide, whatever kinder name the law gives them. It’s still killing when a doctor does it, and when the dying man asks for it. Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s ( Romans 14:8 ). Life is his to give and his to take. But not every possible treatment must be used until the last breath. A patient may refuse or stop a treatment that's a heavy burden and can no longer heal him, but only stretch out his dying. That isn’t killing. The difference lies in the aim. Ending a life is one thing. Ceasing to fight a death that has already come is another. Ordinary care should never be withheld to bring death sooner. That means keeping someone clean and warm and offering food and water while the body can take them. It’s right to relieve pain, even with strong medicine that may shorten life. Scripture says, Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish ( Proverbs 31:6 ). The aim must be to ease suffering, never to kill. God sees the aim of the heart, even when two doses look alike on paper. Don’t make these choices alone. Take them to your elders, and seek a doctor who honors life as God’s gift. Hospice, rightly given, eases pain without hastening death. Long nights of caregiving may bring a dark thought of ending it, for the one you love or for yourself. If so, tell someone today, and call 988 or text 988 . Organ Donation Giving an organ to save another is a matter of Christian liberty, and it can be a fine act of love. No one is bound to do it. The one caution is grave. Death must be truly confirmed before anything is taken, and no one may be hastened toward death for another’s sake. Christians differ on some of the medical tests for death, so talk with your elders and a doctor you trust before you sign.

title: What the Bible Says About Death, Burial, and Cremation
text: Preparing to Die Death isn’t the master of the Christian. Christ is. I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death. Revelation 1:18 (KJV) Keys picture authority. The authority they picture is real. Christ went down into death and came out holding the keys. He took part of flesh and blood, that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage ( Hebrews 2:14-15 ). None of his people will die an hour before his time. So the first and greatest preparation for death is to be found in Christ ( Philippians 3:9 ). If you’ve never come to Christ, or aren’t sure you have, read the gospel today. He died for sinners and rose again, and he turns away none who come. Then get ready in plain, earthly ways too. When King Hezekiah was sick, God sent the prophet to tell him to set his house in order, for he would die ( 2 Kings 20:1 , Isaiah 38:1 ). God gave Hezekiah fifteen more years, but the word still stands for us. Setting your house in order isn’t a lack of faith. It’s love for those you'll leave. Pray with Moses, So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom ( Psalm 90:12 ). Make sure of Christ. Confess your sins and rest on him alone. How to Examine Yourself can help. Make a will. If any provide not for his own, he hath denied the faith ( 1 Timothy 5:8 ). Name guardians who will raise your children in the Lord. Do it this year. Write down your wishes for care. Choose someone who honors life to speak for you if you can’t. Tell them you want no one to hasten your death, and no burdensome treatment that only prolongs dying. Plan a funeral that preaches Christ. Ask for Scripture, psalms, prayer, and a plain word of the gospel. A funeral is a sermon to the living, who lay death to heart that day ( Ecclesiastes 7:2 ). Say whether you wish to be buried, and settle the cost ahead if you can. Be reconciled. If anyone has something against you, go to them now ( Matthew 5:23-24 ). Ask forgiveness, and give it. Tell your family where your hope is. Jacob blessed his sons before he was gathered to his people ( Genesis 49 ). Say it aloud, and write it down. Remember the dying in your church. Visit them, and help with the funeral bill. On the last day the One who holds the keys will open every grave of his people, and death will be swallowed up in victory ( 1 Corinthians 15:54 ).

title: Church Membership
text: Communicant membership, elders and vows.

title: Church Membership
text: Why Belong to a Congregation? A Christian needs a church where the Word is preached, the sacraments are administered, and elders know the flock entrusted to them. Christ joins believers to his body. In Acts 2:41-42 those who received the Word were baptized and continued in the apostles' doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers. The visible church includes those who profess the true religion and their children ( WCF 25.2 ). Congregational membership makes our duties toward particular people concrete. Belonging also places a believer under lawful pastoral oversight. Elders are charged to shepherd God's flock and must give account for their care ( Acts 20:28 , Hebrews 13:17 ). Membership includes receiving that ministry, praying for the church, using one's gifts, and loving fellow members. It's a serious commitment, but it's a mercy.

title: Church Membership
text: What Is Communicant Membership? A baptized child belongs to the visible church but may not yet have been admitted to the Lord's Table. A communicant member is admitted upon a credible profession of faith and the church's examination. The distinction recognizes that those who receive the Supper must discern the Lord's body and examine themselves ( 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 , WLC 171-173 ). The session mustn't demand evidence of sinless maturity. It must also guard the Supper from careless admission. A struggling believer should speak honestly about doubts and repentance, rather than pretending to be certain about everything.

title: Church Membership
text: Why Meet With the Elders? In Presbyterian government, the session oversees the congregation and examines those seeking communicant membership. Be ready to say who Jesus Christ is, why you need him, what you believe about his death and resurrection, and how you're seeking to follow him. You can tell your testimony plainly. A dramatic conversion story isn't required. The elders may ask about baptism, worship, your household, and your understanding of the vows. Their task is to seek a credible profession and care for the soul placed before them. Ask questions of them as well. Find out how the Word is preached, how the sacraments are administered, what the church teaches, and how a member should seek help or appeal a decision.

title: Church Membership
text: Understand Your Promises Church membership vows are made before God. Know what you're promising before you make them. The original Westminster Confession gives the doctrine of lawful oaths and vows in chapter 22. Each congregation must administer membership according to its own lawful church order. Don't assume that every Presbyterian congregation asks identical questions. If you're joining the RPCNA, consult its official membership covenant and ask your session to explain it. Read Visiting and Joining a Reformed Presbyterian Church for the practical process.

title: Church Membership
text: Life After Joining Keep the Lord's Day. Be present for the church's public worship and ordinances. Pray for your elders and fellow members. Give as the Lord has prospered you, according to your responsibilities. When a brother or sister suffers, don't wait for someone else to notice. When you sin, repent. Where another person has been wronged, seek reconciliation. If the session must correct you, listen with an open Bible. Church discipline aims at restoration, the peace of the church, and Christ's honor ( WCF 30.3 ). Membership won't make every church decision easy. It does give you a home in the visible church in which to grow under the ordinary means of grace. If you're still looking, start with How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
text: What to expect at worship and membership.

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
text: Your First Lord's Day You can visit a Reformed Presbyterian congregation without knowing the order of worship or all the answers to a membership interview. Find a congregation through the RPCNA congregation directory . Check the service times and introduce yourself to the pastor or an elder. Ask where to sit and whether the congregation meets again later in the day. You should expect Scripture to be read and preached, public prayer, and the singing of inspired Psalms without instrumental accompaniment. Listen carefully to the sermon and follow the words of the Psalm being sung. The church's purpose is worshiping God, not providing a performance for guests. If the Lord's Supper is administered, speak with an elder before approaching the Table. The session has responsibility for admitting communicants. A respectful conversation protects both the visitor and the congregation.

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
text: Which Standards Should You Read? This website teaches the original 1647 Westminster Confession and Catechisms. The RPCNA has its own contemporary Constitution, including a Testimony and directories governing membership, discipline, and worship. The two sets of documents must be distinguished. The RPCNA's present procedures aren't quotations from the original 1647 Confession. Read the original Westminster Standards study index . For the denomination's current requirements, consult its published Constitution . Ask the elders how the congregation subscribes to and applies those standards.

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
text: The Membership Conversation Tell the session that you want to join. If you were baptized elsewhere, describe the baptism and the church where it occurred. Bring any membership transfer information you have. The session will examine your profession of faith and explain the covenant of communicant membership. Expect to discuss the authority of Scripture, the Trinity, repentance, faith in Christ, baptism, the Lord's Day, and submission to the church's biblical government. You're not being asked to prove you know every detail of the Westminster Larger Catechism. You should understand the basic doctrine you're professing and the promises you're making. The RPCNA's Directory for Church Government assigns admission to communicant membership to the session in an organized congregation. Its Official Vows include commitments concerning faith, Christian life, worship, service, and receiving correction. Read the actual documents rather than relying on a simplified summary. Official denominational source .

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
section: What About Your Spouse and Children?
text: What About Your Spouse and Children? If you've children, ask the elders about their place in the covenant community and their baptism. The original Westminster Confession teaches the baptism of children of believing parents ( WCF 28.4 ). Parents are responsible to teach their children Scripture, lead them in prayer, and bring them into the church's worship. Don't assume that your spouse's journey and yours will be identical. Speak openly about religious differences in the home. Seek pastoral counsel without treating the church as a weapon in a family dispute.

title: Visiting and Joining an RP Church
text: After You're Received Get to know the congregation. Attend public worship, join its prayer and fellowship, and let the elders know when you need counsel. Learn the Psalms you sing. Prepare for the Lord's Table with self-examination and confidence in Christ, not confidence in your own worthiness. Read Church Membership , Baptism , and The Lord's Supper . If you haven't been baptized, the session can arrange the sacrament according to the church's order.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: Careful reports on popular preachers, each weighed by Scripture and the Westminster Standards from the man’s own words, with what he gets right told as plainly as what he gets wrong.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: Why This Page Is Here For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. Acts 20:29-30 (KJV) Paul wept as he said those words to the elders at Ephesus. He knew the danger wouldn’t always come from outside the church. It would rise up from inside it, from men who stand in pulpits and draw crowds. That’s still true. Today a preacher can reach millions of young believers through a phone before any elder in their own church has heard his name. This page gathers careful reports on popular teachers. Each one weighs what a man teaches by the Word of God. It helps believers tell a faithful shepherd from a dangerous one. It also gives parents, pastors, and friends something sound to hand to someone they love. More reports will be added over time.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: How Each Teacher Is Weighed He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. Proverbs 18:17 (KJV) A report here is meant to be fair before it’s anything else. Every one is held to the same rules. Scripture is the standard. Holy Scripture alone binds the conscience. The Westminster Confession of Faith and its catechisms are used as the church’s faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. His own words come first. The evidence comes first from the teacher’s own sermons, books, interviews, and his church’s written beliefs. Where a quotation carries great weight, the report names the sermon and roughly where in it the words come. That way any believer can listen for himself. Critics are leads, not proof. What critics say is read for leads but never treated as evidence. A charge that can’t be traced to the man’s own words or to reliable reporting is left out. A report says so plainly when a common charge doesn’t hold up. What he gets right is told too. A man should be judged by the whole of what he teaches. Truth is still truth when it comes from a man with errors, and the report says so. Each finding is given its weight. A grave finding touches the foundation of the faith. A serious finding departs from clear Reformed teaching in a way that harms hearers. A caution marks a weakness believers should watch for. Sound and credit mark what is right and good. Each ends in a plain answer. Is he safe to sit under? A green check means yes. A red cross means no, he should not be anyone’s steady teacher. The answer stands at the top of every report and beside every name below. No one has to read the whole report to find it. Each report can also be downloaded in full as a PDF, sources and all, to print or pass along. The reports themselves quote the English Standard Version. On this site the same verses are given in the King James Version, like every other page here.

title: Teacher Reviews
text: The Reports Not safe Philip Anthony Mitchell Pastor of 2819 Church in Atlanta and founder of the ACCESS prayer gatherings. Many true things, and errors that reach the person of Christ. 42 min read

title: Teacher Reviews
section: In What Spirit to Use These
text: In What Spirit to Use These Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV) Not every teacher named here is called a wolf. Some are badly wrong at the root. Some are fellow believers whose errors are serious enough that they shouldn’t be anyone’s steady teacher. A report says which, and why, and it leaves the judging of hearts to God. So when you use them, quote the man’s own words, not rumors about him. Don't mock him, and don’t repeat charges the record doesn’t support. Pray for him, because God can still humble a proud preacher and set a confused one straight. And if a teacher is troubling your own church, go to your elders rather than starting a campaign of your own. The surest guard against the counterfeit is to know the true thing well. Sit under faithful preaching in a church where the elders know your name. For more help in testing a teacher yourself, read How to Spot a False Teacher , How to Spot Real Heresy , and How to Weigh “God Told Me” .

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Pastor of 2819 Church in Atlanta and founder of the ACCESS prayer gatherings. Many true things, and errors that reach the person of Christ.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The Short Answer Philip Anthony Mitchell preaches many true things with real force. He calls sinners to repent. He says plainly that no one can earn acceptance with God. He warns against the prosperity gospel and against sexual sin, and he presses the return of Christ on the conscience of a young generation. Believers should be glad whenever Christ is truly preached. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice. Philippians 1:18 (KJV) Even so, he is not a safe teacher to sit under. His own published sermons teach that the Son of God emptied himself “of some of his divine nature.” He speaks often of God charging him and telling him things directly. He taught his church to make an arena “a portal from earth to heaven” and to “put a demand” on God. He told a congregation that fasting can “move God” and that “your bodies are going to be healed.” On perseverance he hangs final salvation on the believer staying in God’s will, which leaves weak believers without the anchor Scripture gives them. His Lord’s Day services and stadium events are built as produced experiences that lift the preacher, and signs of idolizing him are plain to see. Verdict. Not a safe teacher. Don’t sit under his teaching or recommend it to other believers. So the counsel of this report is simple. Don’t make him your teacher, and don’t hand his sermons to new or struggling believers. If a brother or sister already listens to him, don’t mock the man or slander him. Show them his own words, show them where those words depart from Scripture, and point them to sounder shepherds, beginning with the elders of their own church.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: How This Report Was Made The standard used here is Holy Scripture, which alone binds the conscience. The Westminster Confession of Faith and its catechisms are used as the church’s faithful summary of what Scripture teaches. The evidence comes first from Mitchell’s own words. That means sermon transcripts published from the 2819 Church podcast feed, the church’s statement of beliefs, his personal website, and his long interviews. Reporting from the Associated Press, Christianity Today, Premier Christianity, Charisma, and others was used for the facts of his life and ministry. Critics were read for leads but never treated as proof. A charge that could not be traced to his own words or to a reliable report was left out. The sermon transcripts are made by machine from the church’s audio, so small slips in spelling appear in them. Where a quotation carries great weight, this report names the sermon and about what minute it comes at, so any believer can listen for himself. That’s the Berean way. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. Acts 17:11 (KJV) The full report. This page follows the written report of October 2026. The PDF holds every part of it, with each claim tied by number to its source. It quotes Scripture in the ESV, where this page gives the same verses in the KJV. Download the full report (PDF)

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Who He Is Philip Anthony Mitchell was born and raised in Queens, New York, to parents who came from the Caribbean. He grew up in a Christian home, but by his own account he was dealing drugs by age twelve and carrying a gun in his early twenties. He has spoken often of time at Rikers Island, of paying for abortions, and of a dark season around 2003 that brought him near to taking his own life. That crisis turned him back to Christ. He says he sensed a call to preach while reading Proverbs 3:5-6 , and that he ran from that call for four years before he gave in. He is an honors graduate of North Carolina Central University. He also holds a degree in Pastoral and Church Leadership from Valor Christian College in Columbus, Ohio, the school the Pentecostal preacher Rod Parsley founded at World Harvest Church. In one sermon he held up the Bible his college gave him, inscribed “Valedictorian of Valor Christian College, May 15, 2010.” He has been married to his wife Lena since August 2004, and they have two sons and two daughters. For about ten years he pastored a small Atlanta congregation called Victory Church. Looking back on those years, he has said he wanted to be rich and famous. The congregation was scattered during COVID. In December 2018 he traveled to Israel and, by his own account, had an encounter with God there that changed the direction of his ministry. In January 2023 he relaunched the work as 2819 Church, named for Matthew 28:19 , with 183 people. The growth since then has been very large. The church reports about 6,000 people in person each week and about 75,000 more watching online, and its YouTube channel is near two million subscribers. He preached through Matthew for about three years and has since moved through Acts and into Ephesians. He appears on TBN, co-hosts a touring podcast called Street Preachers with Florida pastor Tim Timberlake, and released his first book, Contend , on October 13, 2026.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The ACCESS Gatherings ACCESS is billed as “That Powerful Hour of Prayer.” Mitchell says it began more than twelve years ago as a family prayer hour in his parents’ home in Rex, Georgia, while his father was dying of cancer. After his father’s death the family kept the hour going, and it grew into church gatherings. In October 2025 it filled State Farm Arena in Atlanta and an overflow hall, with about 40,000 people reported. On October 10, 2026, ACCESS came to AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. The church said all 80,000 free tickets were claimed within eight hours. The evening moved through three parts called The Cross, The Warning, and The Cry, and it closed with the prayer “Maranatha! Come, Lord Jesus!” Mitchell says the event cost about three million dollars and that no admission or offering was taken. Two days later he posted on Facebook, “Just learned that a teenage girl was HEALED of deafness and removed her hearing aids last night at ACCESS in TX,” and added, “This to the glory of Christ.” No name, no family statement, and no medical record has been offered, and no independent report confirms it. A great crowd gathered to pray and to hear of the cross and the coming of Christ is no small thing, and no Christian should sneer at it. But the way Mitchell taught his church to understand ACCESS raises real problems, which the part on prayer below takes up.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: What He Gets Right Fairness comes first. A man should be judged by the whole of what he teaches, and Mitchell teaches a good deal that is true. Salvation by grace He denies salvation by works in plain words. His church’s statement says salvation is a gift of grace and is not earned by works. On The Breakfast Club he said, “You can never be enough to be accepted by God.” In a sermon on Matthew 15 , about thirty-eight minutes in, he said of Christ, “He never broke the law,” spoke of him “exchanging his righteousness for your unrighteousness,” and told his people, “you’re not righteous because you have good behavior.” He went on, “we are only righteous if we stand in Christ.” That’s the heart of imputed righteousness, and he preaches it with conviction. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV) Sin, election, and judgment He affirms election. In October 2026 he told his church, “God in eternity past chose you saved you before the foundation of the world.” He preaches hell as real. He calls sin by its name, and his sermon on Matthew 18 that passed two million views told hearers, “Stop treating sin like a pet. Kill it before it kills you.” Readers of John Owen will hear the echo. In his sermon on the ten virgins he taught that the foolish virgins “represent every man and woman who thinks they are Christians, but they are really not.” That’s a needed word in a land full of false assurance. Money He rejects the prosperity gospel by name. Preaching on mountain-moving faith from Matthew 21 he said, “this ain’t prosperity gospel” and “this ain’t name it or claim it,” and he added, “we have no guarantees, yours is to just pray with faith.” He has taught that tithing “is not structured to be bound in the New Testament” and that “we give out of the generosity of our heart.” Preaching on Acts 2 he warned that the early church’s generosity “is not permission for gospel grifting.” The Holy Spirit On the Spirit he is more careful than many charismatics. He teaches that Spirit baptism is “that salvific moment when the Holy Spirit unites a person with the Lord Jesus Christ,” which ties it to conversion. He noted that some traditions place it later, but he did not press that view. He also teaches that the tongues of Pentecost were real human languages. Humility and counsel He tells his people, “He’s just a man. Come feel God’s presence,” and he has urged them not to “idolize a preacher.” He has told visitors from other cities to go home and “find a Bible teaching church where the word of God is being communicated.” In April 2025 a sermon of his told Black parents to “stop blaming white cops for the killing of Black kids,” and it caused deep grief. He publicly apologized and said his framing “was and is harmful.” Not every preacher with his following is willing to do that. These strengths are real, and they help explain why so many young people have been stirred by his preaching. They also explain why his errors are dangerous. Error rarely comes to the table alone. It usually comes on the same plate as truth, and the truth makes it easier to swallow.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The Person of Christ The most serious finding concerns the doctrine of Christ. In “Stay Awake,” a sermon on Matthew 24:36-51 published August 11, 2025, Mitchell took up the question of how Jesus could say he did not know the day of his return. About seventeen minutes in, the published transcript records these words. His own words. “Christ, when he was on the earth, was fully God and fully human at the same time. … if he’s God, he is all-knowing. … I think the canosis of Philippians 2 solves this question. … he emptied himself, the canosis in Greek, of some of his divine nature, so that he can fully step into human. … The evidence that he emptied himself is that he needed to pray just like you.” “Stay Awake,” Matthew 24:36-51 , about 16 to 18 minutes. “Canosis” is the transcript’s spelling of the Greek word kenosis. A few minutes later, about twenty-two minutes in, he adds, “I do believe now that he’s seated at the right hand of the father he probably knows the day and the hour.” That line confirms what he meant. He believes the Son gave up his divine knowledge for a time and has it again now. This view is called kenotic Christology. It teaches that the eternal Son laid aside some of his divine attributes in order to become man. The text Mitchell leaned on doesn’t say that. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: Philippians 2:5-7 (KJV) The words “made himself of no reputation” stand for the Greek word Mitchell reached for, which many newer Bibles put as “emptied himself.” But look at how Paul says it was done. The Son made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. He humbled himself by taking something. He added a true human nature to the divine nature he always had. He veiled the outward blaze of his glory and stooped to the lowest place, all the way to the cross. He didn’t subtract any part of his Godhead, and he couldn’t have. Deity has no parts to give away, and God doesn’t change. If the Son gave up some of his divine nature, then the One who walked in Galilee was something less than God. For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Colossians 2:9 (KJV) The Westminster Confession states the church’s settled faith with great care. The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance, and equal with the Father, did, when the fulness of time was come, take upon him man’s nature, with all the essential properties and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin; being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the Virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God, and very man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man. Westminster Confession of Faith 8.2 So how could the Son say he did not know the day? The Reformed answer, with Calvin and the older church, is that Christ spoke according to his human nature. His human mind was a true human mind. It grew and learned, just as Luke tells us. And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man. Luke 2:52 (KJV) But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. Matthew 24:36 (KJV) As God, the Son knew all things, even while he lay in the manger. As man, he learned and grew. Both are true of one Person, and neither nature was traded away for the other. That’s how Jesus could pray, hunger, and grow weary while he upheld all things by the word of his power. Mitchell is right that Christ’s prayer life shows his true humanity. He is wrong that the Son emptied himself “of some of his divine nature,” and that error sits at the foundation of the faith. Charity requires us to notice that Mitchell said in the same breath that Christ was fully God, and his church’s written statement confesses the same. The fairest reading is that he is confused, and not that he means to deny the deity of Christ. But a confused account of who Jesus is, preached to a vast audience and left standing, is a grave matter all the same. A man who titled his book Contend ought to be the first to contend here. This research found no public correction of this teaching. Because the transcript is made by machine, any believer who wants to confirm the wording can listen to “Stay Awake” on the 2819 Church podcast at about the seventeen minute mark. The wording is clear, and the later line about Christ knowing the day “now” only makes sense if he meant what the first line says.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
section: Claims of Direct Words From God
text: Claims of Direct Words From God Mitchell often speaks of God charging him and telling him things directly. The clearest example is his account of Israel in December 2018. In a sermon titled “A Clarion Call” he describes a man in Israel who laid hands on him and prayed over him. His own words. “He says, receive a double anointed [anointing] and lays his hands on me. And prays over me. … God charge you. Go back to your nation. … I’ve been charged by God almighty in the holy land of Israel.” “A Clarion Call,” about 28 to 29 minutes. Later in the same sermon he says, “And I can hear God telling me, man, there’s a work for you to do over here, my son.” The pattern runs through other sources too. The Associated Press reported in December 2025 that Mitchell “said God told him to preach without bringing prepared notes onstage.” In a sermon on faith he described “using my mouth in prayer and prophecy to agree with everything God already told me.” Speaking of the worship planned for ACCESS, he said, “I feel that in my spirit.” To his credit, he also warns against careless talk. In that same Israel sermon he said, “God said, two dangerous words,” and added, “Anytime I hear somebody say, God said, I’ve got a question, an eyebrow raised.” The trouble is that he doesn’t hold his own claims to that warning. God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; Hebrews 1:1-2 (KJV) All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 (KJV) The Westminster Confession says Holy Scripture is most necessary, “those former ways of God’s revealing his will unto his people being now ceased” ( WCF 1.1 ). It also says that to the whole counsel of God set down in Scripture “nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men” ( WCF 1.6 ). Reformed Christians don’t deny that God guides his people today. He guides by his Word, by his providence, and by wise counsel, and the Spirit opens our eyes to the Scriptures. A man may come home from Israel with a heavy burden for his nation, and God may use that burden greatly. What Scripture does not give us is fresh speech from God that carries his authority. When a preacher says “God told me,” his hearers rightly take him to mean that God has spoken. If God did not speak, then the claim puts words in God’s mouth. If God did speak, then his word binds the hearer just as the Bible does. Either way the claim is far heavier than charismatic preachers usually treat it. The practical danger is authority. In a 2025 sermon Mitchell told his church, “If you don’t like the vessel, pray for the vessel, especially if God sent the vessel.” A ministry whose founding story rests on a personal charge from God is very hard to correct, because a brother who questions the preacher seems to be questioning the God who sent him. Scripture gives every believer a better rule. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21 (KJV)

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
section: Prayer, Portals, and a Demand on God
text: Prayer, Portals, and a Demand on God In “Expectations for ACCESS,” published in October 2025, Mitchell prepared his church for the Atlanta gathering. He rightly said that ACCESS “is a gathering of prayer” and that he named it for the access believers have in prayer. Then, about thirty-seven minutes in, he described the event this way. His own words. “We’re going to make the arena a portal from earth to heaven. … we will put a demand on him to come down.” “Expectations for ACCESS,” about 36 to 39 minutes. He also told them to expect “spiritual healing” and “even physical healing,” and he prayed for “signs and wonders and miracles and healing and deliverance.” Talk of portals and of placing a demand on heaven comes from the charismatic revival culture of open heavens and spiritual atmospheres. It has no place in Christian prayer. Believers already have access to the Father, and they have it in every place, because Christ opened the way by his own blood. Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; Hebrews 10:19-20 (KJV) A stadium is no nearer to heaven than a farmhouse kitchen. Jesus said as much to the woman at the well. Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father. … But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. John 4:21 , 23 (KJV) Neither prayer, nor any other part of religious worship, is now, under the gospel, either tied unto, or made more acceptable by any place in which it is performed, or towards which it is directed: but God is to be worshipped everywhere, in spirit and truth. Westminster Confession of Faith 21.6 No man puts a demand on God. We come as children who ask, and our Father gives according to his will. But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. Matthew 6:7-8 (KJV) And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: 1 John 5:14 (KJV) The irony is painful. The gathering is named ACCESS, and access to God is exactly what Christ purchased for every believer in every room at every hour. Telling thousands of young Christians that a packed arena can become a portal draws them away from the closet and the Lord’s Day assembly, which are the places God has promised to meet them. Mitchell did say he wants people to pray in God’s will, and he isn’t teaching occult ritual. But the words he chose teach a wrong idea of prayer, and the crowd hears the words.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
section: Fasting and Promises God Did Not Make
text: Fasting and Promises God Did Not Make In January 2025 Mitchell called 2819 Church to a week of fasting in a sermon titled “So We Fasted,” from Ezra 8:21-23 . He said, “For the majority of us, 85%, 90%, I’m calling you to what’s called a total fast,” and for himself, “water only.” He did offer a partial fast as another path. Fasting is biblical, and the Westminster Confession counts “solemn fastings” among the proper parts of worship upon special occasions ( WCF 21.5 ). A pastor may rightly call his flock to humble themselves before God. The trouble lies in what Mitchell said fasting does. His own words. “I will weaken you so that who I really am, a spirit inside of a body can grow strong in intimacy with Christ. … When you fast, you hear God more clearly. … When you fast, you can move God to intervene in circumstances. … You’re going to be radically transformed. Your bodies are going to be healed.” “So We Fasted,” Ezra 8:21-23 , about 15 and 48 minutes. Several problems stand out. The picture of a man as “a spirit inside of a body” isn’t how Scripture speaks. God made man a unity of body and soul, and the body is his good creation. The phrase echoes a saying the Word of Faith teachers made popular, that man is a spirit who has a soul and lives in a body. Fasting also doesn’t “move God” as though our hunger pulls a lever in heaven. God answers prayer freely, out of his own fatherly goodness. Worst of all, Mitchell promised a congregation that their bodies would be healed. God made no such promise. When that promise fails, the weak are left to wonder whether their faith or their fast was too small. Scripture warns that hard treatment of the body can look like wisdom and still leave sin untouched. Sin is put to death by the Spirit, through faith in Christ. Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. Colossians 2:23 (KJV) For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. Romans 8:13 (KJV) Mitchell did say that God “can do anything he desires to do in the context of his will.” That’s true, and it should have governed the whole sermon. A pastor should also use great care before calling most of his church to a seven-day water fast, since any large congregation holds many people with medical reasons that make such a fast unwise.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Signs, Tongues, and Healing Reports Mitchell is a continuationist, meaning he believes the miraculous gifts continue in the church today. Preaching on Acts 2:42-47 he said, “the Holy Spirit still does signs and wonders through people,” and “We still lay hands and see healing.” In his sermon on Acts 2:1-13 he said the tongues of 1 Corinthians 14 are different from Pentecost, that “Paul tells that this is a gift for prayer,” and that it “requires a gift of interpretation.” In a sermon reported by Charisma he said, “Suddenly, He can heal a physical body.” He has also published healing reports, like the deaf girl at ACCESS, with no evidence beyond the report itself. He isn’t a classic Pentecostal. He doesn’t teach tongues as the required sign of Spirit baptism, and he ties Spirit baptism to conversion. He has also spoken tenderly of a church member who died, saying, “although she was not physically healed in this life, she is completely healed right now.” That’s the right comfort for grieving saints, and it shows he doesn’t teach that God always heals. Reformed churches confess that God still heals, and that he answers the prayers of his people for the sick. James 5 calls the elders to pray over the sick, and believers should do so with faith. What the Confession denies is that the revealing gifts and sign gifts that marked the apostolic age go on as an ordinary part of church life. Healing claims announced from a pulpit or on social media, with no names and no proof, also put the honor of Christ at risk. When such reports prove false, unbelievers mock, and believers who were not healed grow confused about God. A man isn’t a false teacher simply because he is a continuationist. Many godly brothers hold that view. But for a Reformed believer this is a real line, and in Mitchell’s case it feeds the larger problem described under claims of direct words from God .

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Assurance and Perseverance Mitchell affirms election, yet he speaks of the believer’s final salvation as hanging on the believer. In “Blessed in Christ,” preached in October 2026 from Ephesians 1 , he said, “the one who adopted you will bring you all the way into the kingdom so long as you stay in his will.” A clip that circulated in early 2025 carries his line, “Too many of you think once saved always saved.” In “Woe to You” he warned that “people who used to be on fire are no longer on fire.” His burden is partly right. Many Americans presume they are saved because they once prayed a prayer, and Scripture warns them. The foolish virgins thought they were ready. The Reformed faith has never taught that a man may live in open rebellion and rest on a past decision. But the Reformed faith also doesn’t hang final salvation on the believer’s staying power. They whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved. Westminster Confession of Faith 17.1 And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand. John 10:28-29 (KJV) Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ: Philippians 1:6 (KJV) The sinner who truly believes will persevere, and he perseveres because God keeps him. Warnings are one of the means God uses to keep him, so a faithful preacher holds the warning and the promise together. Mitchell gives the warning loudly and the promise faintly. A doubting saint who hears “so long as you stay in his will” will look inward at his own record and find no rest there. The Reformed answer turns his eyes to Christ, who loses none of those the Father gave him. This research found no evidence that Mitchell teaches sinless perfection or that a single sin undoes salvation. His view is best described as unsettled and leaning toward conditional security. Believers who struggle with assurance should be especially careful here, and may find help in Will God Keep Me to the End?

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Handling the Text Mitchell calls himself an expository preacher, and he does preach through whole books of the Bible. That’s a good practice. But at times his application goes beyond what the text says. In “Be a Witness,” preached in April 2026, he said Jesus told the parable of the ten virgins to show that at his return “he would find half of his people ready for his return and another half of his people who was not ready for his return.” This is a good place to think about what in Scripture is meant literally and what is meant as a figure. A parable is a true lesson told through a story. Its details serve the main point, and they aren’t always meant to be read as hard facts. Five wise and five foolish sets the two kinds side by side. It isn’t a count of how many professing Christians will be ready on the last day. Notice also that both groups slept. While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. Matthew 25:5 (KJV) The wise were not wiser because they stayed awake. They were wiser because they had oil. In his earlier sermon on this parable, “A Cry for Readiness,” Mitchell taught it better. He noted that “all of the women fell asleep” and said the foolish “represent every man and woman who thinks they are Christians, but they are really not.” That’s sound. The later line about “half of his people” shows a habit of loose application that careful hearers need to watch for, and that risk grows for any preacher who goes into the pulpit without notes.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Money, Tickets, and Answering Critics In 2026 Mitchell and Tim Timberlake, senior pastor of Celebration Church in Jacksonville, Florida, took their Street Preachers podcast on an eight-city tour. General admission ran about $60 to $70. A $200 VIP ticket added a meet-and-greet with the hosts, a free book, and merchandise discounts. Every stop sold out. When Christians objected, Mitchell answered from the pulpit. He said the tour was paid for from his own pocket and not by his church, that venues and security cost money, and that “We’re not doing this for a bag.” He also called his critics a “brood of vipers,” the words John the Baptist used for the Pharisees, and he pointed to a child he said was healed at one of the events. On The Breakfast Club he said he takes no offering at Sunday services and that he is “not a grifter.” This research found no evidence that Mitchell preaches a prosperity gospel, and ACCESS itself was free. Scripture also allows those who preach to be paid for their labor. Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. 1 Corinthians 9:14 (KJV) Yet selling time with a preacher is a different thing from covering the cost of a room. Paul set himself apart from those who made a trade of the Word. For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ. 2 Corinthians 2:17 (KJV) Premier Christianity noted that Mitchell’s long rebuttal never addressed the VIP ticket, which drew the strongest objection. Branding fellow believers who raise a concern as a “brood of vipers” also isn’t the gentle answer a shepherd owes. When a celebrated preacher answers criticism by naming his critics Pharisees, he teaches a great many young believers that any question about their preacher is an attack from the devil. Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. 1 Peter 5:2-3 (KJV) By comparison, his giving appeals to his own church have been measured. In early 2025 he asked for a special offering toward a five million dollar building over thirty-six months. He used the language of sowing, but he named no amount and promised no harvest, and he said, “if this makes you feel uncomfortable, then don’t do it.” That’s to his credit.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Training, Associations, and Influences A man’s teachers don’t settle his doctrine, but they do shape the way he thinks. Mitchell’s formal Bible training came from Valor Christian College, founded by Rod Parsley at World Harvest Church in Columbus, Ohio. He graduated as valedictorian in 2010, and in a sermon on honor he said that to throw the Bible his school gave him on the floor would “dishonor Pastor Parsley.” Parsley’s ministry is a classic Pentecostal seed-faith ministry. A current appeal on his website promises “seven powerful blessings of atonement for you when you bring an offering,” including “FINANCIAL overflow” and “A DOUBLE portion from the Lord.” Critics have also tied Parsley to dominionist politics. Mitchell has not taken up Parsley’s money teaching, and he openly rejects it. Even so, the “double anointing” prayer in Israel, the talk of portals and demands, the fasting promises, and the pulpit healing reports all fit the world in which he was trained. This research found no public statement in which Mitchell distances himself from that school or its founder. His other ties are mixed. In one sermon he said, “Thank God for Jakes,” speaking of T.D. Jakes, a preacher long tied to Oneness Pentecostalism and prosperity teaching, and he gave no word of caution. He co-hosts with Tim Timberlake, appears on TBN, and is promoted by Charisma magazine. On the other side, he has been welcomed on Josh Howerton’s program, the author Jackie Hill Perry and her husband Preston Perry attend 2819, and the church’s worship team has partnered with Reach Records. No evidence was found that Mitchell belongs to the New Apostolic Reformation or claims the office of apostle. He is best described as a conservative charismatic evangelical, trained in Pentecostal circles, who has moved toward a sharper doctrine of sin and grace while keeping many charismatic habits of speech and practice.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: The Church and Its Government 2819 Church is nondenominational. Its written statement confesses the Trinity, the full deity and full humanity of Christ, the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture, and salvation by grace through faith. It practices believer’s baptism and a memorial Lord’s Supper with bread and grape juice. Those last two points differ from Presbyterian conviction, though many faithful Baptists share them. Its government is much less clear. Mitchell refers to “the elders,” and the church names him and his wife Lena as its leaders, but it publishes no list of elders, no account of how leaders are chosen or held accountable, and no plan of church discipline. In a 2025 sermon he told visitors there is no membership requirement at 2819. A church of thousands, with tens of thousands more “Digital Disciples” watching online, can’t be shepherded the way Hebrews 13:17 describes unless the shepherds know the sheep and the sheep belong to a flock. A livestream can’t do that work.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
section: Worship and the Danger of Idolizing a Preacher
text: Worship and the Danger of Idolizing a Preacher The Lord’s Day gathering at 2819 Church is built like a concert. Reporters have described a countdown clock, loud music and percussion, strobe lights, and a smoke machine. Volunteers pray over each seat, greeters dance, and the worship team moves from a fast song into a slow one while the room lifts its hands. People line up before dawn to get in, and some travel hundreds of miles each Sunday. ACCESS carried the same pattern into the arenas, with a produced program and tens of thousands gathered around one preacher. What God requires in worship Reformed churches hold what is called the regulative principle of worship. God alone decides how he is to be worshipped, and the church may add nothing he has not commanded. But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture. Westminster Confession of Faith 21.1 Smoke, strobes, and countdown clocks are devices of men. They exist to shape the mood of a room, and they work on the feelings whether the preacher intends it or not. When a gathering is built that way, it becomes very hard for anyone in the room to tell the work of the Spirit from the work of the lighting. God has given his church plain means for worship in the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, the singing of praise, and the sacraments. Those means need no help from a production team. Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear: for our God is a consuming fire. Hebrews 12:28-29 (KJV) Feelings aren’t the enemy. David danced before the Lord, and the Psalms are full of tears and shouts. But holy affection rises out of truth understood. When a room is engineered to stir the feelings first, people learn to measure God’s presence by what they feel, and they go looking for the next service or the next stadium that can make them feel it again. Signs of a culture built around one man Concern about idolizing Mitchell has been raised in public and more than once. Reporters note the enthusiastic reaction whenever he takes the stage, and one observer reported that some members have begun dressing like him. VIP tickets that included a meet-and-greet with him sold for $200, and every stop on the Street Preachers tour sold out. In 2025 a woman interrupted a service to call the church to repent of idolizing its pastor, and security removed her. In August 2026 a visiting minister said he was removed after raising the same concern. The matter has come up often enough that Mitchell addressed it on The Breakfast Club , saying “there is a difference between idolization and admiration.” Mitchell says the right things about it. He has told his church, “He’s just a man. Come feel God’s presence. It’s much better,” and he has urged them to thank God for growth “and not idolize a preacher.” He should be taken at his word that he wants no worship for himself. But his platform pulls against his warnings. He sells paid time with himself on tour. He builds stadium events around his own voice. He tells his church, “If you don’t like the vessel, pray for the vessel, especially if God sent the vessel.” His whole ministry rests on a story of a personal charge from God in Israel. Every one of those things lifts the man, and none of them is required by his calling. A preacher who means his warnings will take down the platforms that feed the problem. John the Baptist showed the right spirit. He must increase, but I must decrease. John 3:30 (KJV) Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man? I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. 1 Corinthians 3:5-7 (KJV) Why this makes him a particular danger Movements like Bethel Church in Redding, California, are easy for conservative believers to spot. Mitchell is much harder to spot. He sounds like a sound evangelical. He preaches sin and repentance and grace, and he draws young believers who would never go near Bethel. So his errors reach ears that are otherwise on guard. His growth has been sudden and enormous. He relaunched with 183 people in January 2023. He now draws about 6,000 a week in person and tens of thousands online, and in the space of a year he filled State Farm Arena and then AT&T Stadium. If he keeps teaching the errors documented in this report at that scale, inside a culture of spectacle that lifts the preacher, he will do as much harm as Bethel has done. He will do it through a door that conservative churches have left open.

title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
section: What This Report Does Not Charge
text: What This Report Does Not Charge Some charges against Mitchell pass from video to video without proof. Fairness means saying plainly which ones the record does not support, so that no one repeats them. He is not shown to belong to the New Apostolic Reformation. No evidence was found that he is part of it or claims the office of apostle. He does not preach a money-for-blessing gospel. He rejects the prosperity gospel by name, teaches that the tithe does not bind the New Testament believer, and promised no harvest when he asked his church to give. He does not teach that God always heals. He has comforted grieving families with the hope that a saint who died unhealed is “completely healed right now.”

text: Summary of Findings The weight given to each finding follows the Westminster Standards. A grave finding touches the foundation of the faith. A serious finding departs from clear Reformed teaching in a way that harms hearers. A caution marks a weakness believers should watch for. Gospel of grace. title: Philip Anthony Mitchell
text: Counsel for the Saints Should Christians listen to Philip Anthony Mitchell? The answer of this report is no, not as a teacher to sit under. A believer may hear a clip and find something true in it, and truth is still truth when it comes from a man with errors. But a teacher is someone we trust to feed us week after week. Mitchell’s errors reach the person of Christ, the sufficiency of Scripture, and the nature of prayer itself, and those are not side issues. My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation. James 3:1 (KJV) Where should saints be most careful with him? Test anything he says about who Jesus is against the Creed and the Confession, beginning with the “Stay Awake” sermon. When he says God told him something, ask where God said it in his Word. Language about portals, atmospheres, and demands should send you back to Hebrews 10 , where Christ alone is our way to the Father. Promises of healing or breakthrough tied to fasting or to a gathering need a promise from God behind them, and he doesn’t supply one. And when he warns about false assurance, take the warning to heart, but rest your soul on the promise that Christ keeps his own. How should saints speak of him? With truth and with charity. Quote his own words when naming his errors. Don’t call him a wolf or a deceiver without proof of his motives, and don’t repeat charges the record doesn’t support. And pray for him. He has shown that he can humble himself and correct a public mistake. Christians should pray that he does the same about the person of Christ and the authority of Scripture. For regular feeding, point believers first to the faithful preaching of their own church, where elders know their names and watch over their souls. For further help, point them to men whose doctrine has stood the test of time, such as R.C. Sproul, Sinclair Ferguson, John MacArthur, Voddie Baucham, and Paul Washer, and behind them to J.C. Ryle, Charles Spurgeon, and the Puritans. Mitchell named his new book after the letter of Jude. The saints would do well to take that verse seriously. Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. Jude 3 (KJV) Contending for the faith begins with the faith about Christ himself. That’s where Mitchell most needs correction, and it’s where the church must stand most firmly.

title: About
text: About Gentle King What This Is Gentle King is a layman’s work. It’s a place to set out the gospel and sound doctrine where anyone can reach them for free. Two tools are made here and given away. Sojourner is a Bible study app for your phone, tablet, or computer. Mortify is an app for the daily fight against sin. They serve the work. They aren’t the heart of it. The name comes from the King himself. He rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed donkey. Isaiah said of him that he won't break a bruised reed or quench the smoking flax. He calls tired people to come to him, and he gives them rest. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Matthew 11:28-29 (KJV) He is gentle, and his authority is real. Those two things aren’t at odds. The throne is what makes the kindness worth anything. This site isn’t a church, and it’s no substitute for one. A website can’t preach to you, baptize you, feed you at the Lord’s Table, or watch over your soul. Christ gave those things to his church. Nothing here binds your conscience either. Scripture does that. The supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture. Westminster Confession of Faith 1.10 So read with your Bible open. If something written here doesn’t agree with it, throw that thing out and keep the Bible.

title: About

If anything here is wrong, it’s mine, and I’d rather know than be flattered.

title: About
text: Statement of faith What I Believe A short summary, put plainly. Not a new confession, only an honest account of the faith everything here is written from. The Scriptures The sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are the Word of God, breathed out by him, true in all they teach, and the only infallible rule of faith and life. All of it points to Christ. God and the Trinity One living and true God, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in his being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness, and truth. In the one divine being there are three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the same in substance, equal in power and glory. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit, yet there is one God and not three. Man and Sin God made man upright and in his own image. In Adam we fell. We come into the world guilty, corrupt at the root, and justly under the wrath of God. Sin is no weakness to manage. It earns death. The Person of Christ The eternal Son of God took a true human nature into union with his divine person and will never lay it down. Two natures, one person, forever. He is the one mediator between God and men. The Work of Christ He kept the law we broke. He died in the place of his people, bearing the wrath our sins deserved. He rose bodily, ascended, and reigns now at the Father’s right hand, praying for all the Father gave him. Not one will be lost. Salvation By grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. God justifies the ungodly by crediting to them the perfect righteousness of Christ, which faith simply receives. Good works follow that verdict gladly. They never purchase it. And Christ is held out freely to everyone who hears, so that no one who comes to him is turned away. The Holy Spirit He convicts of sin, gives new birth to a dead heart, unites the sinner to Christ, works faith and repentance, and finishes what he starts. A dead man doesn’t believe and then come alive. The Spirit gives life first, and faith is what that new life does. The Church and the Sacraments Christ has one church, gathered under his Word, led by officers he appointed, fed by the ordinary means of grace, which are the Word, the sacraments, and prayer. Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are signs and seals of the covenant of grace, not empty ceremony. The Christian Life The law is no ladder to climb for life. It is the rule a freed son gladly walks by. The believer puts sin to death by the Spirit and grows slowly and really. Sanctification always follows justification and never grounds it. Last Things Jesus Christ will return bodily, visibly, and in glory. The dead will be raised. He will judge the living and the dead, send the impenitent into everlasting punishment, and make all things new. Those are certainties. On the millennium I am amillennial. I hold it with an open hand toward fellow believers who read it otherwise. Faithful Reformed men land in different places there. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV) The fuller statement isn’t mine. This site holds the Westminster Confession of Faith, with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, as its doctrinal standard. I receive them as my own church receives them, as a faithful summary of what the Bible teaches. Everything here is written to stand within them. This site is my own work, not my church’s, and its elders don’t answer for it. The Standards are quoted here from the text of 1647. Read the Confession in full at The Westminster Standard , and see the doctrine page for more.

title: About
text: Before you go A Word to You Don’t stop here. A page can hand you a book, a definition, a place to start. It can’t sit with you when your marriage is breaking, or bury your father. It can’t put bread and wine in your hands and tell you Christ was broken for you. What a page can do is hand you Scripture for that hour , and then send you to the church. So find a church where the Word is preached plainly and fully, the sacraments are given as Christ gave them, and sinners are loved and corrected. Sit under men who will answer for your soul. And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. Hebrews 10:24-25 (KJV) And if you’re afraid he won’t have you, hear him say it himself. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. John 6:37 (KJV) The King is gentle, and he is worth more than everything you would leave behind to come to him. If you’re not sure where you stand with him, start with the gospel .

But Scripture also warns against false confidence. These articles take both seriously, following Westminster Confession chapters 17 and 18. You'll find practical counsel here, but the first question is always what the Lord has said. Am I Really Saved? God does not want his children living on guesses. John wrote his first letter to believers so that they would know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). 5 min read When the Same Sin Keeps Coming Back Few things shake a Christian like meeting the same sin again, years after he first wept over it. Your fear draws one conclusion from that. God has drawn another, and he has written it down. 6 min read The Unpardonable Sin and Falling Away Some fears come back at night, when the house is quiet and there is nothing to do but think. Each of these has an answer that will not give way under you. 6 min read When God Feels Far There are seasons when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling and the Bible is only ink. They do not mean that God has gone. 7 min read Doubts and Unwanted Thoughts Some believers are afraid it is not true, and the question will not leave them alone. Others are afraid of what their own minds keep saying to them. 4 min read Is God Punishing Me? The diagnosis comes, or the child dies, or the marriage comes apart. Under the grief a harder question rises, about what God thinks of you. 4 min read Afraid of Dying Christians still die, and many of them dread it. Hebrews says the Son of God took flesh and blood for this very reason. 4 min read Will God Keep Me to the End? Underneath all these fears is the same suspicion, that in the end it all hangs on you.
