title: Why Doctrine Matters
section: Why Doctrine Isn't the Enemy of Devotion
text: Why Doctrine Isn't the Enemy of Devotion Start Here Doctrine is simply what you believe about God. You already have some. The only real question is whether it’s true. You can't speak of Jesus without saying who he is, what he has done, and why he came. Those are doctrines. You've said he is real. You've said something about who he is and what he has done. The man who says God is love is teaching doctrine. So is the man who says God would never send anyone to hell. Nobody stands outside of doctrine. We only stand inside good doctrine or bad. There's a real danger here, and it should be named. A person can know the terms and never know the Lord. He can argue well and pray little. That’s a sad thing, and Scripture warns about it. But the cure for cold knowledge isn’t less knowledge. It’s knowledge that reaches the heart. You can’t love a God you’ve refused to learn anything about. You can’t trust a Savior whose work you’ve never understood. The doctrines on this page aren’t a cage around Christ. They’re windows. Each one lets more light in on his face. If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. John 8:31-32 (KJV) So read slowly. Look up the references. Ask God to show you himself in it.

title: The Bible
text: Why Scripture is our final rule of faith and life.

title: The Bible
text: The Word of God Sola Scriptura Everything else on this page rests here. If God hasn’t spoken, we have nothing to say. God has spoken, and his speech has been written down. The old word for it's inspiration. The Bible didn’t float down from heaven. Men wrote it, in their own words and settings and styles, and the Holy Spirit carried them along so that what they wrote is what God says. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 (KJV) Because God breathed it out, and because God doesn’t lie, the Bible is true in all that it affirms. Inerrancy concerns the Scriptures as God gave them. Copies and translations must be tested against the original text. Scripture is also sufficient for what God calls us to believe and do. Sufficiency means you don’t need a new revelation to be saved and to live before God. Neither private revelations nor hidden traditions can add to the rule God has given. The whole counsel of God needed for salvation, faith and life is either expressly set down in Scripture or follows from it by good and necessary consequence, as the Confession says in WCF 1.6 . And because God meant to be understood, the Bible is clear where it matters most. Not every verse is equally easy. Peter said as much about Paul. But the things you must know to be saved are set out clearly enough that an unlearned reader, using the ordinary means, can understand them. WCF 1.7 says so. That’s why a working man with a Bible and a lunch break can feed on the Word of God. The Confession says the Old Testament was written in Hebrew and the New in Greek, and that these original texts are finally authoritative in disputes ( WCF 1.8 ). It calls for Scripture to be translated into the common languages of the nations. A faithful translation is a gift to the church. We ought to study difficult words carefully rather than treat a preferred English wording as the only inspired text. When a verse is hard, read what comes before and after it, and compare other passages that speak to the same matter. Scripture is its own infallible interpreter ( WCF 1.9 ). The true and full sense of a passage isn't ours to invent. God gave it, and we're to seek it. What then about the confessions and catechisms this site holds? They're subordinate standards. They’re a faithful summary of what Scripture teaches, tested by the church across centuries. They sit under the Bible and never beside it. This site teaches the original 1647 Westminster Confession and Catechisms. Later revisions mustn't be mistaken for their wording. The supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture. Westminster Confession of Faith 1.10

title: God and the Trinity
text: The one living God, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

title: God and the Trinity
text: God, and God as Trinity Theology Proper Before there was a world to save, there was God. He wasn’t lonely. He wasn’t waiting. He was full. God is spirit, infinite, eternal and unchangeable in his being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness and truth. He didn’t come from anywhere. He doesn’t grow or shrink or improve. He isn’t one part of the universe, and the universe isn’t one part of him. He made it out of nothing and upholds it every second by the word of his power. His attributes aren’t pieces bolted together. God isn’t partly holy and partly loving. Everything in God is God. His love is holy love. His justice is good justice. His mercy never embarrasses his righteousness. How God can be just and still justify the ungodly is exactly the question the cross answers. Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord : Deuteronomy 6:4 (KJV) This one God exists as three persons. Not three gods. Not one person wearing three masks. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and there's one God. The Father isn't the Son, the Son isn't the Spirit, and the Spirit isn't the Father. Each person is fully and equally God, undivided in essence, distinct in person. The Confession puts the distinction carefully in WCF 2.3 . The Father is of none, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son. None of it's a matter of one person coming after another in time or ranking below another in being. There are three persons in the Godhead; the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost; and these three are one God, the same in substance, equal in power and glory. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 6 This isn’t a riddle invented by councils. It’s what the Bible forces on anyone who reads it whole. Jesus sends his people to baptize in one name that belongs to Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Salvation itself is Trinitarian. The Father chooses, the Son redeems, the Spirit applies. If you’ve been saved, all three persons have been at work on you. Guard your words here. Every homemade picture of the Trinity ends up teaching an old heresy. That goes for water and ice and steam, and for a man who is father and son and husband. It’s better to say less and say it carefully.

title: The Five Solas
text: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

title: The Five Solas
text: Alone Means Alone The Five Solas The Reformation didn’t recover five slogans. It recovered one gospel, and these are the five hinges it turns on. Sola Scriptura, Scripture alone Scripture is the only infallible rule for faith and life. Tradition can be useful and pastors can be gifted, but only the Bible binds the conscience. Everything else is weighed and either received or set aside. Sola Gratia, grace alone Salvation begins in God, not in you. You didn’t supply the deciding factor. Grace isn’t God meeting you halfway once you make the first move. Grace is God coming all the way down to a dead man and giving him life. Sola Fide, faith alone You are justified by faith, apart from works of the law. Faith isn’t a good deed that earns a reward. It reaches out and takes. Even the faith is a gift, which is why no one will boast in heaven. Solus Christus, Christ alone There is one mediator between God and men. No saint, no priest, no sacrament, no sincerity of yours stands in that place. Christ obeyed where Adam failed and bore the wrath his people owed. He rose, ascended, and prays for his people now. Soli Deo Gloria, to God alone be glory If salvation is by grace, through faith, in Christ, according to Scripture, then the credit has only one address. This isn’t God being vain. It’s God being honest about who did the saving. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9 (KJV) At the center of all five sits justification. God declares the guilty righteous, not by making them righteous first, but by pardoning their sins and counting Christ’s righteousness as theirs. Those whom God effectually calleth, He also freely justifieth: not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ’s sake alone. Westminster Confession of Faith 11.1 Sanctification follows that verdict. It never props it up. You obey because you're accepted, never in order to become accepted. The gospel page works out the imputed righteousness of Christ at length.

title: The Doctrines of Grace
text: How God brings sinners to Christ and keeps them.

title: The Doctrines of Grace
text: How God Saves Sinners The Doctrines of Grace These five points were never meant to be the whole of the faith. They're an answer to a specific question. When God saves a sinner, who does the saving? Read them as one sentence about one God working one salvation. Taken apart they can sound cold. Taken together they're a deep comfort, because they mean your salvation doesn’t finally rest on how tightly you hold on. Total Depravity Also called total inability Sin has touched every part of us, mind and will and affections, so that no one seeks God on his own. The word total is about extent, not degree. No part of us is clean enough to save the rest. Paul lays this out in Romans 3 , and Ephesians 2 calls us dead in trespasses. Unconditional Election Ephesians 1:4-5 Before the foundation of the world God set his love on a people in Christ. He didn’t choose because he looked ahead through time and saw who would choose him. It rested on the good pleasure of his will. Paul defends it at length in Romans 9 , including the objections it raises. Particular Redemption Commonly called limited atonement Christ didn’t die to make salvation merely possible. He died to actually save particular people, and he won’t lose them. His death is of infinite worth, and Christ is freely offered in the gospel to every sinner who hears. But its saving design and effect are for his sheep. Effectual Calling Sometimes called irresistible grace Alongside the outward call of the gospel to all, the Spirit gives an inward call that raises the dead. Ezekiel 36 promised it, and the new birth is where God makes good on the promise. New life comes first, and then the sinner comes willingly, because he has been made willing. Perseverance of the Saints Kept by the power of God Those truly united to Christ will be kept to the end. They may fall badly and grieve the Spirit, but they'll be brought back. This isn’t a promise that a prayer you once prayed guarantees heaven. It’s a promise that what God began in you he will bring to completion, as Philippians 1:6 says. I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. John 10:11 (KJV) He doesn’t say he makes a sheepfold available. He lays down his life for the sheep, and he gets them. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. John 6:37 (KJV) Both halves of that verse are yours to hold. The first half tells you election works. The second half tells you the door is open, right now, to you. If you’re worried about whether you’re chosen, stop looking inward and come to Christ. Nobody who comes is turned away. For a fuller answer to the views these points were written against, see How to Answer Arminianism and Pelagianism .

title: Covenant Theology
text: One covenant of grace across the Old and New Testaments.

title: Covenant Theology
text: One Story, Two Testaments Covenant Theology God has always dealt with his people by covenant. Learn the covenants and the Bible stops feeling like a pile of disconnected stories. Scripture speaks of a people given by the Father to the Son before the world began ( John 6:37-39 , Ephesians 1:4 ). Reformed theologians commonly call God's eternal purpose in the work of the Father, Son, and Spirit the covenant of redemption. That name is a theological explanation, not the name of a separate chapter in the 1647 Westminster Confession. The Confession clearly teaches the eternal decree and the Son's saving work ( WCF 3 and 8). In the garden God dealt with Adam in a covenant of works. Perfect obedience, and life. Disobedience, and death. Adam stood there not only for himself but for all who would come from him. He failed, and the ruin spread to every one of us. After the fall, God promised salvation in Christ. The Confession calls this the covenant of grace ( WCF 7.3 ). Man by his fall having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace; wherein He freely offereth unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ; requiring of them faith in Him, that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal life His Holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. Westminster Confession of Faith 7.3 Here’s the part that changes how you read. There aren’t two ways of salvation in the Bible, law for the old and grace for the new. There's one covenant of grace administered in two ways. Under the old administration it came through promise, sacrifice, priesthood and shadow. Under the new it comes with the substance itself, Christ crucified and risen, preached to the nations. Abraham was justified by faith exactly as you are. The difference is that he looked forward and you look back. And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise. Galatians 3:29 (KJV) The covenant of grace is one in substance under both testaments, not two different ways for a sinner to be justified ( WCF 7.5-6 ). Its outward administration has changed, and the old sacrifices have passed away in Christ. This matters for baptism as well. The original Confession teaches that infants of believing parents are to receive the covenant sign ( WCF 28.4 ). The sign doesn't make every recipient regenerate, but God's promise and command aren't limited to adults who can already describe their faith. So when you open Leviticus, you aren’t reading a foreign religion. You’re watching God teach his people, in blood and smoke and careful ritual, what sin costs and what a substitute is for. When you read the prophets, you’re hearing a covenant Lord pleading with a covenant people. And at the Supper you hear Jesus say the cup is the new covenant in his blood. The whole Old Testament leans forward into that sentence. For a fuller treatment of the covenant sign, read Baptism . Families can also use Family Worship and Church Membership .

title: Law and Gospel
text: What God commands and what he gives in Christ.

title: Law and Gospel
text: Two Words From One God Law and Gospel The law tells you what God requires. The gospel tells you what God has done. Confuse them and you'll lose both. God’s law is holy. Our sin is the reason it condemns us. God’s law puts his own character into commandments, and it does three kinds of work. The law restrains. Even among people who hate God, the law written on the conscience and echoed in a nation’s laws holds back some of the evil that would otherwise swallow us. It shows you what you are. Held up to the commandments, you stop guessing about yourself. The law was never given as a ladder. It is a mirror, and it drives the honest sinner to Christ. For the believer, it guides. He’s already justified and safe, so he takes the law as the rule of a grateful life. This is the third use, and Reformed Christians have always insisted on it. Two errors wait on either side of this teaching, and both are deadly. Legalism takes the law and makes it the ground of acceptance. It says God will love you if you clean yourself up. It turns obedience into a payment and Christ into an assistant. The legalist is either crushed or proud, and often both in the same week. Antinomianism takes grace and uses it as permission. It says that since works don’t justify, obedience doesn’t matter. Paul had already heard that argument, and he didn’t treat it gently. What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? Romans 6:1-2 (KJV) The original Confession distinguishes Israel's ceremonial laws from the moral law. The ceremonies were fulfilled and ended in Christ. Israel's judicial laws expired with that nation's state, except as their general equity may require ( WCF 19.3-4 ). We shouldn't lift an ancient civil penalty out of its covenant setting without asking what enduring justice it teaches. This matters when discussing the duties of modern magistrates. The Confession says in WCF 19.6 and 19.7 that the believer is free from the law as a covenant of works. He is still bound to it as a rule of life. And these uses of the law aren't contrary to the grace of the gospel but sweetly comply with it. The commandments no longer threaten a justified man with the curse. They show him what love looks like in the concrete. You keep the law because you're loved, never to become loved.

title: The Church and Worship
text: The church, worship, and the ordinary means of grace.

title: The Church and Worship
text: Where Christ Feeds His People The Church Christ didn’t save you and leave you on your own. He put you in a body, and he set a table in it. Christ gathers the people he has redeemed into his church. They belong to him and to one another, and they live under his rule. He has appointed plain, ordinary means to give his grace, and they haven’t changed. The outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption are his ordinances, especially the word, sacraments, and prayer; all which are made effectual to the elect for salvation. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 88 The preached word comes first. Not a talk about the Bible, but the Bible opened, explained and pressed home, with Christ held out in it. God has been pleased to save and to strengthen through this plain thing week after week. Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace. It marks the washing away of sin, union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and belonging to God’s people. The Westminster Standards hold that it belongs to believers and to their children, as the covenant sign always has. The water doesn’t save. It signifies and seals what God does. At the Lord’s Supper, Christ nourishes his people through a sacrament that remembers his once-for-all sacrifice. Christ is really present, not bodily but spiritually, and he is received by faith as his people eat and drink. This meal strengthens repentant believers who trust him. And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. Acts 2:42 (KJV) Membership makes that care personal. To join a church is to be known, taught, corrected, and cared for by particular people. Elders must give account for their care of the flock ( Hebrews 13:17 ). Christ gives church officers the keys of the kingdom for teaching and discipline ( WCF 30.1-4 ). Their office is distinct from the civil magistrate's, although the original 1647 Confession also assigns the magistrate duties toward true religion ( WCF 23.3 ). Church censures aim at repentance, the recovery of offenders, and the purity of the church. On worship, the original Confession teaches what is called the regulative principle. God determines how he is to be worshiped ( WCF 21.1 ). Chapter 21.5 names the reading and preaching of Scripture, prayer, singing of psalms, and the sacraments as ordinary parts of public worship. This site follows the Reformed Presbyterian practice of unaccompanied psalm singing. The words of the 1647 Confession are the standard quoted here. Later revisions and differing Presbyterian interpretations must be identified rather than silently substituted. How God Wants to Be Worshiped explains the practice, and the civil magistrate guide explains the original Confession's teaching on public religion.

title: The End Times
text: Christ’s return, the resurrection, and the judgment.

title: The End Times
section: How It Ends, and What Is Settled
text: How It Ends, and What Is Settled Eschatology Start with what every Reformed believer confesses. It’s more than most people expect, and it’s enough to live and die on. Christ is reigning now, seated at the right hand of the Father, with all authority in heaven and on earth. He will return bodily, visibly, personally. The dead will be raised bodily, the righteous and the wicked alike. There will be a final judgment, real and just, and the wicked will be punished forever. Those in Christ will be acquitted openly and welcomed. Then come the new heavens and the new earth, where righteousness dwells and God himself lives with his people. And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away. Revelation 21:4 (KJV) From here on, faithful men differ. The question is how the thousand years of Revelation 20 relates to the present age and to Christ’s return. Two common answers within confessional Reformed Christianity are amillennialism and postmillennialism. Historic premillennialism is included below as an older Christian view for comparison, but it shouldn't be presented as a distinctive teaching of the original Westminster Confession. Amillennialism Held widely in Reformed churches The thousand years is the whole present age between Christ’s first and second comings. Satan is bound from deceiving the nations so the gospel can go out. The souls of the departed reign with Christ now. The kingdom advances through the Word while the world stays a mix of wheat and weeds. Christ returns once, and judgment and the new creation follow immediately. Postmillennialism Held by many Puritans and by Edwards The same gospel that saves one sinner will, in God’s time, bring an age of widespread blessing. The nations will be discipled in great numbers, and Christ’s rule will be honored broadly on earth before he returns. That age is the fruit of ordinary preaching and the Spirit’s power, not a separate dispensation. Christ returns at the close of it to judge and to make all things new. Historic Premillennialism An old view, distinct from dispensationalism Christ returns first, and a real reign on earth follows his coming. The church passes through tribulation and isn't removed from it. This view is ancient, and it isn’t built on a separation between Israel and the church. The man who writes this site holds the first view above. He’s amillennial. The original Westminster Confession doesn't name a millennial scheme. It does confess Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment ( WCF 32-33 ). Those settled truths must govern our reading of Revelation 20 . Distinguish an interpretation held by Reformed believers from what the Confession actually requires. Two cautions, though. Don't treat dispensational premillennialism, with its sharp split between Israel and the church and its secret rapture, as the Reformed position. It isn’t, and it came late. And don't let curiosity about the end replace readiness for it. The last things were given to make you holy and to comfort you while you wait.

title: The Westminster Standards
text: Where to begin with the Westminster Standards.

title: The Westminster Standards
section: The Standards, and the Savior in Them
text: Study all thirty-three chapters with Scripture proofs The Standards, and the Savior in Them Where to Go Next The Westminster Standards were written to instruct the church. Read them carefully, with Scripture open beside them. This site uses the original 1647 Westminster Confession of Faith and the original Larger and Shorter Catechisms. It doesn't substitute the American revision of 1788. The distinction matters in particular for Christian liberty ( WCF 20.4 ), the civil magistrate (23.3), and synods (31.2). Begin with the Shorter Catechism if you're new to the Standards, then read the Confession with a Bible open beside it. You can consult the full Confession and its Scripture proofs , the Larger Catechism , and the Shorter Catechism at The Westminster Standard. Take it slowly. Read each paragraph with its proof texts rather than assuming the Confession says what a later edition says. A historical explanation of an amendment can be useful, but it doesn't change the text this ministry teaches. The Standards were written for the church, and no website can take the church’s place. Find a faithful local church under the ordinary means of grace. Join it, and sit under the Word. If the gospel itself is still unclear to you, go to the gospel page first. That’s the doctrine everything else serves. And remember who all of this is about. The King who ordained the covenant before the world was, and who will judge the living and the dead, says this to you. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Matthew 11:28-29 (KJV) Learn the doctrine so you can see more of him, and then go to him. If something here raised a question you can’t settle, you're welcome to write and ask .

title: Providence
text: The Lord preserves and governs all he has made, including the hard things we cannot explain.

title: Providence
section: God Governs What He Has Made
text: God Governs What He Has Made The Lord hasn't left the world to run itself. What happens to you isn't outside his care, even when you can't understand it. Creation answers where everything came from. Providence answers why creation doesn't fall apart and who governs it now. The Westminster Confession says God upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and actions, from the greatest to the least ( WCF 5.1 ). Jesus said a sparrow doesn't fall to the ground apart from your Father ( Matthew 10:29-31 ). Nothing is too small for his care. That doesn't mean every event is good in itself. Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery. Their malice was real. Years later Joseph could say that they meant evil against him, but God meant it for good ( Genesis 50:20 ). Joseph held his brothers responsible for their treachery while confessing God's wise purpose in the same events.

title: Providence
section: Does God Cause People to Sin?
text: Does God Cause People to Sin? God's decree includes everything that comes to pass, but he is never the author or approver of sin ( WCF 3.1 and 5.4). The wicked act willingly and bear responsibility for what they do. God is holy, even when he overrules their actions for his purpose. Look at the crucifixion. Christ was delivered by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, and those who crucified him acted with wicked hands ( Acts 2:23 ). The greatest evil done by men fulfilled God's saving purpose. Their guilt wasn't imaginary, and neither was God's sovereignty. Don't use providence to excuse your own choices. If you've sinned, repent. If someone has harmed you, the wrong remains wrong. God's government of the event doesn't turn cruelty into righteousness.

title: Providence
text: God Works Through Ordinary Means Because the Lord orders outcomes, we can pray with confidence. Because he also orders the means, we still have work to do. The farmer sows and the Lord gives the increase. A sick person may see a doctor while praying for healing. A parent teaches a child while asking God to open that child's heart. Westminster Confession 5.3 says God ordinarily uses means, yet remains free to work without, above, and against them. Faith in providence doesn't mean staying in danger when you can escape it. Paul knew God had promised the lives of those aboard his ship, but he still told the centurion that the sailors must remain if they were to be saved ( Acts 27:22-25 , 31).

title: Providence
text: When Providence Hurts Some readers will arrive here after a diagnosis, a death, or a betrayal. Scripture hasn't told us why every particular sorrow comes. Job never received an itemized explanation of his losses. The Lord answered him by revealing his greatness, and Job humbled himself before him. The Confession teaches that God sometimes permits his own children to experience temptations and the corruption remaining in them, to humble them and teach them dependence ( WCF 5.5 ). But that isn't permission for us to tell every sufferer what secret lesson God must be teaching. We don't know the secret counsel of God. What we do know is that the Father's care doesn't fail. If you belong to Christ, your suffering isn't the condemnation he bore in your place ( Romans 8:1 ). God works all things together for good to those who love him and are called according to his purpose ( Romans 8:28 ). Paul goes on to define that good as being conformed to the image of his Son. The promise isn't that this week will be pleasant.

title: Providence
section: What Should I Do With This?
text: What Should I Do With This? Do the duty in front of you. Pray for what you need. Take wise counsel from Scripture and your elders. Give thanks for mercies you've noticed. When the Lord's ways are hidden, you may grieve honestly without calling him unfaithful. Psalm 77 gives you words to pray. Trust the Lord where his purposes are hidden, and keep doing the duty he has given you. If you're struggling with the sense that God has left you, read When God Feels Far . If you're grieving a loss, the Comfort section speaks more directly to that sorrow.

title: Union With Christ
text: How believers are joined to Christ and receive every saving benefit in him.

title: Union With Christ
text: United to a Living Savior By the Holy Spirit, a Christian belongs to Christ and receives every saving benefit in him. Jesus said he is the vine and his people are the branches ( John 15:5 ). A branch has no life apart from the vine. Paul calls the church Christ's body ( 1 Corinthians 12:27 ). These are different pictures of a real spiritual union. The believer is joined to Christ by the Spirit and through faith. He doesn't become God or lose his own personhood. The Larger Catechism speaks of the members of the invisible church enjoying union and communion with Christ in grace and glory ( WLC 65-69 ). Those whom the Father has given the Son are joined to him in their effectual calling. Christ is the head, and his people are members of his body.

title: Union With Christ
section: How Does Someone Come to Be United to Him?
text: How Does Someone Come to Be United to Him? We're born in Adam, and Adam fell. By nature we share the guilt and corruption of his fall ( Romans 5:12-19 ). No amount of improvement can transfer a sinner from Adam to Christ. The Spirit gives life and brings those whom God calls into fellowship with the Son ( 1 Corinthians 1:9 ). Faith receives Christ. Faith can't force God to accept us or earn our place in Christ. The Lord makes a dead sinner alive and gives him the grace to believe ( WCF 10.1-2 and 14.1). When a man believes, he isn't purchasing union with Christ. He receives the Savior freely offered in the gospel. Don't try to discover whether you're elect before coming. Christ promises to receive the one who comes to him ( John 6:37 ). Hear the gospel and come to him.

title: Union With Christ
section: What Belongs to Those Who Are His?
text: What Belongs to Those Who Are His? Every saving benefit comes through Christ. In him we're justified, adopted, and sanctified. These blessings are distinct, but they aren't separate saviors. God declares believers righteous for Christ's sake ( WCF 11 ). He receives them as children ( WCF 12 ). He also breaks the rule of sin and begins making them holy ( WCF 13 ). Paul says he was crucified with Christ and now lives by faith in the Son of God ( Galatians 2:20 ). Paul still struggled with sin, but sin no longer ruled him. He belongs to another Lord, and the Spirit works in him. Christ's death is yours by faith, and so is the hope of his resurrection. If we died with him, we shall also live with him ( Romans 6:5-11 ). The believer's body will be raised when Christ returns ( 1 Corinthians 15:22-23 ). Union with Christ isn't a feeling that disappears when your heart is cold.

title: Union With Christ
section: Union With Christ and the Visible Church
text: Union With Christ and the Visible Church The visible church gathers people who profess the true religion and their children ( WCF 25.2 ). Baptism marks entrance into that visible covenant community. We shouldn't assume everyone outwardly baptized is inwardly regenerated. Scripture warns that some share the privileges of the visible church without saving faith. At the same time, don't despise the church because outward membership isn't the same thing as regeneration. Christ gives his people preaching, sacraments, and prayer as the ordinary means by which he calls and strengthens them ( WSC 88 ). You need more than private reading and an occasional sermon online. If you want to know how these benefits are enjoyed, begin with Adoption and Sanctification . Above all, keep looking to the Christ in whom they're found.

title: Adoption
text: What it means to belong to the Father's family through Christ.

title: Adoption
text: Received as God's Children Justification answers the charge against a guilty sinner. Adoption tells you that the Judge has also taken you into his family. God pardons believers and receives them into his family, giving them the privileges of his children ( WCF 12.1 ). John writes that those who receive Christ are given power to become the sons of God ( John 1:12-13 ). This privilege is founded on Christ, the eternal Son, and given through him. Adoption isn't a reward for obedience. A believer doesn't become a son by proving he can behave like one. God first receives him in Christ, and then teaches him to walk as a child of his Father.

title: Adoption
text: What Does Adoption Give Us? The Confession speaks of God's name being put upon his children, the Spirit of adoption, access to the throne of grace, the right to cry Abba, Father, and the promise of an everlasting inheritance ( WCF 12.1 ). Read Romans 8:15-17 alongside it. The Spirit testifies that those in Christ are God's children and heirs with him. You may bring your needs to the Father without pretending to be stronger than you are. Jesus taught his disciples to pray, Our Father which art in heaven ( Matthew 6:9 ). That privilege belongs to Christ's people because of their Mediator. It isn't a claim that God overlooks sin or owes us whatever we ask. A child of God can be poor, sick, lonely, or outwardly forgotten. Adoption brings the lasting care of the Father, even through poverty, illness, or bereavement.

title: Adoption
section: Why Does a Father Discipline His Children?
text: Why Does a Father Discipline His Children? Hebrews 12:5-11 calls believers to endure the Father's chastening. He doesn't discipline because Christ's sacrifice was insufficient. The punishment that condemned us has been borne by our substitute. His correction now serves our holiness. That doesn't mean every grief is punishment for a particular sin. Job's friends reasoned that way and were rebuked. When you know you've sinned, repent and return. When you don't know why you suffer, don't invent a hidden crime merely to explain it. Westminster Confession 11.5 says justified believers may fall under God's fatherly displeasure and lose the light of his countenance until they humble themselves and renew their repentance. That loss of comfort isn't the loss of their standing in Christ. For more on this, read When God Feels Far .

title: Adoption
section: When You Don't Feel Like His Child
text: When You Don't Feel Like His Child Feelings can change in a few hours. The Father's promise doesn't. But you mustn't base assurance merely on saying that you're adopted. The Word calls us to believe Christ and to examine the fruit of faith without turning that fruit into the price of salvation ( 2 Corinthians 13:5 and WCF 18.2 ). If you've never trusted Christ, come to him now. If you're troubled by doubt, bring your fear to him in prayer and tell your elders. Don't hide from the public worship of the church. The Lord ordinarily strengthens his children through his Word and sacraments. Christ is the Son by nature. Believers are sons and daughters by grace. That distinction makes adoption a greater mercy than we can measure.

title: Sanctification
text: Why sin remains in believers and how the Spirit renews their lives.

title: Sanctification
text: Made Holy by the Spirit The Lord doesn't leave the people he justifies in the slavery from which he saved them. Sanctification is God's work in believers, renewing the whole person after his image and enabling them to die more and more to sin and live to righteousness ( WSC 35 ). The Holy Spirit applies the death and resurrection of Christ to those who belong to him. Scripture calls them to put off the old man and put on the new ( Ephesians 4:22-24 ). We must be careful here. Justification is God's once-for-all declaration that a sinner is righteous in Christ. Sanctification is the Spirit's ongoing work within that justified sinner. We can't earn justification by becoming holy, but those whom God justifies he also sanctifies ( WCF 11 and 13). Neither doctrine should swallow the other.

title: Sanctification
section: Why Is Sin Still in Me?
text: Why Is Sin Still in Me? Because sanctification is real but incomplete in this life. Westminster Confession 13.2 says corruption remains in every part of a believer, and from that comes a continuing war between flesh and Spirit. Paul describes that war in Galatians 5:17 . A mature Christian may feel it more keenly as he learns how holy God's law is. Remaining sin gives no permission to stop fighting. Romans 6 says the dominion of sin has been broken. Your old master has no right to rule you. Yet its habits and desires still trouble you. You need the Spirit's strength, and you must use the means he gives. Don't measure holiness by how many dramatic experiences you've had. A man may speak loudly about victory and still refuse to forgive his family, tell the truth, or keep his promises. Scripture calls us to put sin to death in ordinary conduct, including our speech, labor, relationships, and worship ( Colossians 3:5-17 ).

title: Sanctification
section: How Does God Grow His People?
text: How Does God Grow His People? God ordinarily uses his Word, the sacraments, and prayer ( WSC 88 ). Sit under faithful preaching, not only when you feel eager to hear. Read the passage in context and pray over what it commands. Worship with your congregation. Where you need correction, receive it with humility. Put away what makes provision for your sin. If your phone, a friendship, or an hour of the night keeps drawing you back, change your habits ( Romans 13:14 ). Speak plainly with a mature believer or an elder who can help you. Confess what you've done and seek to repair the wrong you caused. These acts don't purchase God's favor. They're part of the obedience his grace produces. Don't treat falling again as proof that you should stay away from Christ. Return to him. Nor should you call a planned return to sin a harmless stumble. If you've decided to keep a sin and refuse correction, you need repentance, not reassurance. Read Struggling With Sin for more detailed help.

title: Sanctification
text: Will This Fight Ever End? Yes. Christ himself will finish the work he began. Our strength never becomes independent of him. The Confession teaches that the sanctified part overcomes through the continual supply of strength from Christ's sanctifying Spirit ( WCF 13.3 ). At death the souls of believers are made perfect in holiness, and at the resurrection their bodies will share that glory ( WCF 32.1-3 ). Until then, confess, believe, pray, obey, and keep coming to Christ. He is the one who saves you and who teaches you to walk. The Christian life isn't a wager that you'll improve enough to be accepted. It's the life of a person whom God has received in his Son and is remaking by his Spirit.

title: Church Government
text: The keys, elders, church courts, and discipline in the 1647 Westminster Confession.

title: Church Government
text: Christ Governs His Church Christ is the only head of his church. He hasn't left her to invent her own government. Jesus gave his church officers to preach the Word, administer the sacraments, shepherd the flock, and exercise discipline ( Ephesians 4:11-12 and Acts 20:28 ). The original Westminster Confession teaches that Christ has appointed government in the hands of church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate ( WCF 30.1 ). The visible church includes all who profess the true religion, together with their children ( WCF 25.2 ). Those people need more than religious content. They need a congregation where the Word is preached, the sacraments are rightly administered, and officers know them well enough to care for their souls.

title: Church Government
section: What Are the Keys of the Kingdom?
text: What Are the Keys of the Kingdom? Matthew 16:19 and Matthew 18:15-20 speak of the keys, binding, and loosing. Westminster Confession 30.2 explains that church officers exercise these keys by the Word and church censures, opening the kingdom to penitent sinners and shutting it against the impenitent. An elder doesn't forgive sins by his own power. Christ alone saves, and his church must declare his Word faithfully. When an offender repents, the church must be ready to receive him. When someone stubbornly refuses correction and persists in scandalous sin, the church can't pretend nothing is wrong. The Confession names admonition, suspension from the Lord's Supper for a season, and excommunication as forms of discipline suited to the offense ( WCF 30.4 ). These are solemn matters. They're meant to reclaim the sinner, protect the congregation, vindicate Christ's honor, and keep his ordinances from being profaned ( WCF 30.3 ). They're not tools for personal grudges.

title: Church Government
section: Why Do Presbyterians Have Church Courts?
text: Why Do Presbyterians Have Church Courts? Acts 15 shows elders and apostles meeting to decide a controversy that affected congregations beyond one city. The Westminster Confession teaches that assemblies of church officers, commonly called synods or councils, ought to exist for better government and edification ( WCF 31.1 ). These assemblies serve the church ministerially. They're bound to Scripture, which remains the supreme judge of every controversy ( WCF 1.10 and 31.3). The original text gives synods authority to determine matters of doctrine, worship, and church government according to the Word, and to receive complaints about maladministration. The original Confession also says the magistrate may call synods and attend them, and that when the magistrate is an open enemy of the church, ministers may meet by virtue of their office ( WCF 23.3 and 31.2). This historical teaching mustn't be replaced silently with the American revisions. It still doesn't make the magistrate a minister or give him the keys.

title: Church Government
section: What Does This Mean for a Church Member?
text: What Does This Mean for a Church Member? Join a faithful congregation and become known there. Come under the preached Word with a teachable spirit. Receive the ordinances with reverence. If you sin, don't wait for a public scandal before asking for help. If someone wrongs you, follow the order Scripture gives, rather than using gossip or a public argument to settle a private matter ( Matthew 18:15-17 ). When an elder makes a mistake, he is still accountable to the Word. Presbyterian government isn't meant to leave a member at the mercy of one man. Lawful appeals and oversight are part of the church's care. If you're looking for a congregation, read How to Find a Church . For the original teaching on rulers and religion, see The Civil Magistrate . The full text of the Confession is available through the Westminster references in this article.

title: Baptism
text: Christ's covenant sign and the work of the Spirit.

title: Baptism
section: Christ Appointed Baptism for His Church
text: Christ Appointed Baptism for His Church Baptism marks those received into the visible covenant community. It points to the cleansing and life that belong to Christ alone. The risen Lord commanded his apostles to disciple the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost ( Matthew 28:18-20 ). Baptism is a sacrament instituted by Christ. The water doesn't save by its own power. God uses an outward sign to declare the promises of his covenant. Westminster Confession 28.1 calls baptism a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of ingrafting into Christ, regeneration, remission of sins, and the baptized person's engagement to belong to God. Read this with Romans 6:3-4 , Galatians 3:27 , and Titus 3:5 . The sign directs our faith to Christ and to the Spirit's work.

title: Baptism
section: Why Baptize the Children of Believers?
text: Why Baptize the Children of Believers? The original Confession teaches that the infants of one or both believing parents are to be baptized ( WCF 28.4 ). That follows the continuity of God's covenant promise. The Lord gave Abraham a sign for himself and his household ( Genesis 17:7-12 ). Peter preached the promise to his hearers and to their children, as many as the Lord would call ( Acts 2:38-39 ). The New Testament also speaks of the children of believers as holy in a covenantal sense ( 1 Corinthians 7:14 ). Under the new covenant the bloody sign of circumcision has passed away. Baptism signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection. The Westminster divines held that children of the covenant belong within the visible administration of the covenant of grace. They receive its sign before they can explain the doctrines it teaches. This doesn't establish that every baptized child is regenerate. Ishmael received circumcision, yet Scripture distinguishes outward covenant membership from saving faith ( Romans 9:6-8 ). Parents must teach their baptized children to repent, trust Christ, and live as those set apart to his service.

title: Baptism
section: What About Someone Coming to Faith as an Adult?
text: What About Someone Coming to Faith as an Adult? An unbaptized adult who professes faith in Christ should seek baptism and membership in a faithful church. The account of the Ethiopian in Acts 8:35-38 illustrates the gospel preached and baptism received. The church examines the profession and administers the sacrament under its lawful oversight. Baptism isn't an act of private self-dedication performed apart from the church. Scripture records households receiving baptism, including Lydia's and the jailer's ( Acts 16:14-15 , 30-34). Those accounts belong in the discussion, but they don't by themselves tell us the age of every household member. Our case for covenant baptism rests on Scripture's broader teaching about the covenant and the visible church.

title: Baptism
text: How Is Baptism Administered? The Confession directs that baptism be given with water in the name of the Trinity. Dipping isn't necessary. Pouring or sprinkling is lawful ( WCF 28.2-3 ). The emphasis belongs on Christ's appointed sign and promise, not on producing a particular emotional experience. A person is to be baptized once ( WCF 28.7 ). Someone who was validly baptized before conversion doesn't need a second baptism simply because he now understands the gospel more clearly. Questions about a previous baptism should be brought to the elders, who can examine what was actually done.

title: Baptism
section: Does Baptism Regenerate Everyone Who Receives It?
text: Does Baptism Regenerate Everyone Who Receives It? No. The grace signified isn't inseparably tied to the moment the water is applied. Not everyone baptized is undoubtedly regenerated, and salvation isn't limited to those who received the sacrament ( WCF 28.5-6 ). God gives the grace promised to those to whom it belongs in his appointed time. That truth gives parents no reason to neglect the command. Nor does the command give them a reason to presume their children's conversion. Pray with your children, teach them Scripture, bring them to worship, and remind them what their baptism declares. The minister applies water. The Holy Spirit gives life. For the doctrine behind this practice, read Covenant Theology . For what follows baptism in the life of the church, read Church Membership and The Lord's Supper .

title: Justification
text: Pardoned and accepted through Christ's righteousness alone.

title: Justification
section: How Can a Guilty Sinner Be Right With God?
text: How Can a Guilty Sinner Be Right With God? Justification is God's judicial act of pardoning sinners and accepting them as righteous for Christ's sake. The question is serious because God's law is righteous and we've broken it. Romans 3:19-26 leaves every mouth stopped, then reveals the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ. God doesn't overlook guilt. Christ suffered for sin, and God receives those united to his Son. Westminster Confession 11.1 teaches that God justifies freely. He doesn't infuse a new moral quality and call it righteousness. He pardons sins and accounts the believer righteous because Christ's obedience and satisfaction are imputed to him. Romans 4:5-8 speaks of the ungodly man whom God justifies and whose sins he forgives.

title: Justification
text: Whose Righteousness Saves? Christ obeyed his Father's will throughout his life and bore the penalty due to his people. He stood in their place. His obedience and satisfaction are the ground of their acceptance ( Romans 5:18-19 , 2 Corinthians 5:21 ). This is why justification brings real peace with God ( Romans 5:1 ). We must distinguish justification from sanctification. God declares the believer righteous once for all in Christ, while the Spirit goes on renewing his character. The believer's good works are necessary as fruit of faith, but they add nothing to the righteousness by which he stands before God ( WCF 11.2 and 16.5).

title: Justification
text: What Place Does Faith Have? Faith is the only instrument of justification ( WCF 11.2 ). It receives and rests upon Christ and his righteousness. It's no payment offered to God. It isn't the excellence of your believing that saves you. The Savior in whom you believe saves you. Living faith never remains alone. It's accompanied by repentance and produces love and obedience. Yet those fruits mustn't be made the ground of pardon. When the jailer asked what he must do to be saved, Paul pointed him to the Lord Jesus Christ ( Acts 16:30-31 ). That gospel is still freely proclaimed. James 2:14-26 condemns a dead profession that has no works. James doesn't teach that good works purchase God's favorable verdict. Abraham believed God, and that faith showed itself in obedience. Read James alongside Romans 4 rather than setting the apostles against one another.

title: Justification
text: When Is a Person Justified? God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world. Christ accomplished their redemption in history. Yet the Confession says they aren't personally justified until the Holy Spirit actually applies Christ to them in due time ( WCF 11.4 ). Election and the cross aren't permission to tell an unbeliever that he is already justified without faith. Believers may fall into grievous sin and lose the sense of God's favor. Their justification isn't undone. The Father calls them to humble themselves, confess, seek pardon, and renew their repentance ( WCF 11.5 ). He receives them because of Christ's finished work.

title: Justification
text: Come to Christ Don't begin by measuring whether you possess enough faith to deserve acceptance. Read John 6:37 . Christ receives those who come. Repent of your sins and trust him. If you've already believed and now fear his displeasure, bring your sin into the light and seek pastoral care. For further help read Am I Really Saved? , Union With Christ , and Sanctification .

title: Christ the Mediator
text: True God and true man, our Prophet, Priest and King.

title: Christ the Mediator
text: One Person, Two Natures The eternal Son of God became man for the salvation of sinners. He remains one divine person, truly God and truly man. John tells us that the Word was God and that the Word was made flesh ( John 1:1 , 14). The Son took a true human body and a reasonable human soul. He was conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of the virgin Mary, without sin ( Luke 1:35 , Hebrews 4:15 ). He didn't cease to be God when he became man. The original Westminster Confession 8.2 teaches that the two complete natures are joined in one person without conversion, composition, or confusion. Jesus grew tired, hungry, and sorrowful according to his human nature. He upheld all things by the word of his power according to his divine nature ( Hebrews 1:3 ). We mustn't divide the Savior into two persons or blend his natures into something less than either.

title: Christ the Mediator
text: Our Prophet, Priest, and King The Larger Catechism explains Christ's three offices in WLC 42-45 . As Prophet he reveals God's will for salvation by his Word and Spirit. As Priest he offered himself once to satisfy divine justice and now intercedes for his people. As King he calls, rules, defends, and preserves them, subduing his and their enemies. Christ's offices meet our actual needs. We're ignorant and need the Prophet's Word. We're guilty and need the Priest's sacrifice. We're helpless under sin and need the King's government. Every office belongs to the one Lord Jesus Christ, who alone mediates between God and men ( 1 Timothy 2:5 ).

title: Christ the Mediator
text: His Obedience and His Sacrifice Jesus obeyed his Father through the whole course of his earthly life. He endured temptation without sin, suffered, and submitted even to death on the cross ( Philippians 2:5-8 ). The Confession says he fully satisfied his Father's justice and purchased an everlasting inheritance for those given to him ( WCF 8.4-5 ). Christ did not die as a helpless victim. He laid down his life willingly ( John 10:17-18 ). His sacrifice was sufficient. It will never be repeated. The gospel therefore offers sinners a Savior whose work has been accomplished.

title: Christ the Mediator
text: Risen, Ascended, and Reigning The third day Christ rose bodily. He ascended and sits at his Father's right hand. He makes intercession for his people and will return to judge the world ( Acts 1:9-11 , Hebrews 7:25 , Acts 17:31 ). Our Mediator is alive. His human nature wasn't discarded after the resurrection. Westminster Confession 8.8 teaches that Christ certainly and effectually applies redemption to all for whom he purchased it. He calls them by his Word and Spirit and brings them to himself. This truth gives confidence to preaching and prayer, while the gospel is offered freely to every hearer.

title: Christ the Mediator
text: Why This Matters When conscience accuses you, look to the Priest who has offered himself for sins. When you need to know the truth, listen to the Prophet in Scripture. When sin presses hard, obey the King who has broken its dominion. Come to Christ as he is revealed in the gospel. Read The Gospel , Justification , and Union With Christ next.

title: The Fall and Original Sin
text: Adam's headship and humanity's need for grace.

title: The Fall and Original Sin
text: Made Upright, Now Fallen Sin didn't belong to the world as God first made it. Our first parents fell, and the whole human race suffers the consequences. God created man in his image, in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness ( Genesis 1:26-31 , Ecclesiastes 7:29 ). Adam received the command not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil ( Genesis 2:16-17 ). He broke that command ( Genesis 3:1-7 ). Scripture treats this as a real event, and Paul explains its consequences in Romans 5:12-19 .

title: The Fall and Original Sin
section: Why Does Adam's Sin Matter to Us?
text: Why Does Adam's Sin Matter to Us? Adam stood as the public head of his descendants in the covenant of works ( WCF 6.3 and 7.2). When he fell, the race descending from him by ordinary generation fell in him. We inherit the guilt of his first sin and a corrupted nature. We also commit sins of our own. This is the doctrine of original sin, taught in Westminster Confession 6 and Larger Catechism 21-29. Some find it hard that Adam represented people not yet born. Scripture itself presents the parallel with Christ. Through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous ( Romans 5:19 ). Our salvation rests on the righteousness of a representative as surely as our ruin came through one.

title: The Fall and Original Sin
text: How Deep Is Our Corruption? The fall affects understanding, desires, will, and conduct. People can show natural affection, work honestly, and help neighbors. Yet apart from regenerating grace they cannot turn to God in saving faith or love him as his law requires ( Romans 8:7-8 , 1 Corinthians 2:14 ). The confession calls this an inability to do spiritual good accompanying salvation ( WCF 9.3 ). We're responsible for our sins. Scripture never permits a man to excuse his choices by saying that he was born corrupt. We sin willingly, and our willing is itself disordered. Even our best outward acts can't remove the guilt of our rebellion.

title: The Fall and Original Sin
text: Sin's Judgment Death entered through sin ( Romans 5:12 ). The whole creation groans under the curse ( Romans 8:20-22 ). The final judgment will expose what people have done and what they've loved. God's law is holy, and its sentence is just. That makes the gospel necessary. We can't repair ourselves by resolving to do better. Christ, the last Adam, obeyed where the first Adam failed and bore the curse for his people ( 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 , Galatians 3:13 ). The Spirit gives a new heart and brings sinners to faith. Read Christ the Mediator and Justification . If you've never believed, hear the gospel and come to him.

title: Christian Liberty
text: Conscience and obedience in the 1647 Confession.

title: Christian Liberty
text: The Liberty Christ Purchased Christ frees his people from the guilt and dominion of sin. His liberty also guards their consciences from human commands imposed as divine law. Westminster Confession 20.1 describes the liberty of believers as freedom from guilt, condemning wrath, and the curse of the moral law. In Christ we're delivered from the present evil world and the bondage of Satan. We have access to God and obey him willingly through grace ( Romans 8:1-4 , Galatians 5:1 ). The Christian has a Lord. Liberty gives no permission to continue in sin. Paul warns those called to freedom not to use it as an occasion to the flesh ( Galatians 5:13 ). Believers serve one another in love.

title: Christian Liberty
section: God Alone Is Lord of the Conscience
text: God Alone Is Lord of the Conscience Chapter 20.2 teaches that the conscience is free from human doctrines and commandments contrary to God's Word or added beside it in matters of faith and worship. A pastor may apply Scripture to real conduct, but he can't create new articles of faith or demand worship God never appointed. The church must teach and discipline according to Christ's Word ( Colossians 2:20-23 , Matthew 15:9 ). This isn't permission to ignore a lawful command merely because it comes through a person. Children owe obedience to parents within the Lord's limits, church members owe proper submission to elders, and citizens owe lawful obedience to magistrates ( Ephesians 6:1 , Hebrews 13:17 , Romans 13:1-7 ). Where a command requires disobedience to God, we must obey God rather than men ( Acts 5:29 ).

title: Christian Liberty
section: What the Original 1647 Text Says in Chapter 20.4
text: What the Original 1647 Text Says in Chapter 20.4 The original Confession also rejects the claim that Christian liberty authorizes opposition to lawful civil or ecclesiastical power. It teaches that those who publish opinions or maintain practices contrary to the light of nature, the known principles of Christianity, or the power of godliness, and those who destroy the external peace and order Christ established in the church, may be proceeded against by church censures and by the power of the civil magistrate ( WCF 20.4 ). That's a substantial difference from some later American Presbyterian revisions. Gentle King teaches the original text and doesn't quietly replace its public doctrine with a modern theory of a religiously neutral state. The same Confession prohibits a magistrate from administering the Word, sacraments, and keys of the kingdom ( WCF 23.3 ). See The Civil Magistrate and Church Government .

title: Christian Liberty
section: How Do I Exercise Liberty Wisely?
text: How Do I Exercise Liberty Wisely? Begin with what Scripture commands or forbids. Where a matter is lawful but not required, consider the duties of love, prudence, and the needs of others. Don't bind another Christian to a personal scruple as though it were a command of God. Don't use a claim of liberty to set aside the clear duties of worship, truthfulness, temperance, or charity. Romans 14 addresses disputes that call for patience, though it doesn't cancel God's commands. Bring serious questions of conscience to your elders. Read the original Westminster chapter 20 guide with its Scripture proofs.

title: Oaths and Vows
text: The solemn promises Scripture permits and requires.

title: Oaths and Vows
text: What Is a Lawful Oath? An oath solemnly calls God to witness that what we say is true. We must never use his name lightly. People take oaths in court and sometimes in public office. Scripture also records lawful appeals to God as witness ( Genesis 24:2-9 , Hebrews 6:13-17 ). Westminster Confession 22 teaches that an oath is an act of religious worship and must be taken with reverence, truth, judgment, and righteousness. Jesus forbids rash and dishonest swearing and requires plain truthful speech ( Matthew 5:33-37 ). James gives the same warning ( James 5:12 ). The Confession understands these commands as prohibitions of sinful swearing, rather than a rejection of all solemn lawful oaths. The apostle Paul called God to witness in a solemn matter ( 2 Corinthians 1:23 ).

title: Oaths and Vows
section: When Must an Oath Be Refused?
text: When Must an Oath Be Refused? No oath may bind a person to sin. If an office requires a promise that conflicts with allegiance to Christ, the Christian mustn't take it. An oath's solemnity doesn't make an unlawful promise good ( WCF 22.3-4 ). Don't enter an oath without understanding its terms. A Christian must speak truthfully in ordinary conversation, contracts, and testimony. Swearing can't repair dishonesty of heart. It adds the weight of an appeal to God and makes falsehood more serious.

title: Oaths and Vows
text: What Is a Religious Vow? A vow is a solemn promise made to God concerning lawful duties and things within his providence ( WCF 22.5-7 ). Scripture warns against careless vows ( Ecclesiastes 5:4-6 ). An obligation made to God mustn't be treated as an emotional gesture that can be forgotten tomorrow. The Confession rejects monastic vows of perpetual single life, professed poverty, and regular obedience as higher states of perfection. Those aren't Christian obligations appointed by God. We must never promise an unlawful thing or make a vow that depends on strength we don't possess.

title: Oaths and Vows
text: What About Church Membership Vows? A profession of faith and a lawful commitment to live under the church's oversight are solemn matters. Their wording and administration belong to the church's lawful officers, and a candidate should understand what he is promising. Don't borrow membership vows from another denomination and pretend they're binding words of the original Westminster Confession. Before making such promises, speak with your elders about the requirements of your own congregation and examine them by Scripture. Read Church Membership and Visiting and Joining an RP Church for practical help.

title: Foundations of the Christian Faith
text: Sixteen lessons through the Christian faith.

title: Foundations of the Christian Faith
text: Begin With Christ This path starts with the gospel and follows the main teachings of the original 1647 Westminster Standards. It's for someone learning the Christian faith, or returning to its foundations. Begin with the gospel even if you aren't yet sure what you believe. The readings are meant to be done with a Bible open. You can take one at a time. Each step links to the complete article, a passage of Scripture, and the relevant paragraph of the original Confession with its Scripture proofs. The pathway can't replace the public preaching of the Word, the sacraments, or the care of your elders. Find a faithful congregation as you study. If Christ is calling you through his Word, don't postpone repentance and faith until you've finished these lessons.

title: Foundations of the Christian Faith
text: Sixteen Lessons in Order 1. Hear the gospel Who Christ is and why sinners must come to him now. Read Mark 1:14-15 (KJV) and WCF 7.3 . 2. The God who speaks Why Scripture is our only infallible rule. Read 2 Timothy 3:14-17 (KJV) and WCF 1.4 . 3. God, our Creator The Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, one living God. Read Matthew 28:18-20 (KJV) and WCF 2.3 . 4. The fall and our need What Adam's sin did and why we can't rescue ourselves. Read Romans 5:12-19 (KJV) and WCF 6.3 . 5. Christ our Mediator The person and work of our Prophet, Priest, and King. Read Hebrews 7:23-28 (KJV) and WCF 8.2 . 6. Repentance and faith Turning from sin and believing the freely offered Savior. Read Acts 2:37-41 (KJV) and WCF 15.1 . 7. Justification Accepted for Christ's righteousness, received by faith. Read Romans 4:1-8 (KJV) and WCF 11.1 . 8. Union and adoption Belonging to Christ and received into the Father's family. Read Romans 8:14-17 (KJV) and WCF 12.1 . 9. A holy life The Spirit's work in the ongoing fight against sin. Read Galatians 5:16-25 (KJV) and WCF 13.1 . 10. Baptism and the covenant Christ's sign, believing households, and the visible church. Read Acts 2:38-39 (KJV) and WCF 28.4 . 11. Worship and the Lord's Day How the Lord gathers and nourishes his people. Read Acts 2:41-42 (KJV) and WCF 21.1 . 12. Joining a church Membership, elders, and caring for the congregation. Read Hebrews 10:23-25 (KJV) and WCF 25.2 . 13. The Lord's Supper The spiritual nourishment Christ gives his people. Read 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 (KJV) and WCF 29.7 . 14. Assurance and perseverance Trusting the Savior through weakness and doubt. Read John 10:27-29 (KJV) and WCF 18.3 . 15. Prayer, family, and work Daily devotion and service in the place God has assigned. Read Deuteronomy 6:4-9 (KJV) and WCF 21.6 . 16. Christ's return The resurrection, judgment, and everlasting life. Read 1 Corinthians 15:20-28 (KJV) and WCF 33.1 .

title: Foundations of the Christian Faith
text: How to Use the Lessons Read the Scripture passage in context before the article. Take notes on the text, especially where an explanation surprises you. Open the original Westminster paragraph and examine its proofs. Ask your pastor or an elder about anything you can't settle from Scripture. If you've already read a lesson, go to the next. If an earlier doctrine becomes difficult, return to it. There's no account, progress score, or badge to earn. The purpose is to learn God's Word and obey him. For a complete chapter-by-chapter view of the Confession, see the Westminster study index . For practical help finding a congregation, read How to Find a Faithful Church .

title: Westminster Study Center
text: Why the Edition Matters The original Confession's chapters 20, 23, and 31 teach duties concerning Christian liberty, the magistrate, and synods that were changed in later American editions. Gentle King follows the original text. When reading a later denominational constitution or historical commentary, identify its edition rather than assuming every paragraph is identical. For an explanation of the relationship between Scripture and confessional subscription, see The Westminster Standards .

title: Corrections and Sources
section: How We Check What Is Published
text: How We Check What Is Published Gentle King is written by a layman. I want to be told when a quotation, reference, historical claim or explanation is wrong. Holy Scripture is the supreme authority. The confessional standard used here is the original 1647 Westminster Confession with the original Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Westminster wording and Scripture proofs are taken from The Westminster Standard . Later American revisions aren't silently substituted. For historical claims and teacher reviews, the first preference is the person's own published sermon, writing, recording or official document. The article should tell you which source supports a consequential claim. An interpretation should be clearly distinguished from a quotation. An allegation that can't be verified should be corrected or removed. This site uses links to the KJV reader and to the original Westminster text and proofs, allowing you to examine the passages yourself. For the full Confession, open the Westminster Study Center .

title: Corrections and Sources
text: Report an Error Tell me the page address, the words that concern you, and why you think they're mistaken. A Scripture reference or a source link helps. I also welcome reports of broken links and mobile accessibility problems. Page address What needs attention? Doctrine or Scripture Westminster quotation Historical source or attribution Broken reference or link Accessibility or layout Other correction What should I check? Open an email with this report The form opens your device's email application. This site doesn't upload or store your report, and you can edit the email before sending it. If the button doesn't work, write directly to colt@gentleking.org .

title: Corrections and Sources
text: What Happens After a Correction? I compare the report with the source and read Scripture in context. Where I've misstated the doctrine, misquoted a source, or linked the wrong reference, I correct the page and regenerate the site. A substantial correction should be explained openly, with the date and the nature of the change. Minor spelling and formatting fixes don't need a public notice. Readers may disagree with the interpretation while sharing the same Confession. I won't present every disagreement as an established error. I also won't use an author's reputation as a substitute for reading his actual words. The site's source and its change history are available in the public GitHub repository . That allows readers to examine what changed.
